ASRS:1775193.n: Planned flight as normal, no limiting MELs were attached to the aircraft at any point during planning. I received a call from the crew at asking for clarification that MEL XX-XX-X-1 meant that center tank fuel was unusable, I confirmed this was the case, that this MEL means that both center pumps are INOP and that any fuel in the center is trapped, I thought it was a generic question and didn't question the MEL on this specific flight. I was advised by Dispatcher X that he believed the flight departed below minimum fuel, I brought up the [planning] and the fuel I had planned it with was below the level at which fuel is added to the center tank, this immediately raised flags and I attempted to contact ZZZ Tower to stop the aircraft from taking off, however they said clearance had already been given and the aircraft was rolling. I believe the aircraft departed with approx 24.7 usable fuel with a MIN TAKEOFF fuel of 27.0. After takeoff and at a safe altitude, I ACARSed the crew asking them to confirm the fuel available in their main tanks only, I determined this fuel was not sufficient to make it to RFD and advised the dispatch lead. The crew agreed that a tech stop was in the best interest of safety and it was decided that ZZZ1 was a suitable gateway for this, the flight was diverted to ZZZ1 to add fuel. Unfortunately, at no point during the pre-planning or planning stage of this flight, did I receive a call from Maintenance Control advising the MEL was being added, nor did the crew request an amended release before blockout advising that the MEL was not on their paperwork and thus not considered for the flight. The call was a routine call in which I thought the crew was just asking for interpretation of a MEL.I would suggest to Maintenance Control that they advise all dispatchers that have that tail assigned of any MELs being added, unfortunately we don't always have the aircraft on its previous leg and thus when they advise one dispatcher of an MEL being added, the next dispatcher does not receive this information.
ASRS:1775193.s: A dispatcher discovered an aircraft departed with insufficient fuel after a crew inquiry about an MEL regarding unusable center tank fuel was misinterpreted as generic. The flight was diverted for a fuel stop because Maintenance Control failed to notify the dispatcher of the new MEL, and the crew did not request an amended release.

ASRS:1775196.n: Upon arrival into the terminal environment at MGM, flight crew was informed of a portion of runway lighting reported as inoperative. Information was not published in NOTAMs and Dispatch was not aware. During the time spent in researching suitability of the given conditions, the flight crew observed Rwy 28 with VMC conditions. The crew determined that the runway lighting that was visible was suitable to execute a safe landing. Some factors to take into account: filed alternate was ZZZ. Crew knew that the weather to get back to ZZZ was not ideal. Having experience occasional moderate turbulence, and 30 knots more headwind than planned. Extended taxi time leaving ZZZ, and stair-stepped altitude climb out had us approximately 300 pounds behind on fuel. Having had a same day previous min fuel declaration, we determined ZZZ was not best action. In our judgement at the time, landing at Montgomery was the safest course of action. Unreported facility malfunctions.Safest decision was madeBuy more time. Request vectors, or holding to further coordinate airfield suitability with all available resources.
ASRS:1775196.s: Flight crew arrived at MGM to find unreported inoperative runway lighting not listed in NOTAMs. Despite fuel concerns and weather at their alternate, the crew judged landing at Montgomery the safest action due to visible lighting and VMC conditions.

ASRS:1775198.n: During takeoff, received master warning indicating a pitch trim inop just prior to 80 knots. Rejected takeoff, taxied off the runway, worked with maintenance to fix the issue, continued the flight with no more issues. Always be ready for warnings during takeoff.
ASRS:1775198.s: The pilot rejected takeoff just prior to 80 knots after receiving a master warning for inoperative pitch trim. Maintenance fixed the issue, allowing the flight to continue without further problems.

ASRS:1775208.n: XA55z We arrived planeside.XB12z Approximately notified maintenance of damage to the #1 engine stator vane.XB22z Approximately notified maintenance of inoperable Right Aft Fuel Pump pressure light. Bulb tested good.XB28z Approximately notified maintenance of missing window shades.XD45z ZZZ Maintenance was completed with aircraft.XD50z Extra fuel was completed.XD58z We blocked out.I really feel the onsite ZZZ mechanics have no business working on our aircraft or need additional extensive training. They damaged the fuel pump switch in the process of trying to get the pressure lights to work. Then they were asking me if the fuel pump was deferrable. I told them from what I saw, it was but that was something they would have to determine with our Maintenance Control. I asked them if before they won our contract if they had ever worked on a B767 or heavy aircraft. They said no. It appeared as if these two gentlemen had never worked on a B767 before. They appeared to have to be led and told every step of the way by whoever was on the phone speaking with them. I assume it was our Maintenance Control. For the CB that had to be pulled and collared they didn't even have a collar. They used safety wire and a handwritten paper tag. This delay was 1 hour 43 minutes. I suspect handled correctly we would have been out on time. Secure competent maintenance personnel to work on our aircraft! Much wasted time and money has been spent creating positions to babysit the crews at the hotel and oversee their preflight preparation and paperwork. This is an unnecessary smoke and mirror show diverting the eyes away from one real and glaring safety problem at this company, maintenance. Having been at over [many] airlines and XX years flying for the airlines I've NEVER seen such abhorrent maintenance practices and absolute disregard for the printed maintenance procedures as I have here. I will continue to call these out via these ASAPS and other means until this company corrects these operating practices safely. The current attitude of this company with regard to maintenance is going to get more people hurt or killed.
ASRS:1775208.s: The flight crew reported that onsite mechanics caused a 1 hour 43 minute delay on a B767 by damaging a fuel pump switch and using improper tagging methods due to a lack of heavy aircraft experience. The pilot attributed the incident to incompetent maintenance practices and a disregard for procedures, warning of potential safety risks.

ASRS:1775210.n: When I arrived at the airplane for departure I was informed that the FA X had called in sick. Apparently he had been exposed [to] COVID-19. I discussed the need for a new general declaration with the agent once they had found a replacement. About 30 minutes before push back they gave me the new declaration with all positions filled, and I signed it. About 20 minutes before pushing the agent returned and told me that they had pulled the new crew member off for another flight, and asked me if we could go with XX [number] of FAs. Not catching my error I said yes and asked for a new general declaration, it arrived just before departure time I signed it and we departed shortly thereafter.This was my first flight in over nine months with passengers, I had a discussion with the Lead FA about the FA that had called in sick, and wanted to be sure none of the other FAs had been exposed to him, apparently none had. We also discussed the fact that we would be getting a replacement. I just missed the fact that our duty time would require XY [number of] FAs.For myself having been on leave and away from flying for so long, I need to slow everything down, take a little more time. Last minute flight attendant sick call and another reassignment. Misunderstood flight attendant minimum requirements. Was unaware that requirements were based on duty day and not flight time. Departed 1 flight attendant undermanned.Last minute changes at a critical time. COVID-19 concerns and maximum limit of XX passengers. We should seek waiver for restricted load passenger flights. Need assistance from dispatch, flight attendants and load to help watch for errors in manning requirements.
ASRS:1775210.s: The pilot departed with one flight attendant fewer than required after agreeing to a last-minute crew reduction without verifying duty-time-based minimums. This error occurred due to the pilot's inexperience after a nine-month leave and a misunderstanding that manning requirements were based on duty day rather than flight time.

ASRS:1775216.n: On descent into CLT, open descent, 6,000 selected in the altitude window. Approaching AAIRE on the JONZE 2, I asked the FO to verify our descent clearance as it didn't feel right being cleared to 6,000 with departures at CLT coming off of 18C. As I asked this, I disconnected the autopilot and arrested the descent at 8,820. The frequency was quite congested (CLT Approach) so the FO was unable to get a word in. However, as I continued the climb from 8,820 to 9,000, CLT Approach did ask us to climb and maintain 9,000. To my knowledge, there were no traffic conflicts, however it was a very uncomfortable situation.Flying into CLT has become problematic with the CDA arrivals. The CHESLY has become legendary for altitude busts, and the JONZE 2 isn't much better. The scenario goes something like this, you check in with Atlanta Center and receive a 'descend via' clearance. Not long after, you are turned off of the arrival and given a 'descend to and maintain' clearance. This process usually repeats itself a couple of times (either with Atlanta Center or Charlotte Approach) before you are assigned a final descent clearance. This system makes it very difficult to fly the arrival. Please know that this isn't pointing blame, but pointing out a problem. As PIC, the responsibility ultimately falls on me. However, a smoother process would be helpful.Eliminate the CDA arrivals into CLT. We rarely fly them as published.
ASRS:1775216.s: The PIC arrested a descent at 8,820 feet while approaching CLT on the JONZE 2 arrival after questioning a 6,000-foot clearance. The crew climbed to 9,000 feet upon ATC instruction, attributing the unsafe situation to confusing CDA arrival procedures and conflicting clearances.

ASRS:1775221.n: During the boarding process of Aircraft X at Gate, a passenger in her assigned seat was holding her carry-on bag on her lap. The carry-on had a vape charger inside the bag and the batteries started to smoke and meltdown. There was smoke and fumes in the cabin. An unknown passenger ran towards the front of the aircraft yelling that there was a fire in the back of the aircraft and for everyone to get off. The flight attendants made an announcement and commenced the Emergency Deplaning at the Gate procedure (which we had discussed in my pre-bridging brief to the FA's (Flight Attendants)). The Purser asked what to do and I told him to continue the process they had started, which was going very well with passengers calmly deplaning up the jet way. The First Officer alerted emergency response and got up from his seat to assist. I was then told by an unknown person, that the smoking bag had been removed from the aircraft by a dead-heading pilot. I ran the Emergency Evacuation checklist to secure the aircraft, grabbed the fire extinguisher (not needed) and stood at the door directing the passengers to continue up the jetway, 'do not take bags or stand in the jetway, and to proceed to the terminal.' I directed the First Officer to go to terminal. There were a few passengers slowing the process trying to grab their carry-on bag, but were directed to stop and continue to the terminal. Once all passengers were off, I directed the FA's to go to the terminal while I swept the aircraft to be sure all crew and passengers were off. I then proceeded to the terminal. At the terminal I found the crew and deadheading crew members at the door, several passengers and agents and the smoking bag lying on the floor next to the ticket counter. I then directed all persons to leave the area, and requested Law enforcement with/dogs and fire and rescue to the bag. Asked the gate agent to call medical assistance and found the affected passenger sitting in the terminal, which I directed Medical to her location. At that point I was alarmed that the threat had followed us to the terminal and was concerned as to its contents. I then briefed fire and rescue, Maintenance as well as corporate security and law enforcement. I directed the deadheading crewmember who had carried the bag to seek medical attention. We coordinated for the FA's to stay nearby to facilitate the eventual allowing of 5 passengers at a time to go back to the secured aircraft to get their belongings. The First Officer was having chest pain and went to the hospital. I declined medical treatment. And met the ZZZ Chief Pilot who assisted me in the process remaining. There were burns on the owner of the smoking bag, and she also went to the hospital. There were no other injuries or incidents associated with the emergency deplaning procedure...but there was some uncertainty among the many constituents affected by the procedure, gate, ground, maintenance. etc. I was relieved from duty with 'p' for the remaining duration of the trip. I received follow up calls from ZZZ Chief Pilot on multiple occasions and was grateful for his support. I also contacted directly Union Safety and spoke with [Representative] who provided assistance and guidance during and after the event. Overall the procedure works, but should be expanded to a joint training scenario. I was most alarmed to learn. That the (brave) deadheading crew member had carried the smoking bag with him during the deplaning and it eventually ended up in the terminal with no oversight. The direction was to deplane away from the threat, not take it with us.The cause was allowing of the charging device and vape apparatus onboard the aircraft as a carry-on. The positive outcome was due to emergency deplaning at the gate procedure and pre-briefing. Well trained and professional back-end crew was outstanding. First Officer reverted to training and promptly called fire and rescue. However once passengers were off, there was confusion and potential danger which needs to be mitigated for future events. Communcication and full understanding and procedures associated are necessary.I suggest the need to continue the use of and to training of the 'Emergency Deplaning at the Gate Procedure'. Would recommend suggested briefings for the crew. Also believe joint training would be very beneficial to role play these scenarios...there is a lot going on and many potential pitfalls. This affects all constituents of the normal process, but also many others. Being released from duty by the Chief Pilot was appreciated, however as a reserve pilot, working to get my time for the month, Pay - No Credit does not help in any way. In fact it prevented me from flying another 4 day trip I could have held, and subsequently puts me at zero(0) hours going into the middle of the month. It was the first leg of the start of the sequence. I had just met the CA (Captain), for the first time, that afternoon. Along with the first time working with the FA's (Flight Attendants). Boarding started as normal, the CA and myself went about our preflight duties. We had finished all our checklists and were just waiting for the Gate Agent to inform us of boarding being complete. As we sat waiting to close up FA-1 shouts up to us 'We have a fire in the cabin'. In the time that it took the CA and I to get over the initial shock factor, the FA's immediately began an 'Emergency Deplaning' of the aircraft. From my advantage point I had no clue how bad the fire was in the cabin. I did not hear any call for an 'Evacuation', or see any doors and slides deploying, so I assumed that the FA's were just doing the 'Emergency Deplaning'.The CA went to the QRH immediately. I got on the radio to ops and told them of our situation. That we had a fire onboard the aircraft, we were 'Emergency Deplaning' into the terminal, and we needed ARF (Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting).The CA and I had completed everything we could think of to help the FA's with the situation in the back. Still not knowing how bad things were in the cabin the CA instructed me to exit the airplane. I did so and then followed my 'evacuation' duties when outside the aircraft. As I exited the flight deck I found a clog of passengers not moving out the door. I made my way through them to find a group of passengers have congregated on the jetway. I instructed them to move and get in the terminal building. This helped the flow of passengers off the aircraft. I found one passenger in visible distress on the jetway. I did a quick assessment of the passenger and then asked if they were OK. The passenger complained of burns on their arm. It did not look bad so I asked if they could walk. The passenger said yes. So I got the assistance of another passenger to help them into the terminal. I also instructed them to take the bag that the hurt passenger said was theirs and was standing next to. Later I would find out this was the bag that was smoking. It was not smoking when I was on the jetway and I was unaware this was the threat on the aircraft. I never would have thought that the threat would be off the aircraft in the direction the passengers were going. Or taken off and left unattended.After the passengers were off the aircraft the FA's were coming off and then asked where the bag was. I asked 'What bag? The one on the ground in the jetway?' They responded Yes, that was the one that was smoking. At that point I realized that I sent it inside the terminal. I remembered what passenger had it and told the supervisor, that was on the jetway, that I could identify them to find that bag.The CA completed his final check of the aircraft and we proceeded into the terminal. The bag has been cordoned off at the gate and people were being kept away. The CA remained at the gate until ARF arrived. I took the FA's and proceeded to an unused gate to keep us together and away from the situation.The incident started with a passenger's bag there was no control over the problem. There was some confusion over what procedures were started and what roles the flight deck crew had in an 'Emergency Deplaning'.It was also confusing how and why the fire, smoking bag, was put onto the jetway. The use of the 'Emergency Deplaning' was very appropriate to this situation and did exactly what it was intended to do. However there is not a clear signal, that we knew of, that signals to the flight deck that an 'Emergency Deplaning' is in progress. There was also not an immediate action item, QRC, or QRH procedure to reference for an event like this for us on the flight deck to help. It felt as if we were making it up as we went along. Merging our evacuation checklist and duties into the 'Emergency Deplaning'.There is also no defined plan for fighting an onboard fire at the gate, that at least theflight deck is aware of. Just so we know what to expect. Example, that if we are to expect the fire or threat to be taken off the aircraft mid-deplaning.The event was a success, it was extremely helpful that the flight deck knows about 'Emergency Deplaning'. However there seems to still be confusion on roles, how to help with and execute an 'Emergency Deplaning'.
ASRS:1775221.s: During boarding of Aircraft X, a passenger's carry-on containing a vape charger smoked, triggering an emergency deplaning at the gate. While the procedure successfully evacuated passengers, confusion arose when a deadheading pilot moved the smoking bag into the terminal, causing uncertainty and requiring medical attention for the passenger and First Officer.

ASRS:1775284.n: ZZZZZ3 Arrival into ZZZ, just over ZZZZZ1 Intersection, told by ATC to fly present heading, maintain 9,000 feet, and to expect Runway XXR due to weather moving east of the airport. Weather radar indicated moderate precipitation (no convection activity) for about 5 miles, no red and no turbulence indications. At that time we observed some static off the nose of the aircraft, then either a lightning strike or static discharge. We also experienced a shot duration of moderate turbulence, aircraft descended approximately 300 feet, then returned to assigned altitude. Flight landed without incident. No initial lighting damage noted by maintenance, but aircraft taken out of service for further inspection. WSI was also being utilized and no lightning was indicated in the vicinity of our aircraft flight path.
ASRS:1775284.s: During arrival into ZZZ, the crew encountered moderate turbulence and a lightning strike or static discharge near ZZZZZ1 Intersection while maintaining 9,000 feet. The aircraft descended 300 feet before recovering, landed safely, and was removed from service for inspection despite no initial damage.

ASRS:1775291.n: Upon descent on the RNAV arrival, the aircraft ahead advised 'moderate turbulence at 10,000 ft.… We as a crew evaluated the deviations options and concluded to stay on route and cross the next fix at 9,000 ft. The area north and south of course on the radar were shaded with darker colors. The current inflight night visibility was zero with moderate to heavy rain lightning and St Elmo's fire. Upon crossing the fix we begin to encounter moderate turbulence. The autopilot was engaged, 250 kts. speed selected. After passing the fix and right about when the smart turn over another fix began we received an immediate CLIMB RESOLUTION ADVISORY and a RED traffic appeared on the Multi-Function Display (MFD) in the 11 o'clock position.I, the Pilot Flying, began the TCAS TA/RA actions and call-outs disconnecting the autopilot, complying with the RA climb instructions. The Captain turned off the Flight Directors as per company procedures. Due to moderate turbulence the aircraft began to rapidly slow below the selected 250 kts., so I, the Pilot Flying, selected TOGA (Take Off/Go Around) to equalize the descending energy and avoid a stall or near stall condition. With the lack of Flight Director (FD) lateral guidance the MFD became primary for lateral guidance for the turn over the fix, the red threat traffic appeared between us and turning left to rejoin the arrival. As we began to level off and reestablish vertical and lateral guidance ATC queried us. The Captain, who was Pilot Monitoring, was tasked with selecting the Flight Directors ON and selecting the desired modes to return us to course and altitude in a rather bumpy erratic flight condition. I, the Pilot Flying, with hands on a push to talk advised ATC of complying with a TCAS RA. As we began to turn back to course the previous red threat traffic reappeared yellow and a 'TRAFFIC, TRAFFIC' was heard, so we remained leveled off and slow turned towards the course. After establishing guidance, and positively managing the aircraft's speed and energy we began a turn towards the next fix. We as a crew were task saturated controlling the aircraft in moderate turbulence and complying with the TCAS RA and were merely queried by ATC, never advised of traffic by ATC or given any lateral guidance after stating we were complying with a TCAS RA. It was only several moments after we were reestablishing on course avoiding the traffic that ATC assigned a heading. Most disturbing during the irregularities of moderate turbulence, TCAS RA with traffic conflicting the turn, and turbulence induced energy state beyond authority of the auto thrust, ATC tries to immediately give us a phone number to call instead of any assistance in weather or traffic guidance.The portion of the RNAV arrival, during the event, has 6.5 miles to descend up to 2,000 ft., slow 40 kts., and smart turn 51 degrees, coupled with a very changing tailwind of 150 kts. at 20,000 [ft.] slowing to 36 kts. at 10,000 [ft.] and the aircraft's FMS plotting the deceleration to approach mode between fixes thus requiring manual speed selected management, it is a very busy part of the arrival.Casual factors were night with St. Elmo's fire, lightning causing a very dark outside and requiring bright instrumentation that is difficult for the eye to follow in moderate turbulence. Possible other factors of AUTO FLT FCU 1 FAIL immediately after the event. ATC was extremely busy. I think another big factor was ATC confusion of what we were experiencing, due to the fact we were both task saturated controlling the aircraft and avoiding a mid-air collision ATC communication became a lower priority. With reduced traffic separation ATC becomes an integral part of every flight, if the manuals would include 'advise ATC' as a step, and clear guidance on priority of traffic avoidance in relationship to lateral guidance and where it is seen or sourced this could help."
ASRS:1775291.s: During a night RNAV arrival in moderate turbulence, the crew executed a TCAS climb resolution advisory while managing rapid deceleration and conflicting traffic. The pilot reported task saturation and criticized ATC for failing to provide traffic guidance or weather assistance, instead offering a phone number during the emergency.

ASRS:1775296.n: While we were on base leg on the RNP Y Runway 2 approach to MGGT [airport], someone on the ground pointed a green laser and it flashed in the cockpit a few times, twice hitting me on the right eye. We were in between GT504 and GT503 with the aircraft fully configured, I was PM and since it was my first time flying into MGGT, I was looking outside to get a mental picture for future reference and situational awareness, trying to identify the runway, when I saw a green laser beam being pointed at the aircraft, I called it out to the Captain and he kept his head down but I was hit twice on the right eye before I could go head down. I reported it to the Tower (in Spanish). The Captain asked me if I was OK, and I just mentioned that my eye felt drier than normal. (I've had the misfortune of being hit by a laser while flying before, so I knew the sensation). We continued to approach and landing without any further incident.Unfortunately, these types of events are almost impossible to stop, unless we wear protective eye gear, there is nothing we can do but lower our heads if a beam is being pointed to the aircraft. While on approach, circling left arc to final, RNV Y 02, MGGT, about 145 knots and 2,000 feet AGL, FO (Non-Flying Pilot) observed a green laser coming from the low 10 o'clock position. We continued approach to landing. FO reported it to ATC, giving them location, and Controller said it's been happening more often now and that they'll report it to authorities. I asked FO if he was OK and he said his eyes were drier than normal.Suggestions - Patrol the terminal area in vicinity of airport more often. Make area more sterile. Prosecute those who attempt to lase airplanes as they land at airports.
ASRS:1775296.s: During the RNP Y Runway 02 approach to MGGT at 2,000 feet AGL, a First Officer was struck twice in the right eye by a green laser from the ground. The crew reported the incident to ATC and completed the landing without further issues, noting dry eyes as the only symptom.

ASRS:1775301.n: Climbing trough 14,000 feet, Number 2 engine suddenly shook and had a classic indication of an engine seizure. I looked down and noticed the EPR rolling back and the N2 at near 0 and low oil pressure light illuminated. CA stabilized the aircraft. After situation assessment, CA had me take control of the airplane and we leveled out at 15,000 feet. We both determined ZZZ1 [airport] would be an acceptable divert option due to winds in ZZZ (Heavy Crosswind out of SE limits). ECAMs and QRH procedures completed and we safely landed in ZZZ1 on Runway XX. CFR determined there was no fire, nor any indication of fuel leak/oil leak etc. Because of the Number 2 engine being failed, CA elected to have us towed to the gate, which was accomplished by the Ground Crew. Climbing through 14,000 feet Number 2 Engine seized, loud bang, aircraft kicked to the right, no N2 rotation, EPR rolled back to zero, low oil pressure light illuminated. Gave FO aircraft control, told him to level at 15,000 feet. I ran ECAM, QRH, and radios. Shutdown Number 2 Engine, and ran Engine Out Immediate Landing Checklist. Notified Washington Center of situation. ZZZ [airport] had crosswinds in excess of 20 knots so diverted to ZZZ [airport] Runway XX. FO flew while I set us up for ILS to Runway XX ZZZ [airport]. I took control of aircraft intercepting the LOC. Single Engine landing was uneventful. Cleared Runway, Fire Marshal looked over Number 2 Engine, no fire or leaks found. Shut down aircraft. Maintenance towed us to the gate.
ASRS:1775301.s: During climb through 14,000 feet, the Captain and First Officer experienced a Number 2 engine seizure with loud bang, zero N2, and low oil pressure. They diverted to ZZZ1 due to crosswinds at ZZZ, completed single-engine procedures, and landed safely on Runway XX with no fire or leaks found.

ASRS:1775338.n: I was PF, hand-flying. On departure, we were cleared to 10,000 feet. Northbound on the SID, climbing through approximately 7,500, I increased pitch to avoid a small build-up off the nose. Climbing thru approximately 8,800 feet, I realized that I was going to have a difficult time leveling off by 10,000 feet. I asked the CA to advise ATC of the potential altitude excursion and aggressively, but smoothly, reduced pitch to level off. I exceeded our assigned altitude by 450 feet, and promptly descended back to 10,000 feet. ATC did not seem concerned by our deviation and cleared us to 16,000 feet.This was one of my first sequences after a 6-month leave of absence. The CA is new to the airplane and new to the seat. These factors contributed to our poor altitude SA and slow cross-check.Our threat-forward briefing focused on our lack of recent flying. We needed to be even more vigilant to trap decision and execution errors.
ASRS:1775338.s: The Pilot Flying and a new Co-pilot exceeded their 10,000-foot clearance by 450 feet during departure due to poor altitude situational awareness and slow cross-checking following a six-month leave. They promptly descended back to 10,000 feet, and ATC cleared them to 16,000 feet without concern.

ASRS:1775343.n: After landing in ZZZZ airport personnel took our temperatures with an ear thermometer. He did not replace the tip with a new one nor did he clean it after each person. This is unhealthy and unsanitary. Use only a forehead thermometer.
ASRS:1775343.s: Airport personnel at ZZZZ airport used an ear thermometer on arriving crew without replacing or cleaning the tip between individuals. The reporter described this practice as unhealthy and unsanitary, recommending the use of forehead thermometers instead.

ASRS:1775348.n: We arrived just before our show time. I confirmed that the aircraft had been fueled the night before and was in the hangar (it was winter and I wanted to avoid frost on the aircraft) and I asked for a bucket to take a fuel sample. My First Officer and I made our way to the hangar and began getting the aircraft ready. I decided to take a fuel sample while he was finishing the preflight. The left tanks, fuel filter, and fuel system low point drains showed clear jet fuel with no contamination. I then went to check the right feeder tank and a large amount of water and cloudy fuel came out of the drain. The right main tank also had a significant amount of contamination but not as much as the feeder tank. I continued to sump the fuel a few more times and it was no longer making a layer, but the fuel was still cloudy. My First Officer had completed the preflight and I made him aware of the fuel contamination and I told him that I'd need to talk to maintenance before flight as I had never seen this much contamination before. I went ahead and had the aircraft pulled out and put on a GPU to warm the cabin before the passengers arrived. While that was happening, I sent the pictures to maintenance. Maintenance directed me to speak with maintenance and that the cloudiness needed to be resolved. I talked with maintenance and they acknowledged the pictures and started working on solutions to see if a maintenance tech could be found. I then checked in with the operations and informed them that the flight may need to be recovered. I then got back in touch with maintenance who said that they had reviewed the pictures and that continued draining of the fuel should cause it to clear up and that it may take several full sumps before it does. I then asked for another bucket and tried again to sump the right tanks. After 2 more sumps on each drain I was able to get clear fuel with no layering. I took pictures of the result and sent them to maintenance and we all agreed the problem had been resolved. I also asked my First Officer if he was comfortable with the result and he agreed. We then continued the flight as normal with only about a 15 min delay.
ASRS:1775348.s: The Captain and First Officer discovered significant water and cloudy fuel contamination in the right tanks during preflight. After maintenance advised continued draining, the crew performed additional sumps to obtain clear fuel, resolving the issue with a 15-minute delay before departing.

ASRS:1775361.n: We were given taxi instructions from the gate at GSO to Runway 23L via Kilo, K6, with expected delays due to traffic into ZZZ. We taxied down Kilo, but the sign for K6 was located 'after' the intersection of Kilo and K6 (not before), so we continued past the intersection, and then saw the late sign for K6. We stopped and asked ATC if we had in fact gone past K6, which they confirmed but said 'no problem'. We asked and received permission to taxi forward on Kilo and execute a 180 degree turn at the taxiway near the entrance to the cargo ramp, which GSO Ground approved, then taxied down Kilo again to K6, and waited for our flow time to ZZZ. The problem could have been easily avoided if the taxi intersection sign had been placed ahead of the K6 intersection (facing towards K5 vs. the cargo ramp), instead of after the intersection.I would suggest that the taxiway K6 sign be placed 'before' the intersection of Kilo and K6, so that a pilot taxiing down Kilo and looking for K6 would actually see it. Where it sits currently, past the actual K6 intersection, does no good to anyone, and is conducive to other pilots missing this intersection. A sign is cheap, compared to the potential problems. During taxi at GSO we were taxiing to Runway 23L from the terminal via J3, K, and K6. We had passed taxiway K6 and continued straight on taxiway K. During the time we passed it, I was running the before takeoff checklist where I tried being outside of the airplane but the entire checklist is verifying the inside components are set and completed. The sun was also glaring in from my right side due to its position where I was partially blinded through the whole taxi even with sunglasses on. When I completed the checklist I looked up and saw the approach light systems for Runway 23L and looked behind and saw we missed K6. I advised Ground that we missed K6 and asked if we'd be able to make the turnaround we told them we'd have to wait until we were at the end and the Captain said we were able to so they said continue back K to K6 hold short Runway 23L. The Captain told me the sign for K6 is also after the taxiway and if you don't see that there isn't a taxiway past the sign it's already too late because you have to continue straight on K. When we taxied back, I wasn't able to confirm what sign was before K6 intersection. [Causes of the incident include] running the before takeoff checklist, sun glare on my side of cockpit, and the possibility that the K6 sign is after the taxiway. This was the last leg of a 4 day trip.
ASRS:1775361.s: Pilots taxiing at GSO missed the K6 intersection due to a sign placed after the turn, sun glare, and distraction from the before-takeoff checklist. They stopped, received ATC approval to execute a 180-degree turn, and successfully returned to K6 to hold short of Runway 23L.

ASRS:1775363.n: My tablet was fully charged at hotel. After 2 hours of flight it would not retain battery. I went to operations in ZZZ to receive [a] loaner and the case was inop. However the tablet received was fully functional.My equipment hasn't been used in some time due to not flying during COVID. I've made arrangements to replace all.
ASRS:1775363.s: A pilot reported that their tablet failed to retain battery after two hours of flight. The pilot obtained a fully functional loaner tablet from operations in ZZZ, noting the original case was inoperative and equipment had not been used since the COVID pandemic.

ASRS:1775378.n: I have witnessed a potential for aircraft spoiler damage during flap rigging. When rig boards are installed on aircraft for a mechanical flap rigging the outboard flap rigging task requires you to turn on hydraulics. Even though the manual tells you to keep the spoiler lever at zero, I have witnessed them deploy if the aircraft has been powered up recently during its self-BITE (Built-in Test Equipment) checks. This can cause the spoiler to hit the rig board if installed. The manual does not tell you to pull circuit breakers for the spoilers during rigging, just to put a placard saying not to operate spoilers, but aircraft cannot read placards.[I suggest] a page that requires you to pull and lock out the spoiler circuit breakers. This will prevent any accidental deployment.
ASRS:1775378.s: A mechanic reported potential spoiler damage during outboard flap rigging when spoilers deployed unexpectedly during self-BITE checks despite the lever being at zero. The reporter attributed the risk to the manual's failure to require pulling spoiler circuit breakers, suggesting a lockout procedure to prevent accidental deployment.

ASRS:1775388.n: Discovered frost on the upper surface of wings during preflight inspection. Planned for a Type I deicing event on the [Deicing Pad] at the approach end of Runway XX. Deicing took four minutes and was completed using 22.8 USG. Takeoff roll was started at XA:00.Upon leaving the deicing pad and headed towards the runway on Taxiway 1, we were instructed by Tower to line-up-and-wait. Prior to entering the runway, were received our takeoff clearance and completed the Before Takeoff Checklist. The FMS calculated takeoff length was 3,753 ft. of an 11,000 ft. runway and V1/Vr/V2 were 112/119/131 kts., respectively with an FMS calculated takeoff weight of 21,950 pounds and an laptop calculated weight of 21,999 pounds. Acceleration was normal and the usual action and call outs were accomplished. Upon reaching Vr, I applied the appropriate amount of back pressure and there was no elevator response. At that moment, and upon applying even more back pressure (again, no control surface response), V2 was called. Seeing that plenty of runway was left (I'm estimating at least 6,000 ft. remaining), I elected to bring the throttles to idle, deploy the air brakes and declare an abort. The airplane was down to a slow taxi as we exited [Runway] XX onto taxiway 2, estimating at least 3,000 ft. remaining.ATC asked us our intentions, and we responded that we'd like to return the ramp, knowing that a brake inspection would be required, as we had aborted above 90 kts. Upon parking the airplane on the ramp, the fuse plugs did their jobs and the tires of the right main gear deflated. The left main tires have remained intact.
ASRS:1775388.s: The pilot aborted takeoff on Runway XX after experiencing no elevator response at rotation speed, despite normal acceleration and prior deicing. The aircraft stopped with 3,000 feet remaining, and the right main gear tires deflated upon parking due to fuse plug activation from the high-speed abort.

ASRS:1775389.n: I was on my 4th leg in a ferry flight, I had a sudden consecutive RPM drop, I applied carb heat with full power, didn't help much, start to lose altitude slowly over the water, I went direct to the nearest airport and contacted the tower, at the beginning it seemed to me I will land in the water so I put my ELT manually ON, by the time I reached there they cleared me to land Runway XX, I was able to make it to the runway, after landing there was a lot of oil leak on the nose wheel, struts and all over the belly.
ASRS:1775389.s: During a ferry flight over water, the pilot experienced a sudden consecutive RPM drop and slow altitude loss despite applying carb heat and full power. After manually activating the ELT and receiving a clearance to land Runway XX, the aircraft landed safely but exhibited significant oil leaks on the nose wheel, struts, and belly.

ASRS:1775401.n: We were given a recovery trip from PBI to ZZZ1. Upon arriving at the aircraft we had to defer the Nav database and the Jeppessen charts. We did just that which made us unable to do RNAV STARS, SIDS, routes etc. When the First Officer tried to get the clearance they gave us a RNAV SID and an AR route as that is what had been filed. The First Officer advised them we were unable to accept the route as we weren't able RNAV SIDS, STARS, routes etc. they informed us that our suffix indicated we were RNAV capable so we would have to refile correctly for us to go without using an RNAV SID. I called dispatch and explained it to the dispatcher and asked for it to be refiled with an appropriate route and suffix. It was refiled with a different route but the suffix still showed us as RNAV capable so clearance still wouldn't issue it. I called dispatch again and asked for it to be corrected and filed again. I made sure the third flight plan did come through with a different suffix before turning my attention to the passengers as they had now shown up. I greeted the owners and got them loaded and made sure the bags were loaded. During the baggage loading it became apparent I would have to increase the weight to match the weight of bags for the trip. I adjusted the weight in the waypoint app and waited for a valid release. The First Officer had briefed the passengers and we got into the cockpit and got ready to go while we waited for the release. We waited quite a while for the release as we began making phone calls and sending messages to try and see if the release was coming. Once I finally got through to the dispatcher on the phone and asked if the new release was coming soon. He responded 'what do you mean? You're in the air already.' I informed him that no we weren't we were still waiting on a valid release due to the weight change. Shortly after that we received a release from a different dispatcher which we verified the suffix was still the same as the last release and made our way to depart. A short time into the flight they gave us a reroute to a couple RNAV fixes and different route. We advised them we weren't RNAV and would like to remain on our route navigating by ground based navigation. It was at this point that I started to wonder if the suffix still wasn't correct for the airplanes condition. We continued without further issues. The entire process was truly exhausting having to review and keep straight in my head four releases and make sure they were done correctly, even if it wasn't already a new airplane as well as a recovery at the end of what was now becoming a long day. The last two releases being issued after the passengers were already onboard the airplane.
ASRS:1775401.s: The crew deferred the Nav database and Jeppesen charts, causing RNAV capability mismatches in filed flight plans and delaying departure until a valid release was issued. Despite the suffix still indicating RNAV capability, the crew navigated via ground-based aids after ATC issued an RNAV reroute, completing the flight without further issues.

ASRS:1775414.n: While flying a VFR flight to LOM, I may have entered the Philadelphia Bravo airspace without clearance. I was communicating with PHL ATC on 124.35 for flight following. I was told to climb from 3,000 to 3,500 to avoid a TFR but don't remember specifically being cleared into the bravo airspace. Normally I would verify with ATC before entering the bravo if I was unsure. However, on this flight, my GPS equipment lost the GPS signal near Wilmington and I got distracted troubleshooting it. I was a few miles into the Bravo airspace when I realized I had not double checked the clearance. I was still talking with PHL ATC and they did not express any concerns with my location.
ASRS:1775414.s: A VFR pilot flying to LOM may have entered Philadelphia Bravo airspace without clearance while distracted by GPS signal loss near Wilmington. Although the pilot climbed to 3,500 feet to avoid a TFR, they realized the airspace entry error only after entering, with ATC expressing no concerns.

ASRS:1775420.n: On initial approach, I experienced engine/mechanical problems and decided to immediately switch airports and land. My left engine was experiencing problems so I requested vectors direct. Then I advised ATC and flew directly to the approach end of the runway. I landed uneventfully, and we are troubleshooting the aircraft to determine the reason for the left engine failure.
ASRS:1775420.s: The pilot experienced left engine problems during initial approach, requested vectors direct, and diverted to land uneventfully. The aircraft is currently being troubleshooted to determine the cause of the engine failure.

ASRS:1775431.n: I was conducting a training flight from ZZZ with a relatively new student, who is part owner of the aircraft (I am not an owner of the airplane). The lesson began normally with a preflight inspection by the student and an abbreviated inspection by myself, which showed no abnormality. There were five quarts of oil in the engine, I tightened the cap myself after double-checking. I personally watched the student add 10 gallons on fuel to the aircraft and sump uncontaminated fuel from both tanks immediately prior to flying. The run up was performed prior to takeoff with normal RPM drops on both magnetos and with application of carburetor heat. On takeoff the oil pressure and temperature read normal, and the engine was generating what appeared to be normal maximum power (~2,500 RPM). Takeoff and climb to the west were uneventful, with the student being the pilot flying. Several minutes into the flight I took the controls to demonstrate a maneuver. After performing a clearing turn at 3,000 ft. to prepare to demonstrate stalls to the student, I pressed the mixture in to prepare for full-power recovery from the maneuvers. Shortly after doing so, I noticed a drastic decrease in engine power (roughly 1,500 RPM maximum). After moving the throttle through most of its range to see if any setting would produce more power, I executed the engine failure checklist from memory (fuel on, mixture rich, carb heat on, magnetos on both, master on, primer in and locked). All items were configured correctly, I cycled each magneto individually to see if using one alone would produce more power, but this did not work. As I was doing this I was turning back toward land to the east and searching for a nearby grass runway. I requested priority handling to Approach, who assisted in locating ZZZ which was only several miles away and within gliding distance. A safe landing was made on the runway, which was in good condition and dry. When shutting down the aircraft, I noticed a sharp increase in RPM while pulling the mixture out to cutoff. I called the TRACON on the phone to let them know of our safe landing. After exiting the aircraft, I checked the oil level again, it was still at five quarts, and the cap had been tight. There was no obvious cause of the engine malfunction visible through the air inlets or the oil door. My student did find some acorns underneath the aircraft on the runway, the plane had recently undergone maintenance to remove debris in the engine cowling placed by squirrels that had gotten into the hangar. Several minutes after landing, deputies from the Sheriff's Department arrived to verify our safety, as they had been contacted by the approach controller. I was able to restart the aircraft normally, though in the full rich position the aircraft was not able to produce more than 1,500 RPM and ran very rough. With the mixture pulled out about two inches, I was able to generate a normal static RPM at full throttle. The aircraft was secured so that it could be inspected and repaired by the on-field A&P when he was available later in the week. I was informed by the student several days later that the mechanic found acorns in the air induction system.
ASRS:1775431.s: During a training flight, the instructor experienced a sudden loss of engine power at 3,000 feet, forcing a priority landing at ZZZ. The student later reported that a mechanic found acorns in the air induction system, which caused the rough running and power loss.

ASRS:1775434.n: Tuned radio to frequency while approaching ZZZ airport from the west. I listened for traffic at ZZZ and announced intentions to land on Runway XY after crossing midfield Runway XY-YX. These announcements were 10 miles and again 4 miles west of the airport. Crossed midfield from the west, made right turn to the south to enter Runway XY from 45 degrees. Announced again on frequency entering left downwind Runway XY, announced base, then final for Runway XY. Saw that I was high and went around. At midfield, while departing and at about 100-200 feet AGL, I saw another aircraft approaching from straight ahead and about 75 feet above me and to the left. The opposing aircraft banked right, as did I. The other aircraft must have been landing on Runway YX and was also going around, because I did not see an aircraft on the runway or taxiway as I approached. I checked the airport traffic CTAF against my entered radio frequency and saw the correct frequency was frequency. I had been announcing on frequency and did not realize I was on the wrong frequency. I had made an error in tuning radio and did not hear the airport traffic, nor did they hear me and my announcements.
ASRS:1775434.s: A pilot approaching ZZZ airport tuned the wrong CTAF frequency, preventing communication with other traffic. While executing a go-around at 100–200 feet AGL, the pilot encountered another aircraft also going around, resulting in a near mid-air collision caused by the radio tuning error.

ASRS:1775440.n: Randall Airport, 06N, in Middletown New York has often been a decent place to train. Runway 8 is noted as having a substantial displaced threshold and the winds on that day favored it. At 150 feet AGL my student elected to go-around and when I questioned why they said, 'I cannot read any of the runway markings nor see the displaced threshold.' They were right to do what they did. The runway is in a sad state of repairs with large cracks and areas of heaving. But worse, the paint is so faded that an unsafe landing could be made without even knowing it on the displaced threshold(s) especially on Runway 8. I implore the appropriate people be contacted so the owner/operator of this field can do some maintenance on this field to keep it open, safe, and operational.
ASRS:1775440.s: During a student training approach to Runway 8 at Randall Airport, the student executed a go-around at 150 feet AGL due to faded markings and poor pavement condition. The pilot reported that the runway's deteriorated state, including heaving and cracked surfaces, created an unsafe landing environment.

ASRS:1775464.n: During descent into for landing, student pulled power from cruise setting to normal descent setting, with no change in RPM noted. Instructor took over the controls to troubleshoot the issue. Power was stuck at 2500 rpm for the descent. In the downwind at 2,000 ft. msl, max speed was 135 IAS. Mixture was pulled to the idle cutoff to start reducing speed as a turn towards the airport was made. Flaps were extended as necessary to ensure a safe landing. Executed a power off landing with no damage to the airport property, aircraft or the three persons on board.
ASRS:1775464.s: A student pilot and instructor experienced a stuck throttle at 2,500 RPM during descent in a training aircraft. They executed a safe power-off landing at 2,000 feet MSL with no damage to the aircraft or the three occupants.

ASRS:1775504.n: I decided to do some practice approaches with my safety pilot. I got gas at ZZZ1 and it was a direct line from there for the approach into ZZZ so I did that one first. I got the weather, which was favoring the opposite direction, and changed to the advisory frequency. Another airplane announced that it was on the the approach for Runway XX but was farther out than we were. I announced that I was on the approach for Runway XY and would break off early. There was a lot of chatter on the radio both at ZZZ and at other airports that shared that frequency. We heard someone else mention Runway XX but couldn't make out what they were doing. I broke off the approach at about 800 ft. and 2 miles from the end of the runway as I knew I'd be far from the aircraft on the opposite approach. That's when my safety pilot saw the near miss plane that had departed Runway XX at some point. We never heard them announce taking off or on upwind and they did not show up on ADS-B (Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast). We immediately turned left for the missed but were past them by that point. After we passed them and announced the missed, the pilot of the other aircraft said something on the radio that I couldn't make out.Contributing factors were me continuing an approach in the wrong direction longer than I should have given the heavy chatter on the radio. The other aircraft was also not announcing enough or not announcing correctly or getting stepped on by other chatter or otherwise unintelligible. Another contributing factor was the other aircraft not having ADS-B Out installed. It wasn't required there but it would have greatly helped avoid the near miss. Given that we did hear another mention of Runway XX, I should have asked for their position since I didn't hear it the first time. In the future, I will break off opposite direction approaches much sooner when there is other traffic in the vicinity.
ASRS:1775504.s: The pilot and safety pilot experienced a near miss while practicing an approach to Runway XY against traffic departing Runway XX. The incident resulted from the pilot continuing the approach too long amidst heavy radio chatter and the other aircraft failing to announce its departure or transmit ADS-B data.

ASRS:1775517.n: To keep current, I try to fly at least one hour a month. I confirmed that there was 15 gallons in each tank which would allow for 3 hours for an anticipated flight of less than 2. I did 8 landings at 3 airports and was on my last 10 mile leg to home base. About 1.5 hours. Because of failure to change the fuel selector to both, the engine died during low level cruise. I [selected and checked] carburetor heat, mags and gas but the engine did not start for unknown reasons. I landed in a farm field with no injuries, property damage and no damage to the airplane as determined by the club mechanic. Lack of experience in type. This the only plane that requires leaving the fuel on right only that I have flown. I was interrupted during the preflight, I should have stated over again. I should practice emergency procedures more often.
ASRS:1775517.s: The pilot, flying a single-engine aircraft on a low-level cruise leg, experienced an engine failure after failing to select the fuel selector to "both." The pilot executed a forced landing in a farm field with no injuries or damage, attributing the incident to a lack of experience with this specific aircraft's fuel system and an interrupted preflight.

ASRS:1775524.n: I departed 52F from runway 35 for a straight out VFR climb enroute to ZZZ for pattern work. After departure, and during the initial climb, I visually observed a powered parachute maneuvering at approximately 1,200 feet MSL on the extended straight out departure path from 52F. I then observed a second powered parachute operating at my current altitude of 1,500 feet MSL directly in my flight path (altitudes later crosschecked from my ForeFlight flight path replay). Since the second powered parachute was head-on I did not see him until the last minute. I was forced to make an abrupt maneuver to the left (west) to avoid a midair collision. I have since learned from other pilots based at 52F that this is a frequent occurrence in all areas around 52F, and at times powered parachutes have operated within the lateral and vertical traffic pattern boundaries of 52F, which seems to be contrary to 14 CFR part 103.13(a) and (b). In addition, this type of operation is prohibited at 52F per the remarks section of the A/FD. These types of operations are less regulated than drones and drone operators. I am concerned that if allowed to continue without some type of mitigation or FAA intervention that it is only a matter of time before there is an accident. I would suggest either requiring some kind of formal training/testing/checking for powered parachutes or prohibiting these operations under (not just within) the all Class B airspace.
ASRS:1775524.s: A pilot departing runway 35 at 52F for VFR pattern work executed an abrupt left turn to avoid a head-on powered parachute at 1,500 feet MSL. The reporter attributes the near-midair collision to frequent, unregulated powered parachute operations within the airport's traffic pattern boundaries.

ASRS:1775529.n: I was flying on an IFR flight plan at assigned altitude of 4000'. After seeing a cell on FIS-B radar (Flight Information System-Broadcast), I requested from ATC if there were any PIREPS for the weather. I then requested a deviation for weather depicted by FIS-B. I was granted the requested weather deviation and was flying outside of the weather depicted by FIS-B several miles in IMC conditions. Apparently, I flew into an embedded thunderstorm cell with both severe turbulence and violent downdrafts and updrafts which was not depicted by FIS-B weather with a 4 minute time stamp.I noticed the IAS had climbed dangerously high into the yellow arc while on autopilot (AP) maintaining an altitude of 4,000'. I reduced power to idle in an effort to maintain a safe indicated airspeed. While the AP was engaged and power reduced the IAS did not reduce sufficiently to the maneuvering speed but was rapidly climbing. I disconnected the AP and pulled the yoke back to reduce IAS. I then encountered severe turbulence and downdrafts forcing the aircraft to lose approximately 500 feet. In an attempt to stabilize the aircraft, I attempted to various throttle settings in an attempt to maintain altitude and heading with little success in controlling altitude or heading.The entire event lasted approximately 2 minutes with several calls from ATC offering assistance. During those calls I requested ATC standby until I was able to regain control of the aircraftThis was an isolated cell whose location was not accurately depicted by FIS-B weather radar returns. In regards to corrective actions on my part as pilot, I'd say to not trust FIS-B time stamps nor the weather depictions as being reasonably accurate. Further I'd extend my safety margin around weather depicted on FIS-B to a greater margin.The flight terminated without incident with my cancelling my IFR flight plan once out of IMC conditions and safely landing at the destination airport.
ASRS:1775529.s: The pilot flying an IFR flight at 4,000 feet encountered an embedded thunderstorm not depicted on FIS-B radar, resulting in severe turbulence and a 500-foot altitude loss. After regaining control by disconnecting the autopilot, the pilot cancelled the IFR plan and landed safely, attributing the incident to inaccurate weather data.

ASRS:1775538.n: At level flight, right engine oil low pressure illuminated, followed by a loss of N1 and subsequent amber lights indicated for GEN failure and hydraulic low. We advised ATC as had lost power from the right engine. We started a decent and went through the appropriate checklists. As we still had N1 & N2 rotation we were able to restart the engine. The engine then indicated normal across all gauges, therefore we continued onto our destination of ZZZ (home base). At cruise flight flight engine oil low pressure illuminates followed by loss of N1 and amber lights indicating for GEN fail and hydraulic low. We advised ATC as we had loss of power in the right engine. We started to descent and went through the checklist. As we had N1 and N2 rotation we where able to restart the engine. The engine then indicated normal across all gauges. We continued to ZZZ home base.
ASRS:1775538.s: During cruise, the crew experienced right engine oil low pressure, N1 loss, and generator/hydraulic failures. After descending and completing checklists, they successfully restarted the engine using remaining rotation and continued to home base ZZZ.

ASRS:1775546.n: Flying a touch-and-go in VMC after flying ~ 1.3 hrs (from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2 then ZZZ). About 0.25-0.5 miles from TO (takeoff) end of runway at ~ 300 ft., aircraft experienced a sudden loss of power and then power surged back. Aircraft remained to feel underpowered and unable to climb. I got priority handling with ZZZ Tower at that time.I was able to enter a low altitude downwind and make short-final for Runway XX with no further incident. On final touch and go at ZZZ2 (directly before the incident at ZZZ) it seemed in retrospect like the aircraft didn't develop full power as expected. This was minor and could also have been an unrelated factor.Potential contributors:1) Prior to departing ZZZ1, I noticed some corrosion on left tip tank fuel sump. There was a few small drops of water in the tip tank. The fuel selector had been left on that tank while sitting on the ground for the previous 2 weeks. The tank was not used in flight. 2) I had used nearly all of the right tip tank in my approach to ZZZ (burned all but last 1-2 gallons), flipped to Main Left tank prior to touch and go. It's possible that that switch was too late and injected a bubble that worked it way through after applying full throttle? 3) [Human Factors] Busy day of touch and goes with MVMC ceilings and BR (mist) in the area.
ASRS:1775546.s: The pilot experienced sudden power loss and surge at 300 feet during a touch-and-go at ZZZ, forcing a low-altitude landing. Potential causes included water in the left tip tank, a fuel bubble from switching tanks, or human factors due to busy operations in mist.

ASRS:1775552.n: In descent while returning to land at ZZZ from west of the airport and north of the Denver Class B airspace, I received a TCAS warning very close to our aircraft. I made a rapid and aggressive descending turn away from the threat aircraft in the direction of the Class B airspace (the only way that I could turn). We were near, but below the ceiling of the Class B segment and did not enter it. We never did see the other aircraft. The remainder of approach and landing were normal.
ASRS:1775552.s: During descent to ZZZ, the pilot received a TCAS warning and executed a rapid descending turn toward Denver Class B airspace to avoid an unseen threat. The aircraft remained below the Class B ceiling without entering it, and the approach and landing concluded normally.

ASRS:1775557.n: While in the cruise portion of my flight on an IFR flight plan I was alerted by ATC of traffic converging same altitude. I was on a NE (northeast) heading but was instructed by ATC to fly at 6,000 ft. The traffic was on a SE (southeast) heading also at 6,000 ft. descending for ZZZ. Due to me being on an IFR flight plan I did not deviate altitude or heading. The traffic descending was descending apparently at a very slow rate. ATC provided traffic alert but did not suggest new heading or altitude. When I had the traffic in sight about 200 ft. below me and very close I elected to climb based on my traffic message from my G1000 avionics with TIS-B (Traffic Information Service - Broadcast). At my altitude of 6,200 ft. the traffic passed below me by 500 ft. ATC was very busy but I should [have] queried them for vectors [or] altitude change earlier so I would not have to take action on my own. ATC did not complain about my momentary altitude deviation.
ASRS:1775557.s: A pilot on an IFR cruise flight received a traffic alert from ATC regarding converging traffic at 6,000 ft but received no specific avoidance instructions. The pilot voluntarily climbed to 6,200 ft after visually acquiring the traffic, which passed 500 ft below, noting that earlier ATC vectors would have prevented the need for self-initiated action.

ASRS:1775565.n: At XA:28Z, Aircraft X checked on the frequency asking for VFR flight following in the vicinity of ZZZ. He was given a beacon code and I displayed a data block on the radar scope, waiting for it to track up. After a minute I told the pilot that I did not have radar contact, and I didn't have a target in the area he stated. I verified his code and location, and had him reset his transponder after another minute went by. At XA:31Z I told him it might be necessary for him to climb before I could establish radar contact. He reported that he was starting a climb to 7,000 feet.One minute after he started his climb, at XA:32Z, I picked up a primary target in the area the pilot reported. I tried to verify the position of the primary target, but the pilot just responded that he was showing zero oil pressure and having electrical issues. As he was saying this, the data block correlated to the code and I radar identified Aircraft X and verified his location. My standard practice, something that I did less than ten minutes prior, is to radar identify, verify location and altitude, and give altimeter. I do it every time, and in that order. When I radar identified Aircraft X, there was no Mode C data, so I asked him to report his altitude. He reported that he was climbing to 7,000 feet and asked for help to get into ZZZ, he was showing zero on his oil pressure. I didn't circle back to the altimeter at this time.I issued Aircraft X a heading to set him up for a pattern into ZZZ. If his engine was about to quit, I wanted him lined up for an airport, not guessing what was below him. I told the CIC I was working a special aircraft, and the OM was quickly in the area. I didn't feel it was in good judgement to add on to the pilot's stress level by pointing out that he was experiencing an urgent situation. It was being handled as such.He asked as he rolled out if he was on the correct heading. I advised that he was 20 degrees off course, and that he should correct. He told me he was using his backup compass, due to electrical failure. That information made a lot of sense at that moment. The backup compass is a magnetic compass. It's one that bounces around as you turn it. The magnetic compass will continue to turn past the heading and then bounce back and correct as the airplane levels off and the compass stabilizes. This is something that an IFR rated pilot would be more knowledgeable about. No gyro turns, or turns with only the backup compass were part of my IFR certificate training. Due to this, I decided to give him small turns that would create an arc to final, and help him maintain better control and orientation.I told him to descend to 5,000 ft. and that I should still have radar contact at that altitude. He responded that believed he'd be able to poke through. I knew it would be minimal conditions, I still believed getting the aircraft set up for a runway was the safest places. As I gave him a turn to the left he stated that he was going to get into the clouds. I asked if he and the aircraft were IFR qualified. He said they were not. I asked if he could maintain VFR conditions. It sounded like he was trying, but didn't seem sure that he would.I told Aircraft X that he could continue down to 4,000 feet and gave him a heading to get him turned more toward the airport. About that time at XA:39Z, just eleven minutes into the situation, an aircraft inbound for ZZZ1 checked on. I issued the ZZZ1 altimeter. This aircraft would end up being held out for the [situation]. I then told Aircraft X he could descend at his discretion to 3,900 feet, but that was the minimum enroute altitude in the area, and the lowest I was comfortable advising him. He said he was starting to poke through at 4,100 feet. I gave him the position and distance of ZZZ1. He responded that he could see some ground.I had him continue his gradual left turn but saw a much more aggressive turn on the radar. I asked if he was circling down to stay in VFR conditions. He said he saw bases at 3,800 feet and it was an unintentional 360. Based on what the radar showed, it was not a controlled maneuver, and probably resulted from an unusual attitude due to spatial disorientation. I asked him to regain level flight, as to maintain control of the aircraft and not get into another unusual attitude. I asked him his altitude, he responded 3,680 [feet]. Up until this uncontrolled maneuver, every report was that he was in marginal conditions, but always seemed to have some visual capabilities. At this point the inability to maintain VFR was imminent.The aircraft showed a northeast heading, I asked him to make a slow turn. Being an IFR rated pilot myself, and seeing how easily he became disoriented already, I wanted to avoid a stall, spin or turning over the aircraft. In the clouds a turn can make your body feel like you are descending, and a climb can make your body think you are turning. A more abrupt climb or turn only magnifies this effect. At XA:43Z as I maintained focus on keeping the pilot's wings level, I offered the option of climbing back up into VFR conditions. He was in favor of the idea. He added that the engine had been running fine, and believed the zero oil pressure reading to be due to electrical issue, not engine issues. With that information I immediately reassessed the IFR conditions to be the most hazardous conditions in the situation.I saw the aircraft again start a west turn that seemed to increase in rate. I gave the aircraft his location and his observed turn. I advised that he level off and focus on flying straight and level. He did not respond. The maneuver seemed unstable and I tried to relay that he needed to get wings level, then start climbing slowly. Anything aggressive would cause greater disorientation. He said the engine was running fine now, no longer a concern. I told him that we believed it to be clear in ZZZ2, ZZZ3, and ZZZ4. He said that sounds nice. I wanted to get him into ZZZ3 if it was in fact clear. It was much closer, and based on his workload, fatigue due to stress, and equipment issues, I wanted him in the air the least amount of time possible. The CIC or the OM, I don't remember which, went up to the weather desk to get the most complete weather information available. Other controllers were also pulling weather at surrounding airports. I was focused on getting Aircraft X oriented and into VMC.I told him to fly his present heading and start a climb, advising that there was no traffic ahead. He responded that he was having trouble keeping his wings level. I advised back to straight and level and asked his altitude. The climb was giving him a sensation of turning and he was having trouble overcoming that. I should have advised him to focus on the instruments over his own sensations, but I did not think of it at the time.He said he was at 4,020 feet. I said give me level straight flight and then we'll start a slow climb. I wanted him to remain calm and know that we were going to work through it. He did not answer. Seeing what appeared to be straight flight on the radar scope I advised a shallow climb. He said he was trying to keep the wings level. At that point a VFR aircraft departing ZZZ1 was checking in. I called the traffic to that aircraft, advised the altitude was unknown, and asked Aircraft X to say his altitude. He did not immediately answer. Instead another aircraft keyed up, saying the other aircraft didn't look good on his TCAS and he needed to level his wings. Aircraft X then responded, he pulled into a stall, but was starting back up. I advised him to take it slow. At that point Aircraft Y verified ZZZ2 to be clear. I asked if Aircraft X was staying level. He said yes, 5,000 feet and seeing sunlight. I saw another turn on radar and had him level his wings once again. A minute later he reported on top of clouds and level. I told him maintain level flight, catch his breath, and if there were any airports he wanted to try to get to, we would get the weather for him. In my experience, it was best to remind him that he could exhale. He still needed to have the ability to fly the rest of his flight with electrical issues. I also offered him the opportunity to request an alternate airport. He had equipment that most likely needed to be repaired or replaced. I didn't want to send him somewhere that he'd get stuck. Aircraft X was maintaining a southeast heading and I asked him his altitude. He responded, 5,860 feet. I offered again, ZZZ2, ZZZ3, and ZZZ4. The pilot was happy with ZZZ2 because it was reported clear. I gave a heading for him to fly that would get him started turning more towards either airport as I waited for the weather information. I recommended going to ZZZ3 because it was the closest. The pilot agreed that ZZZ3 would be his first choice, then ZZZ2. Immediately as he said that, the information was back from the weather desk and I relayed it to the pilot. He said he wanted to shoot for ZZZ2 because it was clear and ZZZ3 was overcast. I gave a few more heading changes and turns to get him direct to ZZZ2. I also lost radar contact on him a minute later as well. I received another report that he should expect to be clear of the west edge of the moving weather some time before ZZZ2, and passed that along. I advised him that he appeared right on course, and I was relieved at XB:08Z.Ten minutes later, while talking to the relieving controller, the pilot thanked us all for the help he received and said he was feeling the love. He even asked to get a forwarding address to send me a bottle of good scotch. Additionally, when calling the facility from the ground, the pilot was very thankful for the services he received. He informed the OM that he had to change pants when he landed, and again wanted to send a thank you bottle for getting him to safety. It was not apparent at the beginning of the situation that the engine oil reading was due to an electrical issue. It was possible that it could have been a number of different factors, but I knew that he could lose his engine at any moment, and it may not sound rough right away. I wanted him to get lined up for a runway as safely and quickly as possible. I gave him the option to get down below the bases, but should have emphasized to maintain VFR, even though it is the pilot's responsibility. During a stressful [situation], that would be a good reminder to give the pilot. Once the pilot gained confidence that the engine was running properly, I did everything in my power, and with all of my flight experience to keep the pilot focused on not getting into an unrecoverable condition, while maneuvering safely into VMC.During an imminent [hazard], controllers have to make judgement calls on what is the most prudent and time critical course of action. Access to checklists during these situations would ensure that all services are provided. Controllers could check that they had provided all of the information possible without taking as much attention away from the imminent safety issue. An easier to use weather reporting system would ensure more weather reports are forwarded along from controllers. The current GI method can be tedious and the tie up keyboard use during busier sessions. ERIDS (En Route Information Display System) offers weather reporting by tapping on the information and hitting send. Using this system would increase the efficiency and result in more weather reports being available. Even just having paper weather slips that controllers can hand to a supervisor would improve efficiency.A working knowledge of flight instruments and factors of flight would allow better assistance to pilots in [hazardous] situations. Recurrent training that focuses on best practices during imminent situations would enhance controllers on seldom used skills.
ASRS:1775565.s: An Air Traffic Controller assisted a VFR pilot of Aircraft X experiencing electrical failures and spatial disorientation in marginal weather. The controller guided the pilot through uncontrolled turns and a stall to regain level flight and climb above the clouds.

ASRS:1775593.n: On the Arrival into ONT SoCal Approach assigned vectors to sequence behind a 747. We were vectored directly behind and above the preceding 747 for 26L when we were cleared for the visual approach to 26R. ATC advised to maintain visual separation. At that point, due to concerns of descending behind the heavy aircraft, I offset right of course and attempted to parallel the 747. My intention was to remain clear of the 747's wake vortices. As we continued the approach and began to converge with the other aircraft, ONT Tower issued clearance to S-turn to the right if necessary. At that point we were too close to the runway to make any effective maneuvers and still maintain a stabilized approach. We then received a 'Descend' RA and continued descending on the visual approach to 26R while the adjacent aircraft executed a climb and go-around from 26L. In retrospect I believe a better course of action would have been to discontinue the visual approach or ask for delay vectors to increase separation from the heavy aircraft. ATC should have issued more realistic vectors to sequence us further behind the 747. Descending on the Arrival into ONT, SoCal Approach Control gave a maintain current HDG [instruction]. We visually acquired a 747 at our 12 o'clock position approximately 5 NMs. SoCal then gave us a right turn to a 140 HDG, then subsequently a 170 HDG that placed us at the 6 o'clock position of the 747 approximately 5 NMs behind. Once established on the 170 HDG, SoCal cleared us and the 747 visual approaches, 747 to Runway 26L and us to 26R and told us 'Caution wake turbulence and maintain visual separation with the 747'. The Captain did not want to be in a position to be at a 45 degree angle behind the 747, which would've increased the chances of getting into the wake of the 747, so as we were descending for the approach we received a descend RA and Aircraft Y executed a go-around for a climb RA. When we noticed that it would be challenging to do the approach and simultaneously staying out if the heavy aircraft's wake turbulence, should've asked the Controller for a vector or turn before starting the final portion of the approach.
ASRS:1775593.s: Pilots on a visual approach to ONT Runway 26R behind a 747 on 26L received a Descend RA due to wake turbulence concerns and insufficient separation. The crew continued descending while the 747 executed a go-around, with the pilot attributing the event to unrealistic ATC vectors and a failure to request delay vectors earlier.
