I manually deployed the spoilers on touchdown, the FO extended the thrust reverse levers (the levers fully extended, but the reversers did not deploy) and applied maximum manual braking. We stopped on the runway to allow the fire department to analyze the aircraft and brakes for fire indications, which were reported as negative. We opted to then taxi off of the runway and into a large taxiway intersection (XX and YY Taxiways) to allow access to the aircraft from all angles. We calculated brake energy and cooling requirements, and monitored the brake temperatures on the synoptic page. Because our calculations put us on the edge of the warning zone for fuse plug melting, we sat and did not set the parking brake and called for towing. Normal after landing and shutdown procedures were accomplished. The tow took approximately an hour to complete, during which the brakes cooled back to normal temperatures without any damage. There were many people and agencies involved, the aircrew, Flight Control, Maintenance Control, SME's, ZZZZ2 Gateway, and others, all of whom were ready on a moment's notice, helped tremendously, and performed their roles flawlessly. Thank you to all. After a normal climb to Flight Level 350 I began to exit my flight station when I heard the Captain call attention to the EICAS which at the time showed, I believe, two amber advisory messages, >YAW DAMPER LWR and RUD RATIO SNGL. Almost immediately thereafter several other EICAS advisory messages appeared on the primary EICAS screen along with a full page of status messages on the secondary EICAS screen. I immediately took my place back at the FO (First Officer) station and was advised by the Captain to resume Pilot Flying duties along with communication with ATC. Our IRO (International Relief Officer) was advised by the Captain to begin a patch with dispatch and begin troubleshooting measures with maintenance control. Among the three jump seating crew members was an instructor pilot who was also summoned to the flight deck for assistance. During this trouble shooting period it was determined that multiple systems including flight controls, hydraulics, pneumatic's and navigation equipment were all seriously degraded from normal. Also, it was decided that the two remaining jump seaters should go and inspect the main deck. Those crew members reported that no smoke was visible however a distinct electrical burning odor was present towards the front of the main deck. A diversion to ZZZZ2, including an overweight landing was agreed upon following all operating crew members vote. Clearance to ZZZZ2 was obtained with ZZZZ1 Radar and thus we began our diversion. I requested with ZZZZ1 a descent to FL250 so as to reduce the total time required to descend from altitude yet still provide for adequate differential pressure in case the need for equipment cooling override mode was required. After each initial flap configuration change we agreed upon disconnecting the autopilot momentarily to check flight control effectiveness. I found the aircraft to exhibit normal flying characteristics though slight porpoising occurred while on final approach as it was also discovered that the aircraft's right side glide slope was inoperable. I then disconnected the autopilot and hand flew the remainder of the approach to landing. During this landing it was pre briefed that the Captain would manually deploy the speed brakes and I would manually apply brakes as the auto deploy functions for both were disabled. I found the aircraft to have very effective stopping power as we stopped prior to the [Taxiway] XX high speed turn off. We remained on the runway with the parking break off while emergency vehicles inspected the fuselage and brakes for possible fire. Once it was determined that no visible fire was present we taxied clear of the runway onto a very large intersection at XX so that fire vehicles could more easily access the landing gear area if needed. We again held manual brakes only and did not set the parking brake during this wait for ground tow as our brake temperatures slowly climbed to a 6 on several indicators. After about an hour after landing we were towed to our parking gate. Incidentally, it was pointed out later on by the Captain that he was very quickly able to determine a possible diversionary landing site by his use of the 'Surface Conditions' line select item in the Weather Layers feature of our Jeppesen Flight Deck Pro app. Its simple and very intuitive red vs. green color gradation made the direction to turn from altitude a quick one, much quicker than having to dial up various ATIS frequencies. Perhaps this method could be stressed somewhat more during training? It was a great way to get a big weather picture of our surrounding area during an intense information overload situation.
ASRS:1775985.s: The flight crew of a 747 experienced multiple EICAS faults and an electrical smoke odor at cruise, causing a diversion to ZZZZ2. They executed an overweight landing with manual braking and speed brakes due to system failures, then waited for brake cooling before being towed to the gate.

ASRS:1775993.n: On visual approach, turning base to final inside 5 miles to touchdown on Runway XXL at ZZZ, the #1 Engine lost thrust and rolled back. It indicated 20 to 21% N1 for the remainder of the flight irrespective of the thrust lever position. I manually flew the airplane to the runway and landed. I requested my FO/PNF (First Officer/Pilot Not Flying) notify the Tower we had an engine failure just after passing below 500 ft. AGL. The Master Caution illuminated in flight, with ENG illuminated on the Master Caution annunciator. No other warning and no other caution lights illuminated. The engine ran at idle thrust and within acceptable parameters, but the thrust lever would not command additional thrust.Unknown why engine rolled back to idle in flight.Manually flew airplane single engine to a full stop landing on intended runway. Verified condition of engine my self and later commanding PNF to call out what he saw as failure. Notified ATC/Tower of engine failure.
ASRS:1775993.s: During a visual approach to Runway XXL, the pilot reported that Engine #1 lost thrust and rolled back to idle, indicating 20–21% N1 regardless of lever position. The cause was unknown, but the pilot manually flew the aircraft to a safe single-engine landing and notified ATC.

ASRS:1776006.n: The purpose of this report is to point out a possible safety issue in regards to the no fly zones going to South America. Flying over South America there are two no fly zones, one in the Peruvian Airspace and the second one extends from south of Peru across the Andes mountains all the way down to the south of Chile. Those areas where depicted in our old paper navigational charts and every no fly zones had waypoints. Those waypoints where depicted, for example the no fly zone over Peruvian airspace had the following waypoints depicted on the old paper navigational chart as follows: NFZ01, NFZ02, etc., up to NFZ06. Those way points are still on our Nav (Navigation) Database and can be still used for safety awareness by building the no fly zones on the secondary flight plan. When we switch to Electronic Flight Bag you can still see the no fly zones but the way points are taken away. Based on my experience, about 80% of the times that we fly to South America, the iPad loses his own ship due to lack of signal and you cannot use the electronic chart for reference to make sure that you are not getting over any of the no fly zones, especially when we are deviating from weather. The only place that we can find those no fly zones way points is in the diversion guide page XX. I always put those way points on the secondary flight plan so I can see them on the Nav Display just in case we have to deviate due to weather and the iPad loose the signal. On my last flight to Lima we had to deviate due to weather over the shore line and because we had those no fly zones on the secondary flight plan, we were able to stay away from that area. I been flying into South America for over XX years in different fleets and we always had use that procedure and the information was everywhere. Now we have lost that information when we switch from paper to electronic nav charts. We also are getting new pilots from other bases that never been in those routes before and the majority are not even aware of those way points, and have no clue how to find them and use them. I believe that in the name of safety, those way points should be inserted into the electronic navigational charts and the company should provide more information about those way points.If you need any additional information please don't hesitate to contact me.Thank you for your time and attention to towards this matter.Experience flying this division.As I mentioned before, I believe that in the name of safety, those way points should be inserted into the electronic navigational charts and the company should provide more information about those way points.
ASRS:1776006.s: A pilot reported that switching to Electronic Flight Bags removed No Fly Zone waypoints from South American charts, creating a safety risk when iPad signals fail during weather deviations. The pilot successfully avoided a restricted area using a secondary flight plan but recommends restoring these waypoints to electronic charts and improving crew training.

ASRS:1776008.n: While climbing to our cruise altitude the Captain and I began to hear a noise coming from the cabin that sounded to us like a pressurization leak in the airplane. Shortly thereafter the Captain received a call from the cabin crew, I believe notifying him about the same noise we were hearing. We then asked ATC for a lower altitude in hopes of the noise stopping. Shortly after that the Captain received another call from the cabin crew, when he hung up the phone he told me we were returning to our departure airport ZZZ due to claims of smoke or fumes in the cabin. I then donned my oxygen mask and notified ATC with our intentions to return to ZZZ. We were then given a lower altitude and vectors. We conducted the smoke/fumes checklist. We also decided ZZZ1 airport would be closer and notified ATC we would be landing there. We landed in ZZZ1 without incident where we had the ARFF (airport rescue firefighters) search our aircraft for any hot spots while still on the runway. After no hot spots were found we taxied to the gate where we deplaned normally. The pressurization leak that caused a loud noise and I never heard what the cabin crew smelled in the cabin. I really can't come up with any suggestions that would have prevented this event without knowing what caused the leak and what caused the smell.
ASRS:1776008.s: During climb, the flight crew heard a loud noise resembling a pressurization leak and received reports of smoke or fumes from the cabin crew. They diverted to ZZZ1, landed safely, and deplaned after ARFF found no hot spots, though the specific cause of the leak and odor remained unknown.

ASRS:1776024.n: I took over this flight at shift change and outgoing Dispatcher advised they had just received information about undeclared HAZMAT (hazardous material) being on the aircraft. Service recovery advised that there were 98 packages of lithium batteries in position 2R, which was located too close to ADG (accessible dangerous goods) loaded in position 1L. At this point, flight was about 3 hours out of ZZZ, notified crew of issue via ACARS, and after service recovery consulted with Duty Officer, determined no immediate safety issue existed, so flight continued to ZZZ1. I do not know what caused the issue, aircraft was already in the air when I found out about it and the error was with the loading of the dangerous goods and lithium batteries, anyway. You would need to contact hub to find out the cause.
ASRS:1776024.s: A dispatcher notified the crew of undeclared lithium batteries loaded too close to other dangerous goods while the aircraft was en route to ZZZ1. Service recovery and the Duty Officer determined no immediate safety issue existed, allowing the flight to continue despite the loading error.

ASRS:1776025.n: The 'Before Takeoff' Checklist was not performed. The Captain did not call for the Checklist and I did not catch the error. The Aircraft was properly configured and the Takeoff occurred normally without incident.We were both focused on properly performing the ZZZ Noise Abatement procedure. We pushed back from Gate X (very close to the departure end of Runway XXR). During the pre-departure takeoff briefing neither of us discussed the Threat of the very short Taxi to the Runway. We did discuss that ZZZ was a bit of a 'Ghost Town;' with minimal activity compared to the times we'd previously been to the airport (for both of us it was during the 'Pre-COVID' era). Within a short period of time after Departure, I mentioned we'd forgotten to perform the Before Takeoff Checklist. We both discussed our expectation that there would have been wait during Taxi, which is part of the 'Normal' routine. In this case, we did perform the Runway/Performance Change items after push-back with the Parking Brake set - we were then cleared to Taxi, instructed to switch to Tower, and then Cleared for Takeoff. The delay we were anticipating never occurred. The Captain called the Cabin after we were out of the sterile flight deck period and learned that the Aft Flight Attendant (FA) was seated, the Forward FA stated he was standing in the Galley during Takeoff. Both FA's indicated that all passengers were seated.Suggestions - 1. Brief the Flight Attendants that the Taxi Time is ZZZ is very short, and to be seated prior the call for 'Cabin Secure'. 2. At ZZZ, include the short Taxi time, close proximity of the Gates and Runways as a Threat during the takeoff briefing. 3. Perform both the Runway/Performance Change items and Before Takeoff checklists prior to beginning Taxi for Takeoff.
ASRS:1776025.s: The flight crew omitted the Before Takeoff Checklist during a short taxi at ZZZ airport due to distraction by noise abatement procedures and an expectation of a delay. The aircraft departed normally without incident, though the crew later realized the error and noted that cabin crew were not fully secured for takeoff.

ASRS:1776030.n: Turned in closer to final than anticipated after receiving vectors to final. Cleared for the approach and wasn't quite to ZZZZZ [Intersection] before descending to the final altitude. Received a low altitude alert from ATC. Called up ATC and discussed the situation, didn't lose any separation or any other problems.Turned in closer to final than anticipated. Cleared for the approach and wasn't quite to ZZZZZ [Intersection] before descending to the final altitude. Create a clear path for the descent and verify the DME.
ASRS:1776030.s: The pilot descended to final altitude before reaching the ZZZZZ intersection after turning in closer to final than anticipated. ATC issued a low altitude alert, but no separation loss or other problems occurred.

ASRS:1776038.n: During cruise at 10,000 feet MSL, on a revenue flight enroute to Bakersfield California, I flew underneath a small unidentifiable object. Weather conditions at the time were VFR but hazy, I was just crossing the mountain tops into the flat land around Bakersfield when the event happened, I was located on the 141 degree radial from the Shafter (EHF) VOR at approximately 35 DME. While looking ahead and piloting, a small light from outside and above me caught my eye. When I looked up I was flying 25 to 50 feet below a small round object with what looked like a light on the bottom side of it. I initially reported this to Bakersfield Approach as a drone, but I flew by it so quickly and the range at which I spotted it, I can't say with 100% certainty what it was. I would say it's possible it could've been a balloon with the sun reflecting off of it as well. Fortunately, nothing happened and I proceeded to Bakersfield for a normal landing.Being as I don't know 100% what the object was it's hard to say what 'caused' it. If it was in fact a drone and not a balloon then it was most likely being illegally operated.Unfortunately due to the haze preventing me from seeing it sooner, and the rate of closure with the object there wasn't any time to react. I reported the event to Bakersfield Approach.Not much to suggest other than asking pilots to remain vigilant in their scans outside as best they can with the given weather conditions.
ASRS:1776038.s: During cruise at 10,000 feet MSL en route to Bakersfield, a pilot flew 25 to 50 feet below an unidentifiable object, possibly a drone or balloon, due to hazy conditions preventing early detection. The pilot reported the event to Bakersfield Approach and completed a normal landing with no further incident.

ASRS:1776046.n: Aircraft was cleared for the RNAV (GPS) RWY XXR at ZZZ. PF armed APP mode and commenced the approach. Passing ZZZZZ [fix], PF was utilizing EVS (Enhanced Vision System) and HUD in an attempt to see runway lights. PF continued to focus on EVS and HUD when GROUND PROX illuminated almost the same time as a TERRAIN ALERT call from ZZZ Tower was received between ZZZZZ and ZZZZZ1. Aircraft was level at 1,100 feet, where it climbed to regain VPATH to continue approach. PF and PM both had vertical ground contact and were familiar with local terrain (ZZZ is aircraft's home base) and were comfortable reacquiring the VPATH and continuing approach.Suggest using EVS and HUD as secondary tool during. Verify APP has properly captured prior to shifting focus to EVS and HUD. During RNAV XXR approach to ZZZ with approach close to minimums the Tower called low altitude alert almost simultaneously with Ground Prox warning. The approach had been setup properly and I saw the PF arm approach mode when we were cleared to switch to tower. I went heads down to change frequency and checked in with tower. Shortly thereafter the Tower called a low altitude alert and ground proximity called terrain. At that time I noticed that we were well below the vertical path but I could see the ground and almost immediately the tower on my right side which we were well clear of. I told PF to level off and even climb a couple hundred feet. We were able to rejoin the V Path about ZZZZZ1 on the approach and continued down to MDA where we were able to proceed visually when the runway was observed visually. If we were not at our local airport with local knowledge of the terrain I am sure I would have called for a go around.I believe that the PF was focused inside the HUD on the EVS looking for runway lights and lost his instrument scan. As the PM I also lost situational awareness. Really have no idea how we ended up I believe in a pitch hold mode with the autopilot and no idea how it did not capture the V Path.
ASRS:1776046.s: During an RNAV (GPS) approach to ZZZ, the PF and PM descended below the vertical path while focused on the EVS and HUD, triggering Ground Prox and tower alerts. The crew leveled off, regained the vertical path, and continued visually, attributing the deviation to lost instrument scan and autopilot mode confusion.

ASRS:1776048.n: I was complying with a functional check of the aileron cable tension in the forward cargo area. With this task you must remove the forward bulk head right hand panel and cargo area floor boards. After the aileron cable tension checks, I completed the job card signing off all the tasks including the completion of the bulk head blow out panel and floor boards. I failed to secure the floor boards and the bulk head panel resulting in the aircraft flying in an unsafe condition in which could of resulted in a catastrophic result. As a maintainer it is my responsibility to make the sure any and all aircraft is it a 100% airworthy. In the future, any task that is not completed will not be signed to make sure it is completed to ensure the aircraft is airworthy.
ASRS:1776048.s: A maintainer failed to secure the forward bulkhead panel and cargo floor boards after performing an aileron cable tension check. This oversight resulted in the aircraft flying in an unsafe condition that could have caused a catastrophic outcome.

ASRS:1776065.n: Passenger started complaining that he was extremely hot and was grabbing at the collar of his shirt. The vents were open and the aircraft was chilly not warm. I could see that he was sweating and he asked if he could have some water. I went to the back galley to get him water and some iced cloth folds to put on his neck. When I turned around to head out with his items, [his condition had deteriorated]. I immediately called the pilots and we paged for medical assistance. We had a few nurses onboard that assisted us with the passenger. He stated he needed to get to the restroom. I helped the nurse get the passenger to his feet and the passenger went into the lav. He was vomiting for several minutes.I spoke with the Supervisors the next day and advised them if my concerns regarding the fact that this passenger seemed to be exhibiting COVID symptoms. I was advised there was nothing that could be done regarding the possible exposure and that I should just self monitor while continuing to fly. I feel that more precautions should be taken when a passenger shows symptoms of COVID mid flight. I think we should carry a thermometer onboard and when a passenger shows COVID symptoms especially when it results in a call to medical. More precautions should be taken to protect crew members proactively instead of retroactively.
ASRS:1776065.s: A cabin crew member assisted a passenger exhibiting heat-like symptoms who deteriorated and vomited in the lavatory during flight. The crew contacted pilots and onboard nurses, but the reporter noted that post-flight advice to self-monitor for possible COVID exposure lacked proactive protective measures like onboard thermometers.

ASRS:1776069.n: I was attempting to help a passenger in Seat X3 when the service animal of passenger in Y1 lunged at me. I was afraid it would injure me or other passengers. Every time I, the other crew and passengers walk down the aisle the passenger in Y1 has to grab the leash.
ASRS:1776069.s: A cabin crew member reported that a service animal belonging to a passenger in Y1 lunged at them while they were assisting a passenger in X3. The crew member feared injury to themselves or others, noting the animal requires the owner to grab the leash whenever anyone walks down the aisle.

ASRS:1776090.n: C Flight Attendant positioned behind the exit row on Aircraft X. Family boarded with 2 small children, one of whom would occupy a car seat. I believe car seat may have had blankets over it during boarding so it was difficult to tell that it was a car seat. It was also difficult to see what was going on in front of the exit row when I was behind it due to multiple passengers, seats, and distance in the way. We also became distracted at the end of boarding by a high maintenance passenger traveling with 2 dogs that attempted to sit in the exit row that took some time to relocate. It was getting close to our departure time, so C needed to brief the exit row passengers and get to the front. Due to the above factors, it was missed that the family with the car seat was one row in front of the exit row. This was not noticed until A flight attendant did the final walkthrough shortly prior to being cleared for departure. At that point, the plane was in motion, the seatbelt sign was on, and every row was occupied. There was not somewhere we could realistically move a family of 4.We could have more specific instructions for the D Flight Attendant during boarding, to position on an opposing part of the exit rows from the C on the 800 to be able to see what is going on all around the exit row. The 737-800's exit row is 3 entire rows, and it is difficult to see what is going on all around it with just one person located there. Additionally, the D positioned in the exit row during boarding would keep the exit row monitored during potential distractions, like having to relocate a passenger from the exit row.
ASRS:1776090.s: A Flight Attendant missed a car seat in the row ahead of the exit row on a 737-800 during boarding due to visual obstructions and distractions from relocating a passenger with dogs. The family could not be moved once the aircraft was in motion, prompting a recommendation for additional crew monitoring of the exit row area.

ASRS:1776093.n: Today I used new temperature check system. Recommend adding hand sanitizer in this area as the touch pad is a touch point every employee must touch if the bar code doesn't work. Presently no hand sanitizer dispenser is available.
ASRS:1776093.s: A crew member reported that the new temperature check system's touch pad lacks a hand sanitizer dispenser. The reporter recommended adding sanitizer because the pad is a mandatory touch point when the barcode scanner fails.

ASRS:1776098.n: Passengers bag was too large to fit in overhead bin, I advised bag needed to be checked. I noticed the face mask was down and asked her to cover her nose and mouth. She said that her mask just fell down when she sat in her seat. I advised her that her mask had been down since she tried to stow the bag. She started yelling at me and ask if I was the mask police? I said no, but if your mask doesn't fit, I can provide you another mask, she declined. I told the Captain and forward Flight Attendant because the passenger would not comply. Forward Flight Attendant asked passenger if she needed another mask, she complied wearing her own mask. I had to ask the passenger to pull up her mask a second time. When deplaning, passenger had mask down again.
ASRS:1776098.s: A flight attendant reported a passenger refused to keep her face mask on while stowing an oversized bag and yelled at the crew. The passenger eventually complied after the Captain and forward flight attendant intervened, though she lowered her mask again during deplaning.

ASRS:1776099.n: Three passengers boarded with their masks down. I asked them to pull them up. When collecting trash, before door closure, I noticed passenger in XX4 mask down again. I asked her again to pull up mask and advised of policy, she laughed at me, then mocked what I had said. I asked again if she would pull up mask. Then advised the Captain of the interaction since I had to speak to her twice while on ground. Passenger in YY3 had mask down for second time in cruise when I collected trash after service. He claimed he was forgetful. XX4 passenger played the peek aboo game where she had mask down but each time I approached, before I reached her, would pulled it up. ZZ4 passenger asked me how many times I was going to ask him to pull up his mask. When deplaning, had mask down.
ASRS:1776099.s: Cabin crew reported multiple passengers on a flight failed to keep masks up during ground, cruise, and deplaning phases. One passenger mocked the crew, another played peek-a-boo, and a third questioned the frequency of requests, requiring the Captain to be advised of the interactions.

ASRS:1776102.n: Incident / Discovery: Maintenance work light / flash light found in the the nose landing gear wheel well which resulted in an air return of the aircraft.Aircraft location: Aircraft X B737-800 was located in the parking area at ZZZ Airport.Work Conditions: Night time, outside, no spot lighting or ambient lighting. Sky conditions clear. Temperature 30(s) Fahrenheit.On the night, Coworker and I were assigned to troubleshoot log X 'Unable to access APU bite' Per previous log entry of being suspect, I replaced the R735 relay in the J20 box, took us some time to locate the J20 box and the relay because the WDM and IPC were not clear on the exact location. 2-3 hours to locate on aircraft. This junction box is located behind the L/H rear pressure panel of the nose landing gear box structure. However, access was difficult to the box from the nose landing gear area due to the angle of access and aircraft height. In turn, I climbed into the E/E bay with a blue hand light, head lamp and a No. 2 Philips screw driver, maneuvered/positioned myself over the flight deck air supply duct along the left side of the nose wheel box structure to get better access to the J20 cover, Relay 735 and associated cannon plug for troubleshooting purposes. Coworker was in support from the nose landing gear wheel well to hand me various items I needed to work through the access structure.As documented in the log, the relay did not correct the issue so we continued to troubleshoot which required continuous access to the J20 box. I was mainly working from inside the E/E bay, not from the nose landing gear wheel well.As the night progressed and not finding any faults with the physical wiring, we reported to our lead where we were at. Was told that the aircraft is needed for a flight, document where we were at and close up the aircraft.We headed back out to the aircraft. When we got back to Aircraft X, I double checked the APU ECU security, checked the aft cargo bay for equipment and tools, closed the aft cargo bay door. I then proceeded into the E/E bay to secure the J20 box cover and check for security and check for tools and equipment. As I was doing this, Coworker was securing the nose landing gear wheel well pressure panel.After Coworker finished installing the panel, I went inside the flight deck to re-engage two circuit breakers and to pressurize the aircraft for the leak check of the pressure panel. Once pressurized, Lead performed the leak check of the pressure panel. When leak check was satisfactory, I depressurized the aircraft, powered down, closed the main cabin door and pulled the air stairs. Shortly after we met in the vehicle we had and began going over paper work.Coworker and I are somewhat new to avionics and have a lot to learn about the various differences between our fleet types and associated details of each. We are very capable of doing the work but would feel more comfortable to be paired with someone who is well seasoned in the avionics shop. It should be this way for anyone that is new. Since I have been in the shop, I have been paired mainly with inexperienced technicians who are learning the same way as I am, learn as you go. Common sense would dictate to pair a very experienced tech with a inexperienced tech, this promotes growth, development and prevents mistakes.I'm sorry that this unfortunate mistake took place and is an oversight I strive to never let happen, unfortunately it did. I will be much more vigilant in the future about tooling and equipment used for aircraft maintenance to make sure this will never happen on my end again. My co-worker and I received our assignment to work on the Aircraft X located [in parking], a remote maintenance area (ZZZ). I remember on that day I was closing up a pressure panel at the nose landing gear wheel well and the battery of the octagon light died on me and so I had to use my flash light. Because we have been outside for so long, I was in the rush to get back to the office, which in the process I left the light in the nose wheel well and also I forgot to double check all my tools and I take full responsibility for my actions. Co-worker and I are new to this bid area and every day we are been paired with new people to figure things out on our own. On the day of the event, the working area was pitch black, it was very cold outside, the AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual) was a little confusing, trying to locate this J20 box to change a relay. and when the relay didn't fix the problem, we had to follow the wiring diagram. Everything was overwhelming. But all that been said, I still take a full responsibility for my action and I hope this will not repeat itself again. Thank you.
ASRS:1776102.s: Two mechanics troubleshooting an APU fault on a parked B737-800 left a flashlight in the nose landing gear wheel well, causing an aircraft return. The incident resulted from rushing to close up the aircraft in poor lighting and a lack of experienced supervision.

ASRS:1776112.n: I experienced a loss of full engine power during initial climbout from RWY 32 at ZZZ. I had the student notify Tower we wanted to return for landing. We were still able to climb and engine was running smoothly so I wanted to keep as low key as possible. When asked by tower we did not request assistance and did not require priority handling. We climbed to approximately 1,000 feet AGL as we entered left downwind. Just past abeam approach end of RWY 32 while on downwind engine experienced further reduction in power without moving throttle. I told Tower we were turning base at that time, added 10 degrees flaps and aimed for the approach end of RWY 32. As we rolled onto final there was a business jet in position for takeoff on the runway. I heard the Tower clear him for an immediate takeoff, then tell him to abort and hold position. The Controller then advised me they could not issue a landing clearance. I responded that I had to land and Controller told me about the jet in position. I replied that I observed the traffic and would maneuver to pass to the right so I would not overfly the jet, and come in around and land in front of him. I flew a few hundred feet to the right at approximately 300 feet AGL, did not fly over the jet and passed well clear of him holding in position. I then slipped the aircraft into the left crosswind, lined up and landed on Runway 32 about 1,500 feet down the runway. The engine was generating enough power to taxi and I utilized Taxiway XX and called ground control when instructed for taxi back to ramp. When I reviewed the event, I believe I incorrectly assumed that the tower controller was providing me priority handling, when in fact the Controller was not fully aware of my situation. I should have just requested priority handling either prior to or as I turned downwind so Controller knew not to have the jet line up and wait on the runway before me.
ASRS:1776112.s: The pilot experienced engine power loss during climbout from RWY 32 at ZZZ and returned for a landing. The pilot attributed the runway conflict with a business jet to failing to explicitly request priority handling, which allowed the controller to clear the jet for takeoff before realizing the emergency.

ASRS:1776126.n: Practicing landings and flight pattern. As practicing the landing I was told to pull quickly for the flare process of the plane and caused a miscommunication as to pull on the yolk quicker. With the miscommunication caused the airplane to balloon and land on the nose wheel hard and causing internal damage to the nose wheel internals, ripping almost all the screws off the nose wheel screws keeping it attached to the plane. After the incident the instructor took control of the plane and went on a go-around and landed the plane with the nose being as high off ground as possible. I was instructing my student on landing, focusing on the timing of flaring. He flared too much, which made him balloon. And to correct for it, he pushed down on the control to bring the nose down and landed nose first. The process was too quick for me to intervene. I heard a cracking sound as the nose wheel touched down on the runway. I executed a go around and made a soft field landing, wheelbarrowing the plane all the way down to the taxiway connected to our flight school's entrance. When I exited the plane, I visibly verified that the nose strut was sitting abnormally. I alerted our maintenance tech, who has verified that the nose strut was damaged.
ASRS:1776126.s: An instructor and student practicing landings experienced a nose-wheel hard landing after the student flared too much and overcorrected, causing the aircraft to balloon and strike the runway nose-first. The impact damaged the nose strut internals, prompting a go-around and a subsequent soft-field landing to taxi the aircraft for maintenance inspection.

ASRS:1776144.n: After landing when I requested that I be able to keep the same squawk for convenience as I was dropping two people off and continuing on VFR, the Tower Controller ask if I heard him calling us. I said no, due to Approach Controller keeping us on their frequency. As we are a helicopter and we are given clearances like 'landing at the ramp is at own risk' it can be confusing as to a clearance to land. I thought I was given a clearance to land. I'm not sure if it is due to COVID and staffing issues but it seems like I hear more ATC frequencies managed by one person, so this could have led to confusion during frequency changes.
ASRS:1776144.s: A helicopter pilot reported confusion during the landing phase when the Tower Controller asked if they heard a call, which the pilot missed due to remaining on Approach frequency. The pilot attributed the communication gap to potential staffing issues and noted ambiguity regarding landing clearances for helicopters.

ASRS:1776162.n: Many of our fellow pilots have said to me that many pilots and others have been affected by COVID in one way or another, either necessitating quarantine or even hospitalization. Further, and in particularly our fleet, there is a disruption to the training schedules due to a lack of instructors, hence little, if any continuity. Have the Union and the Company considered shutting down for another month as the surge upon surge rages? There's no need to rush training if pilots will go non-current without the additional flying. Plus an additional month might get us to the beginning of a vaccination.I don't know if I have missed communications or not from the Union or the Company, but what is the plan for vaccinating pilots or other front line employees? Is there a timetable? Where do we stand in the national 'Phase 1' rollout? Has an update to the memorandum on pay during COVID sick leave been considered? Specifically, what happens to the pilot who receives round 1 or 2 of the vaccination and has to call in sick due to side effects. What happens to a pilot who has adverse side effects which lead to LTD? Could this pilot apply for the new LTD benefits and not wait until month X? Is a pilot required to take the vaccination? If yes, what happens if he declines? Where will pilots get the vaccination? Does a pilot have to wait until the Company procures the vaccine? What has FAA medical said about any of this?
ASRS:1776162.s: Pilots reported that COVID-19 has disrupted training schedules due to instructor shortages and raised concerns about vaccination plans, sick leave pay, and long-term disability benefits. The reporter questioned whether the company should pause operations to allow for vaccination rollout and sought clarification on mandatory vaccination policies and FAA medical guidance.

ASRS:1776166.n: Briefed the ILS 26L IAH prior to top of descent (DRLLR 5). Center delayed our descent due to traffic. When descent clearance was given, told to maintain 310 kts. or greater. We were already over 6,000 ft. above descent profile. We were able to get back on profile just prior to approach handoff. When switched to Approach Control, they told us to expect RNAV Y 26R. After positive aircraft transfer control, I loaded the RNAV 26R and briefed the approach. We were expecting vectors to final RNAV Y 26R. I became PF (Pilot Flying) again. We were still descending on the arrival passing through approximately 8,000 ft. and 6 miles from SKLER when approach cleared us the RNAV Y 26R approach. We then realized the RNAV approach started at SKLER and included an arc segment to final. The Captain reloaded the approach with the SKLER transition. As we approached SKLER, everything looked good as we accomplished approach procedures. Autopilot was still engaged. Approaching DRKAR, we were expecting the aircraft to start a right hand turn on the arc. It didn't turn as we continued straight ahead. Captain said we need to turn as I selected HDG SEL (Heading Select) to start a right hand turn on the arc. We were a couple seconds late to start the turn. At this time ATC said we were late on the turn and gave us vectors to intercept visual [Runway] 26R. Visual approach and landing were uneventful. We debriefed after block in and recreated load the FMC. Although the arc portion showed on the route, there was also a vectors line after DRKAR. We think this is why the aircraft didn't turn on the arc and maybe we needed to sequence the FMC.
ASRS:1776166.s: The crew flying an IAH arrival experienced a missed FMC arc turn at DRKAR while executing the RNAV Y 26R approach. They believe the autopilot failed to turn because the FMC displayed a vectors line after the waypoint, requiring manual heading selection and subsequent ATC vectors for a visual landing.

ASRS:1776188.n: Need more space to accommodate 6 feet apart. On this day, [it] was very chaotic during the international check-in. We are really short of manpower to accommodate document checking. Violating the safety standards for us the employees and the customers. Please review cameras to see the amount of people in the same area. I was scheduled to work lobby for international flights to help them to check in and check their requirement COVID-19 for every single customer. At the kiosk I realized that it was around 200 people and only 2 agents were scheduled to work that area. I was very concerned about safety and health of myself and others because there was no social distancing and not following CDC guidelines. I talked with Supervisor and asked to please call a union representative. To see the unsafe conditions that the company is operating. I hope you will be able to see the cameras in order to understand the horrible situation.I think all the authorities including health department will be concerned about this very important issue.
ASRS:1776188.s: A ground staff member reported unsafe conditions during international check-in where 200 passengers were served by only two agents, violating CDC social distancing guidelines. The employee cited severe manpower shortages and chaotic crowds as the cause, requesting union representation and camera review to document the health hazard.

ASRS:1776224.n: ZZZ based Flight Attendant (FA) A was coughing during pre-flight and during the flight commenting about a sinus/cold issues. She accomplished her boarding / pre-departure duties. FA E advised that FA A was feeling ill due to cold, sinus, headache and now running a fever. (unverified) and that the FA A had taken a cabin seat and was attempting to rest. Dispatcher was notified via SATCOM and advised that FA A was feeling ill, running fever and that I was requesting a Manager meet the flight. I inquired if COVID (rapid) testing was available (due to current world events) for FA A upon arrival at ZZZ. Dispatcher respond that ZZZ did not have rapid testing and Customer Service Manager (CSR) would meet the flight. Upon arrival, the flight was met by 2 CSRs and they were briefed. I also spoke with the ZZZ Chief Pilot on the phone, post flight.
ASRS:1776224.s: A Flight Attendant on a ZZZ-based flight became ill with fever and sinus issues during the flight and rested in a cabin seat. The Captain notified the dispatcher, who arranged for Customer Service Managers to meet the aircraft upon arrival for briefing.

ASRS:1776265.n: We were cleared for takeoff. We set takeoff power and started our takeoff roll. At around 80 KTS the center runway red warning lights came on indicating another plane was on the runway. We queried ATC and they aborted our takeoff.
ASRS:1776265.s: The flight crew aborted takeoff at 80 KTS after center runway red warning lights indicated another aircraft was on the runway. ATC confirmed the obstruction and instructed the crew to stop the takeoff roll.

ASRS:1776271.n: Change in maintenance procedures after servicing or replacement of parts in the hydraulic systems.I was flying with LCA (name deleted) for my Latin America route qualification, to finish the Captain Upgrade syllabus. We got a late start because of our gate being occupied by another aircraft experiencing maintenance issues. Once we received our airplane X and performed all associated preflight flows, briefings, and checklists we pushed about an hour behind schedule. I noticed that a leaky valve on the Yellow hydraulic system was replaced and a RON check had been performed that morning. Taxi, take off from runway XX and the initial climb up through FL180 was normal. Somewhere around FL200 the ECAM flashed a message, too quick for us to see what it was, about 30 seconds later it flashed again, and then another 2-3 times before the ECAM Message stayed displayed, hydraulic Y RSVR LOW LVL. I was Pilot Flying, and called for ECAM actions. LCA (name deleted) performed the ECAM actions and then consulted the COM for further instruction. At this time we were nearing our cruise altitude of FL330. I remained in control of the aircraft and ATC communications while LCA (name deleted) contacted maintenance through ACARS about our issue. Dispatch and Maintenance both confirmed that a return back to ZZZ was the best course of action. I requested a return to ZZZ with ZZZ1 center and stated we had hydraulic issues. Center Cleared us back to ZZZ via direct ZZZ and the ZZZ Arrival. The next communication with ZZZ1 I declared an emergency to get services in place for our arrival. I proceeded to load the MCDU for our return to ZZZ. LCA (name deleted) kept in communication with Maintenance and Dispatch during this time. LCA (name deleted) also gave the TEST briefing to the lead Flight Attendant (FA), and made all PA's in both English and Spanish to the passengers. Once we were established back towards ZZZ and we were caught up on our duties, I briefed the arrival and approach, we both discussed outcomes of the landing to be prepared for anything that may arise with our associated failure. The loss of the Yellow hydraulic system would require us to bring the airplane to a complete stop on the runway because of the loss of Nose Wheel Steering. LCA (name deleted) calculated a landing distance assessment, and went through the procedure for an overweight landing. LCA (name deleted) took over control of the aircraft on the arrival because he has been flying recently and I haven't had a landing in the plane in 3.5 months, My most recent experience was a warm up and PC the week prior. The arrival, approach, and landing were normal. We landed and stopped on the runway XX, called for 'flight attendant stations', Crash fire rescue inspected the exterior of the aircraft, and confirmed no hot spots. Once given the all clear, the 'remain seated' announcement was made, we completed the landing checklist, shut down both engines with the APU running so the ground crew could hook up and tow the aircraft to the gate. Once hooked up we were towed to Gate XX where we then deplaned and talked with maintenance about our issue.I believe the RA's functioned abnormally due to their antenna's prolonged exposure to snowy and icy conditions on the runway, taxiway, and ramp at ZZZ airport. I suggest an advisory could be sent out to keep the crews from being startled when this occurs in the conditions explained above. However, remind the aircrews to still comply with the terrain warning, whether it's an erroneous warning or not.
ASRS:1776271.s: The Captain and First Officer experienced a Yellow hydraulic reservoir low level warning at FL200 following a valve replacement, causing an emergency return to ZZZ. The crew landed safely with an overweight landing, though the reporter incorrectly attributed the issue to RA antenna exposure to snow and ice.

ASRS:1776272.n: Have more of a warning from ATC of the turbulence expected to encounter. We did not know of the severity of the turbulence until we were in it ourselves. Experienced continuous moderate turbulence between 8,000 feet to 3,000 feet on descent on the RNAV arrival. We landed without incident.
ASRS:1776272.s: The flight crew encountered continuous moderate turbulence between 8,000 and 3,000 feet during descent on the RNAV arrival. They attributed the lack of preparation to insufficient ATC warnings regarding the expected severity, though the aircraft landed without incident.

ASRS:1776276.n: Be fast to recognize an air quality event.I was flying an A320 from ZZZ to ZZZ1. During the arrival we had an air quality event. The estimated duration of the event was 5 minutes. During the event the power levels did not change. I have experienced this in the same type of aircraft before. There was no evidence of smoke or fire in the cockpit and it was localized. The odor smelled like dirty socks and were mild. It was only in the cockpit. During the time of event, our air supply was the engines. I was able to turn off Pack 1 and isolate the problem within about 15 seconds. I reserve the right to change my statement as more informant becomes available.
ASRS:1776276.s: The A320 pilot reported a localized air quality event with a mild "dirty socks" odor in the cockpit during arrival. The issue was isolated within 15 seconds by turning off Pack 1 while the aircraft was using engine air supply.

ASRS:1776299.n: Please thank the Customer Service helpers for arriving immediately. 10 minutes prior to departure, the lead Flight Attendant (FA) informed us there was a female passenger who was dizzy and had vomited. The FA was concerned about the passenger's fitness to fly and requested we call for the Customer Service helpers. They arrived and immediately removed the passenger. I suggested to the Gate Agents that they consider calling for Medical Assistance. I discussed the situation with the lead FA and First Officer. The lead FA said the passenger had described a history of kidney illness. We all agreed we had not received any information that would cause us to suspect COVID-19 illness. We departed on time. I described the event to our Dispatcher via ACARS. After arrival, I called the Duty Officer and the Chief Pilot on Duty and reported the event to them.
ASRS:1776299.s: The Captain, First Officer, and Flight Attendants removed a dizzy, vomiting passenger with a history of kidney illness 10 minutes before departure. The crew determined the passenger was not suspected of having COVID-19, and the aircraft departed on time after the incident was reported to operations.

ASRS:1776306.n: We leveled off at about 10,000 ft. after an idle descent from FL350. As engine power came up during the level off, an abrupt strong oil or chemical like smell came from my vents. It definitely got my attention, immediately. I donned my O2 mask right away. I was Pilot Flying and called for the fumes procedure. I took my mask off briefly, a few mins after the procedure was done to see if fumes were still present. It appeared to have fully dissipated by that time. We checked with the FA crew, they did not report any the odor/fume. We continued the descent and approach into ZZZ without any further issue. On the ground, the Captain and I talked to the on Duty Chief Pilot and did not require any medical assistance. Wrote up the event in the MX log and odor/fume reporting sheet.
ASRS:1776306.s: The Pilot Flying reported a strong chemical smell from the vents during level-off at 10,000 ft after descent from FL350. The crew executed the fumes procedure, donned oxygen masks, and continued to ZZZ without medical assistance after the odor dissipated.

ASRS:1776315.n: After landing and during rollout on RW (Runway) XXR, we were instructed to 'make left turn if able and hold short of [Runway] XXL, then notify if gate was open'. As PF (Pilot Flying), I had already briefed during approach briefing that we would likely make left turn on [Taxiway] XX then hold short of [Runway] XXL to await further taxi instructions. As we decelerated and approached [Taxiway] XX, we noticed another airplane on Taxiway XY (around [Taxiway] XZ) facing east. We were initially uncertain if it was holding or continuing east so we were going to skip [Taxiway] XX and make next left. ATC stated that they were holding for us, so we made the turn on [Taxiway] XX. As we exited the RW (Runway), the CA (Captain) continued taxiing to cross RW (Runway) XXL even though we had been told to hold short. We were across the hold short lines when I queried him about holding short, but I was late in warning him to avoid the confusion and mistake of going so far. At same time, an airplane had rotated for takeoff on RW (Runway) XXL just prior to our position making it a more serious event. ATC never said anything to us as the event happened or immediately after, so I asked them if we should continue across RW (Runway) XXL. They replied in the affirmative and to contact Ground Control after exiting on other side. At no time did ATC comment on the event. We continued to the gate without further incident.Contributing factors were the confusion about the intention of the aircraft on Taxiway XY near the [Taxiway] XX exit we were instructed to use, the short distance between the parallel runways, and lack of coordinated and deliberate attention to the immediate situation we were in. I failed to give the CA a reminder we had been instructed to hold short of RW (Runway) XXL prior to him crossing the hold short lines. Neither of us confirmed both directions were clear prior to crossing even though it is SOP to do so and we had consistently been doing that up to that point. He said during our debrief he had momentarily looked down at his taxi diagram to confirm location of the potential crossing taxiways we might use before realizing too late we had taxied over the lines. I had also momentarily diverted my attention to try to contact ramp (per ATC's request about our gate availability), while assuming the CA had heard the hold short instructions and would comply. Again, we had already briefed this likelihood of taxi route and necessity of holding short of and eventual crossing of RW (Runway) XXL during the arrival/approach briefing during descent into ZZZ area. I had never received a query from ATC about gate availability in ZZZ, even though it's common procedure at other airports. Therefore, it affected my normal after-landing expectations and flow. That's not an excuse, but was definitely a factor.Weather was not a factor, nor was the lighting due to being midday. I don't believe fatigue or other physiological factors contributed either. CAVU. RNAV [Runway] XXR. FO (First Officer) was PF (Pilot Flying). Upon landing standard transfer of controls on roll out. I planned on exiting [Taxiway] XZ to [Taxiway] XY to get behind a Airbus on [Taxiway] XY. ATC states 'exit [Taxiway] XX hold short of [Runway] XXL on [Taxiway] XX' (and gate status I think). The Airbus on [Taxiway] XY held short of [Taxiway] XX as directed by ATC. As we were in front of the Airbus as directed (on [Taxiway] XX) I was looking at chart and outside to see which way [Taxiway] XX veered (it looks like it veers left or right and is a wide taxiway). I was quickly comparing real life view to the chart diagram. As I was at that point we had already passed the hold short line. It then realized it and stopped. My FO asked 'if it's okay to cross [Runway] XXL', ATC cleared us across [Runway] XXL at [Taxiway] XX left on [Taxiway] XA. All the while ATC communication was busy with the changing of our exiting directions to switching to ground. I have been to ZZZ multiple times before although I was unclear of how [Taxiway] XX is setup and viewed in real life. I was shocked what I had accidentally allowed to happen. I deviated from my exiting plan and slightly rushed thus missed seeing the HS (Hold Short) line and my situational awareness. I am at 100% fault in not continuing to [Taxiway] XZ as planned, taking on the slightly rushed exit, and most certainly not stopping as directed. I am still criticizing myself as I write this. I can guarantee that I will be more diligent and aware of actual versus chart of my location at all times.
ASRS:1776315.s: The First Officer and Captain crossed the hold short line of Runway XXL during rollout after exiting Runway XXR, nearly colliding with a departing aircraft. The incident resulted from the Captain's distraction with a taxi chart, the First Officer's delayed reminder, and confusion regarding another aircraft's position.

ASRS:1776326.n: Passenger X (seated in X1) boarded the aircraft with a small cup of coffee and a bag of cheez-itz. He took an excessive amount of time sipping the coffee and eating the snack, keeping his mask off for most of the flight. Whenever I passed through the cabin I would notice his mask off and when I approached him he would take a sip of coffee. He had his mask off this way from the safety demo to the initial descent. When we started our initial descent I walked through the cabin to collect trash and he appeared to be asleep with his eyes closed and his mask off. I woke him up and instructed him to wear his mask over his nose and mouth. He seemed to be doing everything he could to circumvent wearing his mask properly the entire flight.
ASRS:1776326.s: A cabin crew member reported that a passenger in seat X1 repeatedly removed his mask to eat and drink from boarding through initial descent. The crew member woke the passenger during descent and instructed him to wear his mask properly after observing him attempting to circumvent the requirement.

ASRS:1776333.n: While unloading Aircraft X a BE-1900C in ZZZ1, I discovered HAZMAT that had not been declared to the crew. The HAZMAT was a 'Battery, wet filled with acid' UN2794, class 8. The HAZMAT had the appropriate paperwork, but the pilot notification paperwork was not completed, nor was the crew notified. Appropriate company management personnel were notified and a SMS was completed.
ASRS:1776333.s: During unloading of a BE-1900C at ZZZ1, ground personnel discovered undeclared wet acid batteries (UN2794) with missing pilot notification paperwork. Company management was notified and a Safety Management System report was completed.

ASRS:1776345.n: While in the downwind leg of the pattern working with a student, Tower cleared our aircraft number one for touch and go on. They also directed an RV9 to enter left base. The RV9 was asked to report us in sight. After several moments, they reported us in sight and Tower cleared them number two to land. We then turned base and the RV9 turned base inside of us. When we rolled our wings level, tower called the RV9 to tell them they had turned inside of our turn. The RV9 was then cleared to land number one, however, he had already entered an evasive 180 degree turn to his right and when I gained visual contact again, he was directly above us with less than 200 feet separation. We were unable to maneuver evasively at our low altitude but he was able to pass over us with no further conflict.
ASRS:1776345.s: A pilot instructing a student on a touch-and-go was cleared number one while an RV9 entered left base. The RV9 turned inside the pilot's base turn, prompting an evasive 180-degree right turn that resulted in less than 200 feet vertical separation as the RV9 passed overhead.

ASRS:1776382.n: Volume during this session was not particularly high, but complexity and workload changed quickly, and a sequence of events took my attention away from aircraft that didn't need much of it, including the aircraft in question. Aircraft X descending into ZZZ. My initial descent clearance was to 15,000 ft. An eastbound departure was potentially in conflict with 3 other aircraft, including Aircraft X. Deconflicting this aircraft took much of my attention during this time. Aircraft X ended up being no factor. Once clear of all other aircraft, I gave Aircraft X descent clearance to 11,000 ft. Read back was not as clear as I thought, but I had other things to worry about, including two aircraft simultaneously calling for VFR flight following and a conflict alert between VFR aircraft I was providing flight following to and a Mode-C intruder which took much of my attention because they were tracking to pass about 1 mile apart and the Mode-C intruder was climbing into the other VFR aircraft. Once that situation cleared up and as Aircraft X was descending through 12,000 ft. I received a call from FSS (Flight Service Station) which I decided to answer on the assumption that it would be a faster phone call than it turned out to be.Their request was for a Special VFR departure (SVFR). I had to take time to verify that SVFR was possible from this airport and since SVFR is a very rare request in my area of specialization I then had to look up the phraseology to give the clearance. By the time the clearance was delivered and read back, at least 2 minutes had passed. As I disconnected the FSS call, Low Altitude Alert showed Aircraft X at 7,900 ft., descending below the MIA (Minimum IFR Altitude) of 8,000 ft. I immediately issued a low altitude alert with a clearance to climb to 10,000 ft. immediately. After the pilot responded I advised the pilot that his descent clearance had been to 11,000 ft. and asked if he had ZZZ in sight. Pilot responded that he had the field in sight. I cleared Aircraft X for a visual approach and gave instructions to contact Tower. It did not appear that he observed the climb clearance that accompanied the Low Altitude Alert, and the aircraft was at 7,300 ft. when I cleared Aircraft X for a visual approach.It is difficult to recommend any actions or changes to prevent re occurrence. This particular sector is quite complex, with high terrain, military airspace, two approach control facilities, arrivals to and departures from ZZZ1 in all directions. Convergence between ZZZ arrivals/departures to the south of ZZZ and ZZZ1 arrivals/departures to the southeast of ZZZ1. Also ZZZ2 arrivals and departures to the northwest of ZZZ2 all come together in the vicinity of ZZZ3. Also several satellite airports where pilots cannot reach us on the ground resulting in FSS relays. 11 adjacent sectors adjusted for typical sector configuration with multiple combined but the actual number of individual adjacent sectors is much higher and a relatively heavy VFR workload. It can unexpectedly become quite busy, even with a small number of aircraft in the sector. When this happens, it usually entails coordination calls from one or both of the approach control facilities, the military controlling agency, FSS, and one of the 11 adjacent sectors, and often includes aircraft that require a higher-than-normal workload. The timing of these factors is not controllable, so when several things happen at once, it usually can't be predicted, it can become difficult to manage, and it's often over before a D-side (Radar Assist) can make it to the sector to help.
ASRS:1776382.s: An air traffic controller managing Aircraft X's descent into ZZZ issued a low altitude alert after the aircraft descended below 8,000 ft MIA due to the controller's distraction by a complex FSS call and other conflicts. The controller subsequently cleared the aircraft for a visual approach after the pilot confirmed the field was in sight.

ASRS:1776386.n: Aircraft X entered a terrain area at 7,200 ft. with a Minimum IFR Altitude (MIA) of 7,400 ft. Aircraft X was cleared for the RNAV [Runway] XX approach. Aircraft X executed the missed approach. Aircraft X requested vectors for the RNAV [Runway] XX Approach. I issued a turn 30 degrees left when able direct to the Initial Approach Fix (IAF) and notify me when he was direct. Aircraft X reported they were ready for the approach clearance. I issued '[Aircraft X] maintain seven thousand until established. Cleared RNAV approach Runway XX at ZZZ.' Aircraft X read back the correct clearance.Aircraft X continued on their heading past the IAF without beginning a procedure turn for the approach. I was busy with multiple requests from other aircraft and fighters departing a military base for active Warning Areas. And didn't notice Aircraft X missed the fix. I was giving a relief briefing and noticed Aircraft X was not on his cleared route. I asked him where he was heading. Aircraft X stated he was waiting for vectors to the approach. I pulled up the MIA's and noticed he was about to enter a 7,400 ft. MIA block. I issued a safety alert for the terrain and climbed Aircraft X to 8,000 ft.In my scan I knew that Aircraft X was out of position but assumed he was unfamiliar with how to execute the procedure turn at the IAF and was going to get back on a correct course soon. Every time I checked back in my scan he was a bit further off course. The workload was high. Frequency congestion was causing a lot of missed and stepped on clearances further increasing workload. I had requested help from the Controller-in-Charge twice prior to this happening. I needed assistance with a flight break up flight plan and to notify the surrounding facilities the Special Use Airspace went cold. A dedicated D-side (Radar Assist) would have helped notice the aircraft off course.
ASRS:1776386.s: An air traffic controller issued a terrain safety alert and climbed Aircraft X to 8,000 ft after the aircraft entered a 7,400 ft MIA area while executing a missed approach. The controller attributed the oversight to high workload, frequency congestion, and a lack of radar assistance during a relief briefing.

ASRS:1776390.n: There was some confusion going into work as I was notified at XA:00 pm for my XA:30 shift and told not to report to work until XD:45 due to Level 3 cleaning that was taking place. When we arrived at work the control floor was empty and ZAU ARTCC resumed operations at XD:55am with no briefings at all. I was working the MID configuration which includes the following sectors (sector numbers removed) along with the following approach controls (ZZZ1/ZZZ2/ZZZ3/ZZZ4/ZZZ5). During my stint which started at XF:00 am and ending at XI:00 am around XX:50 ZULU I spoke with Aircraft X looking for the ILS to Runway X at ZZZ2. I asked the pilot if he had the current weather at the field along with the NOTAMs and the pilot responded with a yes to the weather and that he had read the NOTAMs yesterday. I then read what I thought was all the pertinent NOTAMs to the aircraft. I vectored Aircraft X for the ILS at ZZZ2 and cleared the aircraft in for the approach. I switched the aircraft to advisories and requested a timely cancellation due to a second aircraft being vectored for the same approach. Aircraft X soon cancelled his IFR and reported a down time along with the condition of the runway and that the ramp area was in a much worse condition. I inadvertently missed the snow removal NOTAM and was later on informed by management that Aircraft X had landed on a runway with snow removal equipment on it. Any usage of the active runway should require call to either the facility or on frequency to prevent any confusion on what is going on at the airport. Any and all NOTAMs that directly effect the runways should be better identified. ZZZ2 had over 15 NOTAMs listed at the airfield which all look identical, if the ones like snow removal were BOLD or even a different color it may help the next person avoid the same mistake I made. I was notified today upon arrival to work that Aircraft X had landed on a runway occupied by snow removal equipment at the time. I was unaware that this had happened. I was working the assist position when the aircraft was cleared for the visual approach. The Radar Controller had issued the weather and read the NOTAMs to the aircraft and neither of us were aware that snow removal was taking place at the airport. The aircraft canceled IFR prior to landing. I was not made aware of the hazardous situation until the following work shift. This is the third report that I have written on this type of event at this airport! Several years ago, I myself had an aircraft execute a missed approach due to snow removal equipment on the same runway. I of course submitted a report detailing the situation and offered recommendations to prevent the situation from occurring again. I received no feedback. I told my Operations Manager, who was aware of the incident, and was dismissed. I then took it to the local safety council who actually looked into it. However, after some time I was informed that the current procedures would remain in effect. No definite reason was given. If a runway is possibly occupied by snow removal equipment, an aircraft should not be cleared for an approach. Having an aircraft switch frequencies to contact the snow removal crew themselves to land obviously has many drawbacks. The snow removal crew should simply notify the control facility prior to entering the runway. ATC could then close the runway until notified that the snow removal crew has exited the runway. This could be done by radio or phone, thus preventing the situations that have previously occurred.
ASRS:1776390.s: An air traffic controller cleared Aircraft X for an ILS approach to Runway X at ZZZ2, inadvertently missing a snow removal NOTAM among over 15 identical entries. The aircraft landed on the active runway while snow removal equipment was present, a hazardous situation the controller was unaware of until the following shift.

ASRS:1776398.n: ATC assigned a vector '[Heading] 140 and maintain 3,000 ft. until established on localizer....' As Pilot Monitoring I heard the vector and maintain 2,000 ft. until established. Captain heard 2,000 ft. as well and entered 2,000 ft. I read back 2,000 ft. to the controller. The Captain briefed and all checklist items were briefed prior to this event. The Captain flew through the localizer due to his failure to move the localizer frequency from Standby to Primary. He quickly recognized it and visually maneuvered aircraft back toward course. We received a Terrain Alert and we discussed to shallow our intercept angle. The course was intercepted safely. The controller transmitted that the altitude was 3,000 ft. until established. We were at approximately 2,000 ft. at that time. I transmitted that we had heard '2,000 ft. until established' and read that back to him earlier. We maintained 2,000 ft. until glideslope intercept. We landed uneventfully. Beautiful day, 30 mile visibility, clear skies, airport in sight 30 miles away. Routine departure from ZZZ. At altitude, we were given direct to a fix and descend to 3,000 ft. Approaching the fix estimating 5,000 ft. altitude ATC gave us a clearance: 'Left turn of (EST) about 30 degrees and intercept localizer' which was inside of the fix 'and descend to 2,000 ft.' The First Officer clearly repeated to ATC '2,000 ft.' and no ATC correction was said. I set 2,000 ft. in the altitude alerter and pointed at it until the First Officer repeated '2,000 ft. A slight north wind caused my track just slightly south of center line of final, well within reason, estimate one dot right. As I was correcting and back on centerline the GPWS (Ground Proximity Warning) sounded, when back on center line the GPWS stopped. The hill was always in sight and we were never left of center line, never was there any danger. At that moment ATC asked if we had the airport in sight and we said yes. ATC cleared us for a visual approach to the runway and said our clearance was only to 3,000 ft. Uneventful landing. I clearly heard and after discussion, the First Officer also clearly heard '2,000 ft.""
ASRS:1776398.s: The flight crew descended to 2,000 ft instead of the assigned 3,000 ft due to a misheard ATC clearance, triggering a GPWS alert during localizer interception. The controller clarified the altitude restriction, but the crew maintained 2,000 ft until glideslope intercept and completed an uneventful landing.

ASRS:1776425.n: I notified my lead before departure that there was low visibility due to the jet bridge placement. He asked me if he wanted me to push or if he wanted me to push it. I told him I would wing walk. Once he gave us the clear to push signal, he almost immediately began to push the plane before the wing walker opposite to me could make sure traffic was stopped. A pick up truck with a plow was going, probably too fast, down the vehicle service road. The opposite wing walker was waving his hands and wands to get the trucks attention. The plow got stopped finally nearly once he got to the line of the envelope. The back of the truck went up in the air as he stopped due to how fast he was going and how fast he stopped. By the time the truck stopped the entire tail of the aircraft was in the vehicle service road.
ASRS:1776425.s: During pushback, a ground handler began moving the aircraft before the opposite wing walker could stop a speeding plow truck. The truck stopped abruptly near the aircraft envelope, causing its rear to lift while the aircraft's tail entered the vehicle service road.

ASRS:1776435.n: Aircraft X arrived. As reported before, this aircraft's aft cargo pit mechanical loading system is inoperative, causing the ramp crews assigned to have to manually unload thousands of pounds of cargo loaded onto pallets that the equipment is specifically designed to move. This continues to create an unsafe environment as the crews are moving individual pallets weighing thousands of pounds, up to one piece listed at 9427 lbs. These loads were never meant to be muscled by ramp service employees while inside the aircraft. It's irresponsible to continue to use this aircraft and expect people to put themselves in danger. The danger, as always, lies in requiring employees to manually move thousands of pounds they were NEVER intended to move that exposes them to injury in multiple ways. The very floor of the cargo pit isn't specifically designed for walking and moving loads as they have MANY trip hazards opening employees up to MORE injury. Again, it's VERY irresponsible to continue to use this broken aircraft. It NEEDS to be removed from service.
ASRS:1776435.s: Ramp crews manually unloaded heavy cargo pallets, including one weighing 9,427 lbs, from Aircraft X's aft cargo pit due to an inoperative mechanical loading system. The reporter states this created an unsafe environment with trip hazards and injury risks, urging the aircraft be removed from service.

ASRS:1776444.n: During initial taxi out and under the direction of the marshaller our right main landing gear departed the paved surface and became stuck in the grass. The airport diagram does not accurately depict the taxiway layout and I did not realize how close the landing gear was to the edge of the pavement after push back. It was very dark and perhaps the marshaller could not see that either. I followed marshaling signals up until the event took place. During initial taxi after push back, we were being directed by marshaller and our right main departed the paved surface and was stuck in the grass. I believe the cause of the event was being pushed back to close to the edge of the taxiway, very dark ramp and the airport diagram doesn't accurately depict layout. I could not see how close to the edge of the taxiway we were and possibly the ground crew either. In the future, I will be more vigilant to dark areas and better lighting on the ramp will assist.
ASRS:1776444.s: During initial taxi in dark conditions, the pilot followed marshaller signals but the right main landing gear departed the pavement and became stuck in grass. The pilot attributed the incident to being pushed back too close to the edge, poor lighting, and an inaccurate airport diagram.

ASRS:1776501.n: Air return to ZZZ due to strong odor and haze entering the cockpit and cabin through the air system. This occurred right after takeoff. After running the appropriate checklists, were vectored back around and landed and taxied without incident back to the gate. We were deiced prior to the flight. Caused by fumes entering the cockpit and cabin.
ASRS:1776501.s: The crew returned to ZZZ shortly after takeoff due to strong odor and haze entering the cockpit and cabin through the air system. The flight landed safely, with the reporter attributing the incident to fumes entering the aircraft after deicing.

ASRS:1776503.n: Aircraft X was leaving late. Four Company aircraft were leaving DTW around the same time with very similar call signs. To be exact, Company, Aircraft Y, Aircraft Z, and Aircraft A were also leaving. Meanwhile, the controller working Tower was also working Ground frequency. More than once, aircraft were taking frequency changes for other aircraft. While no serious deviations occurred, my First Officer remarked that both the high workload of the controller and the similarity of call signs could be a number of threats that on a worse day could lead to a serious safety concern. I do agree with him. I think Company has been aware of the issue of similar call signs leaving and arriving at hubs at the same time for a while, but it would require too much work to actually re-work the system to better avoid this issue. I fear that we will have to wait for some serious incidents to have the impetus to actually change this feature of our dispatching. Flight Planning presumably has a reason for making the flight numbers a particular way.
ASRS:1776503.s: The pilot reported that four Company aircraft with similar call signs departed DTW simultaneously while a controller managed both Tower and Ground frequencies, causing frequency confusion. The crew identified high controller workload and call sign similarity as potential safety threats, fearing systemic changes will only occur after a serious incident.

ASRS:1776509.n: The timing of the situation was ripe for a mistake, as a similar-sounding call sign received the exact type of clearance we would have expected as we approached the end of the runway while I was task saturated with completing the required checklist. Ideally, I would not have misheard the call sign, but ultimately I should have realized my attention had been entirely focused on the checklist, not the radio, and asked Tower for a short delay, clarification, or repeated clearance. We were operating the second leg of the day as Aircraft X from ZZZ to ZZZ1. We were given a short taxi from the terminal to Runway XXR. Approaching the departure end of XXR I switched to Tower frequency while still completing the Before Takeoff Checklist. As we made the turn from B onto B5 and while still finishing the last few steps of the checklist, Tower cleared another aircraft with a similar-sounding call sign, to line up and wait on XXC. I mistakenly thought the line up and wait clearance was for us and read back a clearance to line up and wait on Runway] XXR. Tower did not acknowledge my call, and while the Captain and I both saw an aircraft on final for [Runway] XXR, it appeared there was adequate spacing for the line up and wait clearance to be reasonable. As our aircraft passed the hold short line, Tower cleared the similar call sign for takeoff on XXC. The Captain and I simultaneously realized there had been a possible mix up of call signs. We advised tower we had read back the line up and wait clearance and asked for confirmation that it had been for us. Tower advised that it had not been for us, but cleared us for an immediate takeoff to accommodate the aircraft on final for [Runway] XXR. We immediately transitioned to a rolling takeoff and were able to get airborne before any go-around or other action was required by the aircraft on final. It did not sound right to me when the Tower said to line up and wait, but after the First Officer read back the instructions and the Tower did not correct us we pressed on. Next time I am in a situation that does not feel right, I will stop what I am doing and verify the instructions before taking the runway.We were taxiing to Runway XXR in ZZZ.
