As we were approaching the hold short line we heard the instruction to line up and wait. The First Officer read back 'Aircraft X line up and wait XXR.' Both of us looked at final approach and saw an aircraft on approximately a 5 mile final, I verified this with my MFD. As we turned on to the runway the Tower cleared an aircraft for takeoff that had a very similar call sign as ours. At this point, I verified our instructions to lineup and wait. Tower said that he did not clear us to line up and wait. The Controller immediately cleared us for takeoff and so we took off.
ASRS:1776509.s: Pilots of Aircraft X mistakenly read back a line-up and wait clearance for Runway XXR intended for a similar-sounding call sign while task-saturated with checklists. After realizing the error, Tower cleared them for an immediate rolling takeoff, allowing them to depart safely before the aircraft on final required a go-around.

ASRS:1776515.n: We taxied out single engine. There was some distraction/discussion on taxi out regarding a large brush fire burning to the east of the airport. Upon turning north to Runway XXL we noticed Aircraft Y holding short of the runway. There was some discussion of the aircraft as we had a similar setup the day prior in ZZZ and it changed up the departure sequence and we had to maneuver around that aircraft. As we neared the runway the Tower then cleared as for departure without delay as there was another aircraft on final. We lined up on the runway and as I added power I noted the asymmetrical thrust. I rejected the takeoff and advised Tower. After clearing the runway we started the second engine and completed the takeoff without incident.In my opinion we developed some expectation coupled with distraction that it may be a bit before we departed. This must have pulled my mind from the task at hand (starting the second engine). With the Tower then expediting our departed we switched into a rushed sequence that resulted in the error of not starting the second engine. The other aircraft and the aircraft on final also pulled my eyes and attention outside the aircraft more than usual.In hindsight and trying to examine why this happened I have also had some personal distractions that could have been a casual factor in contributing to my lack of focus. This was my first trip after recovery from a moderate case of COVID as well as an [another personal issue.] While I can say these weren't outwardly conveyed or discussed they were heavy on my mind. We taxied out to XXL from the gate single engine. On the way we noticed a big smoke plume and also saw a fire truck spraying water on field which was unrelated. When we turned on bravo away from view of the smoke we noticed Aircraft Y awaiting takeoff similar to yesterday at what appeared to be the end of the runway. We couldn't tell they were at the intersection prior until we were upon them. I was looking at them when Tower cleared us onto the runway. I read the line up and wait back and instinctively started my before takeoff flows. Notifying the flight attendants, transponder and to config. As I read that checklist ATC interrupted and said cleared for takeoff. I read that back then restarted the checklist and finished it. The captain added power and immediately rejected. We notified ATC and exited the runway. We then started the engine and ran the checklists from there and resumed the flight.
ASRS:1776515.s: The crew taxied single-engine and rejected takeoff after applying asymmetric thrust due to distraction from a nearby fire, other aircraft, and personal issues. They subsequently started the second engine and completed the departure without incident.

ASRS:1776545.n: Enroute we heard a company flight with a very similar callsign on same frequency. Center notified us that the company these two similar callsigns on the same route at the same exact time every day. Similar callsigns increase workload unnecessarily. No deviations happened as a result of similar callsigns.Company should review similar callsigns and assign [different] numbers during forecasted conflicts like before.
ASRS:1776545.s: Pilots reported hearing a company flight with a similar callsign on the same frequency enroute. Center confirmed the daily conflict, noting that while no deviations occurred, the similar callsigns unnecessarily increased workload.

ASRS:1776554.n: From Captain X - 'When I approached the gate for my flight the boarding agent was talking on the phone. As a courtesy I waited until he was off the phone to identify myself (as working crew). I overheard his side of the conversation and clearly heard him state that he was (now) aware that the first four rows of coach class could not be occupied due to weight and balance and that he would re-seat the passengers that were booked in those seats. During my FA briefing I said nothing about those seats because there was no mention in my flight release that the first four rows of coach should not be occupied. During pre-flight in the cockpit I called my Dispatcher to ask for additional fuel and an alternate and during this conversation nothing was said about the first four rows of coach not being occupied. We pushed at XA:15Z and got airborne eight minutes later. The closeout had a note about the first four rows not being occupied, but since I recalled the agent saying that he would re-seat the passengers in those rows I did not pursue it any further. After climbing out of ten thousand I called the #1 FA and told him to make sure that no passenger changed their seats to the first 4 rows of coach during the flight and was then told that there were 3 passengers sitting in the first 4 rows of coach. I called my Dispatcher to make sure we were restricted and was told we were. I asked Dispatch to find out why those seats were assigned by the gate agent after I heard the agent acknowledge over the phone that those seats were restricted due to weight and balance and should not be used. I also asked my FA to re-seat the 3 passengers and make sure the first four rows of coach remained unoccupied for the duration of the flight. I don't know why the agent who said he was going to re-seat the passengers didn't do it. The passenger manifest clearly showed that at least one of those 3 passengers was assigned a seat in the first 4 rows of coach by the agent during our boarding process.' To tag along with what Captain X said, the TPS did not have any weight and balance information about seat restrictions. The closeout did, but since Captain X knew that the gate agent knew about it already, we figured no one would be assigned those seats. For some reason, those passengers got assigned those seats, I assume because they were non revs and the gate agent was under pressure to get the flight out so they probably forgot about the restriction. Time pressure, gate agents are under a lot of pressure, and seem understaffed during COVID. Due to this, they should be commended for doing the work that they are. They should be thanked for making sure non revs make it on. The intense amount of pressure agents work under day in and day out, adds up and a mistake is bound to happen. This mistake, although a procedural mistake, was not one of extreme error. The margin of error built into weight and balance is wide. If weight and balance is truly as tight as 3 passengers, the FAA would make sure we weighed every single bag individually and get true cargo weights instead of averaging bag weights. We would also weigh passengers instead of simply assuming there are average summer and winter weights per passenger. The flight was completed successfully, transporting XX or so people across the country.Don't work gate agents so hard. Give them the tools they need to succeed and ease up on micromanaging. Let agents make real decisions and they will feel empowered to complete their tasks, like making sure 4 rows are empty on a flight. I could place the blame on the agent and make a bunch of suggestions and punishments up, but I'm tired of the culture of pitting work group against work group here. This is the only airline I've worked for where this practice is known and visible. We are all working toward the same goal of trying to save the airline industry. Let the agent know of the mistake and move on. We need to work together now more than ever.
ASRS:1776554.s: The Captain and gate agent were involved in a flight where three passengers were seated in restricted coach rows due to weight and balance limits. The agent failed to re-seat them despite acknowledging the restriction, but the crew corrected the seating in-flight and the flight completed successfully.

ASRS:1776557.n: During taxi out for takeoff at ZZZ we received an ACARS message stating that 'the load close out was invalid' and that we must wait for a valid load close. I got distracted and forgot about getting a valid load closeout and we departed and flew uneventfully to ZZZ1. The Captain and I had had a successful trip. We worked well together. This was our last leg home on our last day. We had confidence in each other and perhaps that led to complacency. We had just been delayed at the gate for a COVID concern. I think we had a runway change and I got distracted.Perhaps, in the future, I will Scribble 'void' over the invalid load close out so that we do not mistakenly use it.
ASRS:1776557.s: The First Officer and Captain departed from ZZZ with an invalid load closeout due to distraction and complacency following a gate delay. The flight to ZZZ1 was uneventful, though the crew acknowledged the error and proposed marking invalid documents as 'void' to prevent recurrence.

ASRS:1776560.n: After takeoff we delayed our Tower assigned turn to 120 until reaching1,000 ft. per the company Ops pages. We received a RA (TCAS resolution advisory) at about 1,000-1200 ft. We responded to the RA. Informed the Tower immediately, they did not acknowledge our report and switched us to Departure. After we were cleared of the conflict we noticed an aircraft on the MFD 400 ft. above us. The Tower Controller cleared us for take off with a turn to 120 before we reached the runway, suspect the departure corridor was not clear. Better communication between flight crew and ATC, about traffic awareness in the vicinity of the airport. Departed RWY XXR ZZZ, per company pages started right turn to heading 120 assigned by ATC. Immediately received an RA 'monitor vertical speed' we were climbing at about 1500'/min and v/s (Vertical Speed) tape showed we needed to limit climb to about 200'/min. We pitched over immediately, shortly thereafter we got 'clear of conflict'. All this happened between about 1,500 feet AGL and 3,000 feet. After the RA was complete I noticed traffic on the ND (Navigation Display) about 400 feet above us and slightly behind us. During the event Tower handed us off to Departure, we told him we were responding to an RA. Without any comment he repeated the hand-off to Departure.We were following our assigned clearance. We do not know who the other aircraft was or if they had deviated from their clearance. It all happened very fast at a busy phase of flight. Pull the [Quality Assurance] data for this flight and ATC records to see what caused this event. I believe we got close to this other aircraft but I don't know why. I think it's worth investigating.
ASRS:1776560.s: Flight crew departing RWY XXR received a TCAS RA between 1,500 and 3,000 feet AGL while climbing, requiring a reduced vertical speed to avoid traffic 400 feet above. The crew suspects the departure corridor was not clear, noting the Tower did not acknowledge their RA report before handing them off to Departure.

ASRS:1776562.n: About 2 hours into the flight, I received a call from A Flight Attendant that a passenger was told on 5 occasions to properly wear face mask and would not comply. The situation never escalated to heated verbal exchanges or threats. I informed the flight attendant to pass on to the passenger that the Captain will have law enforcement meet the aircraft upon gate arrival if he does not comply with policy on wearing of a face mask. The passenger complied for the duration of the flight which had approximately 1 hour remaining. I called ahead to have a Customer Service Agent meet the aircraft at gate arrival and talk with the passenger, which was done.Some passengers believe that certain policies regarding flying do not pertain to them.Keep backing up the flight crew when passenger disregard airline and FAA policy when on board an aircraft.
ASRS:1776562.s: The Captain reported a passenger refused to wear a face mask five times during cruise but complied after being warned that law enforcement would meet the aircraft at the gate. A Customer Service Agent met the passenger upon arrival, and the incident concluded without escalation or threats.

ASRS:1776574.n: Prior to block-out of Aircraft X, ZZZ airport Tower and Approach Control closed due to a COVID cleaning. Dispatch informed the flight crew to remain in the gate and not block until a new flight release could be sent with an alternate. Additionally, a non-tower operation worksheet was needed which includes approval from the manager and flight operations duty officer. Once the crew signed the new release and had a copy of the approved non-tower ops worksheet, the aircraft blocked out and operated to ZZZ. Later that night, the captain called the Flight Operations Duty Officer around XA:15pm to inform the Duty Officer that when he landed the aircraft in ZZZ, the airport lighting was not operational. However, the flight crew was able to safely land the aircraft in ZZZ because the moonlight was bright. There were no NOTAMs indicating the airport lighting was INOP. Additionally, Dispatch was never notified by the crew that the lighting was INOP. Dispatch was only notified by the Duty Officer four hours after the aircraft blocked in at ZZZ. I called the airport Tower after it reopened, and the controller stated he wasn't aware of any lighting issues and the lighting was operating normal.Even though this was a short flight, communication from the flight crew to dispatch was poor. They're several things Dispatch could have helped with prior to the outcome, including calling airport operations to inquire about the lighting issues and suggesting diverting to the alternate airport. Just before we were ready to pushback ground ops messaged us to let us know that ZZZ was going to non-towered ops for COVID cleaning. After we reviewed the FOM to ensure that we collected all the required documents and procedures. We had all the required items per the FOM. With that we departed 1hour and 8 minutes late. We knew that Tower and Approach would be closed upon arrival. We were being vectored in by ZZZ Center. We requested to come in between ZZZZZ and ZZZZZ1. We requested the visual into Runway XX at ZZZ the weather was VMC. On the base leg I has a visual on the PAPI and the captain intercepted final around 8 miles out and was flying the glideslope towards the runway. We were cleared the visual and switched to CTAF frequency. We made multiple calls on final reporting our position. We also tried to activate the lights on the field 3 times with no success (there was nothing on the approach plate indicating it would be pilot controlled. But we hoped that it being listed as the CTAF would give us control). Around ZZZZZ the runway was clearly coming into view. By 1,000 feet we could clearly see the runway and all the markings. The Captain then proceeded to land and we taxied into parking. The landing occurred at XA15z which was in the twilight hours. At no point did we feel that we were in danger or unsafe. We mistakenly used the takeoff lighting requirements. After landing we looked everything up in the FOM to double check ourselves. We do feel it would have been dangerous to go around in a CFIT moderate environment with minimal coverage from Center. This was my second flight in ZZZ with the Captain this week. We were comfortable with the approach leading into Runway XX.The event was caused by ZZZ Tower not leaving the lights on when they closed and us as a crew using the takeoff lighting requirements vs landing requirements for CATI table.We could have delayed longer out of ZZZ1 to arrive when ZZZ was definitely going to be open. We could also call the Tower before departure to ensure that they leave the lights on. We could also plan to shoot the ILS all the way from the initial approach fix.
ASRS:1776574.s: The flight crew departed late for ZZZ under non-tower operations due to a COVID closure and landed safely in twilight despite non-operational runway lights and no NOTAMs. The incident resulted from the tower failing to activate lights and the crew mistakenly applying takeoff lighting requirements instead of landing requirements.

ASRS:1776575.n: ZZZZ hub failed to notify us (Dispatch ZZZ) of Dry Ice being loaded in aft belly of aircraft. Required fuel over burn not included on release as a result.Failure of the ZZZZ hub to notify Dispatch ZZZ of Dry Ice being carried in forward or aft belly of a 777.
ASRS:1776575.s: Dispatch ZZZ was not notified by the ZZZZ hub that dry ice was loaded in the belly of a 777. Consequently, the required fuel overburn was omitted from the flight release.

ASRS:1776589.n: Alerted to passenger with continuous cough throughout flight. Passenger in [seat] X3 had spent the last year in [foreign country] and reported that she had the cough for a week and had been taking medicine for 2 days. Flight Attendant witnessed her taking cough medicine during flight. No other COVID symptoms reported. Dispatch and Medlink consulted. Passenger was relocated to aft of aircraft to isolate, per recommendation of Medlink doctor. She was also given an N95 mask. Paramedics met aircraft. Passenger's temperature was taken by EMS and was normal. She refused to answer any further questions and treatment. All 3 flight attendants [were] exposed to this passenger.
ASRS:1776589.s: A flight attendant reported a passenger with a continuous cough who had recently traveled abroad. Medlink advised isolating the passenger in the rear with an N95 mask, resulting in exposure for all three flight attendants before paramedics met the aircraft.

ASRS:1776608.n: While flying the ZZZZZ RNAV departure this morning, ATC asked us if we were assigned a heading from the last Controller. The PM replied stating we were direct ZZZZZ1, with ZZZZZ behind us on the FMS legs page. This made us look closely at our legs page and moving map on our iPads, which showed us off course. ATC replied with 'roger.' Shortly following that, we were handed off to the next controller. When we checked in we mentioned our box input error and he said, 'No problem, proceed direct ZZZ1. How's that?' No further discussion with ATC. I immediately knew what happened and why. The FMS would not download our flight plan (not uncommon) so I built in manually. As I looked at the clearance I noticed the departure and selected it, but failed to assign the ZZZZZ1 transition. ZZZZZ1 appeared on our route packet as a different fix, not part of the departure and I fell for it. I had a lot of fixes and airways to type in so I focused on getting them correct and failed to notice how I had loaded the departure, without the transition. Ultimately we were missing 4 fixes in the legs page. I checked the first 5 fixes in the legs page to confirm the altitude restrictions since we were cleared to climb Via. Normally I check all the fixes but the other contributing factors today were no coffee or breakfast at this point. I wanted to get setup and ready so I could get coffee. Due to COVID, food and coffee was not available at the hotel so we catered it for our morning departure. Additionally, the pax showed up XX minutes early which squashed my plans to eat before we took off. Additionally, the lead pax birth date was incorrect on our brief so we were further distracted.Human error. I caused this event during the FMS setup. The pre-flight distractions becoming more and more common place with passenger related issues of catering and name details, today it got me. Another potential cause could be how the flight plan route is displayed on our packets. I'm used to seeing something like 'ZZZZZ.ZZZZZ1 ZZZ2, etc.;' as the FMS shows, but the filed route on our flight plan shows 'ZZZZZ ZZZZZ1 ZZZ2, etc.' Seeing it with the period would have drawn my attention to the ZZZZZ1 transition. Suggestions - For me, all things being the same again, if the filed route on our flight plan packet showed 'ZZZZZ.ZZZZZ1' this deviation wouldn't have happened today. Regardless of this and the distractions, I need to be more careful. Clearance was ZZZZZ departure ZZZZZ1 transition, data link would not download flight plan. Flight plan was manually entered by PF loaded ZZZZZ departure to ZZZZZ then direct ZZZZZ1. When verifying flight plan off filed route page neither of us caught this manual entry error. When asked if on heading by ATC we started wondering why so checked departure and GPS position and found our error. Asked ATC if we needed to correct error and they said no and cleared us farther down line on clearance. Possible contributing factor were passengers showed XX minutes early, the way ARINC flight plan filed route shows on first page. Things could do to correct this issue on future. Verify and check each fix on the departure and also check mark each fix on lat long pages in flight plan compared to what is in the box.The way filed route showed on ARINC page, not loading transition properly when manually entering flight plan.Cross check each leg of the departure versus the plate. Also check mark each way point matches the lag/long pages in the ARINC flight plan. Any time having to manually enter information verify everything a couple times.
ASRS:1776608.s: The pilot manually entered a flight plan with a missing transition due to pre-flight distractions and confusing route packet formatting, causing the aircraft to deviate from the ZZZZZ RNAV departure. ATC cleared the crew direct to the missed fix after the error was discovered during a heading verification.

ASRS:1776616.n: During arrival to HAN, I was a jumpseat observer. We were at 2,000 ft. on the localizer, cleared for the ILS [Runway] 11 Left approach. Just outside the Final Approach Fix, I heard the Captain (Pilot Flying), say glideslope captured, and he set the missed approach altitude of 5,000 ft. in the altitude alerter. I was confused, because looking at the FO's (First Officer's) PFD (Primary Flight Display), I could see that we were below the glideslope, and it was no captured. I could not see the Captain's PFD to verify whether or not the glideslope was captured. The aircraft started descent from 2,000 ft., even though we were not on the glideslope. I called out to check the glideslope and/or altitude. I did not have a hot mike, and maybe they weren't hearing me. The aircraft passed the Final Approach Fix approximately 500 ft. low. I called out the glideslope deviation again. The other jumpseat observer was also telling them to climb, and I yelled 'Go Around'. Then we got a GS caution with a line strike through the FMA on the PFD. At approximately 1,200 ft., the go around was finally initiated with full scale deflection indicated on FO's PFD.During the surprise go around, we were instructed to maintain heading and climb to 5,000 ft. At some point the autopilot was disconnected, and situational awareness was deteriorating. The aircraft was veering to the right of track, 20 degrees nose up, and not following the flight director commands of 10 degrees nose up. I called out something like 'Who's flying the airplane, fly the airplane!' The flying pilot then steered back toward the flight director, regained control and the autopilot was re-engaged. After reaching 5,000 ft. we were vectored back for another approach to Runway 11 Left.Also of note, there was runway/taxiway construction at HAN airport that could have possibly created a glideslope anomaly. Though I could not see the Captain's flight instruments, it is possible there may have been a loss of glideslope indication at the start of the event. On the FO's PFD, I could see that the ILS was identified, and localizer/glideslope were displayed at all times.The Pilot Monitoring should have noticed on his instruments that the aircraft was not on glideslope, and should have called out the deviation immediately. When I saw the deviation, I was trying to alert the crew to fix the situation. I should have called out go around immediately. While inbound on the localizer for RNWY (Runway) 11L, the glideslope was captured and the 'G/S' FMA was active. Shortly after capturing the glideslope, the 'G/S' FMA blinked and had a yellow strikethrough. The glideslope then started to fall beneath us, while the autopilot tried to increase the rate of descent. The Pilot Flying switched to V/S [Vertical Speed], and rolled in more V/S down to stay on glideslope with a more than normal descent rate. I instructed to 'level off, level off' followed by 'climb back to 2,000 ft. It was then I noticed the glideslope dot had blinked and reappeared at two dots high, indicating we were low. The Captain in the observer seat then said 'Go Around, Go Around'. The Pilot Flying initiated the go around with the 'TOGA' [Takeoff Go-Around] switches and sometime thereafter turned off the autopilot. He then hand flew the go around to 5,000 ft. and present heading. After notifying Tower of our missed approach, we were told to contact Approach frequency. During this event, with my seat position, I was only able to observe the Captain's PFD [Primary Flight Display]. After landing safely and gathering all facts observed between crewmembers, it was apparent that the autopilot tried to capture a false glideslope and failed, thus giving us the yellow strikethrough the 'G/S' FMA."
ASRS:1776616.s: During an ILS approach to HAN, the crew descended below the glideslope due to a false signal, likely caused by airport construction. The aircraft passed the Final Approach Fix low before a delayed go-around was initiated, resulting in a brief loss of control before stabilizing at 5,000 ft.

ASRS:1776622.n: Upon doing cockpit pre-flight to ferry Aircraft X out of long-term storage from ZZZ to ZZZ1, I noticed the aircraft was fueled improperly. The wing tanks were not full and were imbalanced, there was no fuel in the center tank and there was fuel in the ACT (auxiliary) fuel tanks. This is not the proper configuration for fueling the aircraft. The wing tanks must be full before there can be any fuel in the center tank and certainly there cannot be fuel in the ACT tanks in this scenario. We notified the mechanics onboard who were assisting us to make sure everything was good prior to departure. What ensued was a three-hour debacle trying to figure out how to drain the fuel from the ACT tanks and ensure the only fuel was in the wing tanks. Planned release fuel was 25k, which in this scenario should result in fuel only in the wing tanks. After the fueling issue was finally resolved, we received two separate ECAMS after engine start. Shut down the engines and called the mechanics back to fix the new issues. SMOKE DET Fault and ANTI ICE STBY L STAT. MX fixed those two issues and we finally departed over four hours late.Someone in ZZZ is not making sure [aircraft company] aircraft coming out of storage are fueled properly. This is the second time I have caught a problem. Someone less vigilant may miss the problem.This is the second fueling issue I have had with an aircraft coming out of storage from ZZZ in the past two weeks.
ASRS:1776622.s: Pilots discovered improper fuel configuration on Aircraft X during pre-flight for a ferry flight from long-term storage at ZZZ, with fuel in auxiliary tanks instead of wing tanks. Mechanics spent three hours correcting the fuel and fixing subsequent ECAM faults, causing a four-hour departure delay.

ASRS:1776626.n: Just after departing ZZZ, heard F/A's on cabin inter phone complaining of an odor in the cabin. About that same time, the FO and myself noticed an electrical/plastic melting odor in the cockpit. Performed Avionics Smoke procedure in the QRH. Smell dissipated after selecting Blower and Exhaust fans to override and turning off cabin fans and galley equip. Confirmed odor was dissipating with the cabin crew, so after some discussion, we decided to continue to ZZZ1. Talked with dispatch and Maintenance Control, filed out fume event report. We [advised ATC] to minimize delay getting into ZZZ1 and as we begun defending thru 10,000 ft, the fumes returned. FO and myself both donned out oxygen masks and got the a/c on the ground in ZZZ1 as quickly as possible.No casual factors involved. About a serious event as can be!Unsure where the actual source of fumes came from. After departing ZZZ, heard F/A's on cabin inter phone complaining of an odor in the cabin. About that same time, the CA and myself noticed an electrical/plastic melting odor in the cockpit. Performed Avionics Smoke procedure in the QRH. Smell dissipated after following QRH and selecting Blower and Exhaust fans and turning off cabin fans and galley equip. Confirmed odor was dissipating with the cabin crew, so after some discussion and already having ZZZ1 as nearest suitable airport, we decided to continue to ZZZ1. Talked with Dispatch and Maintenance Control, filled out fume event report. We [advised ATC] to minimize delay getting into ZZZ1 and as we begun defending thru 10,000 ft, the fumes returned. Both crewmembers donned oxygen masks and got the a/c on the ground as quickly as possible.'
ASRS:1776626.s: The flight crew and cabin crew experienced an electrical odor after departing ZZZ, which temporarily dissipated following QRH procedures but returned during descent through 10,000 ft. The crew donned oxygen masks and landed at ZZZ1, though the fume source remained unidentified.

ASRS:1776647.n: I as Pilot Flying, was initially on a stable approach descending to 3,500 ft. on base for [landing]. I had briefed a Flaps 22 landing. As I was turning base to final (a left turn) and starting further descent, the winds shifted and resulted in a loss of tailwind, and my airspeed increased in the turn. At that same time Tower told us to turn 10 degrees right I believe due to traffic. Through all of this, my approach became unstable with too steep a descent, and got [we] a GPWS sink rate alert. I immediately executed a go around. ATC issued a new clearance and we came back and landed without incident. Suggest some more insight, and different scenarios taught on Flaps 22 landings possibly during training. Because of the higher airspeed vs. Flaps 45, it seems there is an increased chance of unstable approaches, especially if the winds shift as in my case. I carried too much power on this approach and also got distracted with the instruction from Tower to turn opposite of my base to final turn.
ASRS:1776647.s: The Pilot Flying experienced an unstable approach with a GPWS sink rate alert during a Flaps 22 landing due to wind shifts, excessive power, and distraction from a conflicting ATC turn instruction. The crew executed a go-around and subsequently landed safely after receiving a new clearance.

ASRS:1776648.n: I went into the cockpit for a bathroom break at XA:30pm. Neither pilot was wearing a mask. I asked, 'please put on a mask;' and pointed to mine as I entered and saw they weren't wearing masks. The First Officer reached for his mask and put it on as I paused upon entering and pointed to my mask. I again asked the Captain to put his mask on, once again pointing to my mask with both hands this time. The Captain just turned and looked forward out the window in front of him. He would not verbally reply nor put on a mask. He refused to follow company policy. We did not speak the entire time I was up there for their break - he looked out the window, I stood silently by the door. I had to stand there in the cockpit and potentially be exposed to COVID-19 and the serious consequences that could ensue. It is my understanding that COVID policies apply to everyone! When the First Officer swapped out, I said something to him about the captain refusing to comply with policies and procedures and being disrespectful. The First Officer chose not to comment on the Captain's inconsiderate and dangerous behavior, although the First Officer was wearing a mask at that time and he kept it on while I was in the cockpit.I chose not to go up again, so a colleague said he'd help with the meals in 20 minutes. At the time the colleague handed the meals up, the person taking them from him didn't have a mask on. The Captain did not wear a mask when others went into the cockpit to help. Several crew members chose not to go up there at all, several were offended and uncomfortable but chose not to say anything, and one said they didn't care that much. Fortunately, we only flew one leg with the Captain.The Captain's behavior was inappropriate, disrespectful, non-compliant with company policy, and potentially quite dangerous. His behavior was unsafe and unacceptable on all fronts.
ASRS:1776648.s: A flight attendant reported that the Captain refused to wear a mask in the cockpit during a break, violating company policy while the First Officer complied. The Captain's non-compliance and refusal to engage created a potential COVID-19 exposure risk for crew members entering the cockpit.

ASRS:1776668.n: I checked in for our departure on flight XX. I got to the plane and was the first flight attendant to arrive. I went down to the plane and noticed a paint thinner smell and walked to the back of the plane and noticed the smell throughout the plane. I went to the front and asked the First Officer if he noticed the smell and he said, 'Yes'. That he would run the APU to get air flow. I felt uncomfortable with the odor and stopped the flight attendants in the jetway. The other flight attendants could notice the strong smell in the jetway. The Captain arrived shortly after the flight attendants and further assessed the situation when he got there and made sure no one boarded the plane as the odor was strong. I felt we should contact the base supervisor so [NAME] the B flight attendant contacted [NAME2], the on duty supervisor. She came to the jetway and noticed the smells right away. Maintenance told the Supervisor that the way the heater was positioned attached to the plane that the wind was blowing in the heater exhaust into the plane. The Captain, was told by maintenance that there could be CO2 onboard but there was no way to measure CO2 with any devices.We need a safety measure to prevent crew and passengers to be affected by toxic fumes. If a device that measures toxic fumes available would help prevent an occurrence such as this. There also needs to be procedures in place that prevent the potential device (maybe heater) from discharging exhaust fumes into the aircraft.
ASRS:1776668.s: Flight attendants and the flight crew detected a strong paint thinner odor on the aircraft before boarding, caused by wind blowing heater exhaust into the cabin. Maintenance advised that carbon monoxide levels could not be measured, leading to a cancellation of boarding and a recommendation for toxic fume detection devices.

ASRS:1776669.n: During Takeoff a strong odor of chemical/burning plastic filled the cabin and all-call was made to confirm everyone else also smelled the same odor. It lasted for about 15 minutes. Pilots also confirmed the smell, along with some passengers and non-rev crew members. During descent and approach the same smell came back through to landing, 15 minutes, the chemical burning odor. The Flight Attendants felt symptoms (coughing, watery eyes, sore throat, lightheaded, headache) from this odor and had Medical meet us at the gate. The First Officer also had Medical check him as well. We did not feel well enough to continue on for our next segment of our trip. Due to the pandemic of COVID-19 and the short time frame of a fume event needed for bloodwork, the risk to go to a hospital is too high for both ourselves and others.
ASRS:1776669.s: Flight attendants and the First Officer experienced a chemical burning odor during takeoff and descent, causing symptoms like coughing and headaches. Medical met the crew at the gate, but they declined hospital testing due to COVID-19 risks and were unfit to continue their trip.

ASRS:1776670.n: Captain reported that the CPDLC [Controller-Pilot Data Link Communications] accept and reject buttons were switched, this caused 2 occasions of erroneous reject responses being sent to ATC. On arrival switches were confirmed in the wrong place (IPC (Illustrated Parts Catalog) 31-10-51-02) and switched back (SWPM (Standard Wiring Practices Manual) 20-84-13). This report is to raise awareness that these switches can be inadvertently transposed.
ASRS:1776670.s: The Captain reported that transposed CPDLC accept and reject switches caused two erroneous reject responses to ATC. The switches were confirmed in the wrong location per IPC 31-10-51-02 and corrected per SWPM 20-84-13 to prevent future inadvertent transposition.

ASRS:1776688.n: Student Pilot soloing to a nearby airport to practice landings under an endorsement from his instructor to fulfill solo requirements in 141 curriculum. Upon landing, student turned right to get off of runway in order to execute his full-stop taxi-back maneuver. When the aircraft did not turn right to his liking after applying full right rudder and differential brake, he shut down the aircraft to realign it and then continued his taxi. Upon reaching the hold short line at the departure runway of this uncontrolled airport, he discovered again that his plane was not turning to satisfaction and after making his entry call to the runway continued across it to the other side whereupon he manually adjusted its position again to get back onto the runway due to its seeming preference for right turns. He then initiated a take-off at which point the aircraft veered sharply to the left. The student pulled throttle to idle and applied full brake pressure, the lack of grabbing action in the right main brake assembly caused the plane to veer even more sharply left, off the runway to the left and into the grass infield. No objects were struck by the plane and the student shut down and exited in a safe and timely fashion. The aircraft was reviewed by a company CFI and Maintenance Technician and returned to service after a change of brake pads. Speculation is that improper use of the braking system over time caused a [glazing] effect on both the pads and rotor that limited the grabbing ability of the system at the time of the incident. No harm came to persons or property, student was quickly and safely retrieved to the point of the flights origin and the aircraft was returned to service that same day.
ASRS:1776688.s: A student pilot soloing in a training aircraft experienced poor braking and directional control during taxi and takeoff at an uncontrolled airport. The aircraft veered off the runway into grass due to glazed brake pads and rotors, but no injuries or damage occurred before the plane was repaired and returned to service.

ASRS:1776691.n: Just to raise awareness of a potential problem with anti-skid systems on Cessna aircraft. Normal approach and landing. Initial braking action good, anti-skid released, then reapplied brakes a couple of times, then released completely, cycled anti-skid switch with no effect, emergency brake had no effect either. Manufacturers emergency/abnormal checklist states'in the event of anti-skid failure, be prepared to use the emergency brake'.
ASRS:1776691.s: A pilot reported a Cessna anti-skid system failure during landing where braking was ineffective despite cycling the switch and using the emergency brake. The pilot noted the manufacturer's checklist advises using the emergency brake for such failures, yet it had no effect in this instance.

ASRS:1776730.n: A near midair collision occurred while in the traffic pattern. I was cleared to take off after [a] Cessna and was told to follow traffic. I took off and turned to John Wayne's standard 15 degree offset heading while climbing to TPA. Around 500 feet AGL I realized I no longer had traffic to follow in sight. I heard the Cessna request a short approach and ATC approved [him] for a short approach and clearance to land [Runway] 20L, after this I assumed that the traffic to follow was downwind and that I would have visual contact if I turned towards crosswind and downwind. As I was in the turn ATC asked me if I had traffic to follow in sight still. I reported back that I no longer had traffic in sight. ATC then told me to just fly a wide downwind for spacing. At this point the Cessna reported that [they] needed to make a right turn to avoid me. This whole time the Cessna was not in my visual, so they must have been beneath us and out of line-of-sight. I can only speculate on how exactly we converged as I had zero visual reference at this point with the Cessna. The Cessna and I continued flying the pattern together with no further incident but I did notice this Cessna was not flying the standard 15 degree offset on upwind and seemingly a little lower than TPA. I am unsure if this was an attributing factor to the loss of separation we encountered.
ASRS:1776730.s: A pilot and a Cessna experienced a near midair collision in the traffic pattern at John Wayne Airport after the Cessna deviated from the standard 15-degree offset and flew below TPA. The Cessna executed a right turn to avoid the pilot, who had lost visual contact while climbing to 500 feet AGL.

ASRS:1776731.n: During a tailwheel transition training flight, the aircraft departed the runway surface on landing. The winds upon time of landing favored Runway XX and a right-crosswind component of about 10 knots was present at the time of the occurrence. No other traffic was in the pattern and the approach was stable throughout. The touchdown was in a three point attitude and did not bounce. On the rollout, the student improperly managed rudder control and the aircraft rapidly developed a significant turn to the left. As Instructor, I took control of the aircraft and stopped the ground loop from further developing. The aircraft departed the hard surface of the runway at roughly a 10 degree angle at a fairly slow speed and came to rest in the grass about 20 feet from the edge of the runway. Upon shutting the airplane down, both the student and I exited the airplane to assess the situation. No signage or lighting was hit nor was there any damage present on the airplane. The grass was smooth and no holes were present.The situation developed from a normal crosswind landing to a runway excursion quickly. The cause was an improper control input by the student that was not caught in time by me, the instructor. Despite not reacting in time to prevent the excursion, the aircraft did not ground loop and no damage was sustained by the airplane. Any corrective action would be on my part as the Instructor, to take control sooner before such a significant turn could develop.
ASRS:1776731.s: During a tailwheel training landing with a 10-knot crosswind, a student's improper rudder input caused a left turn and runway excursion into grass. The instructor took control to prevent a ground loop, resulting in no aircraft damage or injuries.

ASRS:1776745.n: I was entering the traffic pattern at 45 degrees for a downwind entry for RWY14 at FIT. I had previously announced my intentions and location on the 122.7 CTAF. I did not see or hear the conflicting traffic during its go around and climb out from RWY14. I was alerted to the traffic by an ADS B traffic alert on my iPad. At this point I could not see the traffic in my field of view. I turned 45 to downwind and added power to get away from the traffic. Earlier I had heard the conflicting aircraft on the CTAF advising it was on the RNAV20 approach and would be breaking off the approach for a straight in to RWY14. Calls to the conflicting traffic before and after ADS B alert we're not answered.It all happened very quickly and I only glanced at the ADS B display, figuring my attention should be outside the airplane looking for the traffic. But the combination of repeated ADS B traffic warnings and not being able to visually see and avoid the traffic was quite stressful. Today, I was able to get the conflicting traffic's flight path from flight aware and compare it to my own from Garmin Pilot. It appears the conflicting traffic did a low approach to RWY14 and a go around, making a left climbing turn close to my own flight path. From the flight paths, the time stamps, and the fact that I never made visual contact with the conflicting aircraft, I think it passed behind me, and estimate it may have gotten as close as 500 ft.Being more vigilant to visually identify and track what I thought was landing traffic, would likely have avoided this dangerous conflict. The fact that the conflicting traffic never responded to my radio calls should also have raised a red flag.
ASRS:1776745.s: The pilot entering the traffic pattern for RWY14 at FIT experienced a conflict with an aircraft executing a go-around and left climbing turn. An ADS-B alert prompted evasive action, resulting in an estimated 500-foot separation as the pilot failed to visually acquire the unresponsive traffic.

ASRS:1776759.n: I was on the ramp at the FBO which is located at the end of the taxiway. I had received my IFR clearance for departure on Runway 7 on the clearance frequency. I then switched to the ground frequency and requested taxi clearance. (It was now well after sunset) I was told to taxi to Runway 7 via Foxtrot. I left the ramp and made an immediate left. Upon reaching Foxtrot 2, I realized that I wasn't actually on Taxiway Foxtrot, but was on a parallel road which was intended for vehicle traffic, not aircraft. I stopped at Foxtrot 2 and notified Ground control what had happened. I informed them that I could make a right onto Foxtrot 2 to get on the Foxtrot Taxiway. The controller notified me to hold my position and that he would send an Ops (Airport Operations) vehicle out. About 5 minutes later the Ops vehicle arrived behind me. The ground controller notified the Ops vehicle that I had stated that I could make the turn onto Foxtrot 2. The Ops vehicle approved that which I did and I made the right onto Foxtrot 2 and then left onto Taxiway Foxtrot and proceeded to the hold line for Runway 7 without further incident.After making the wrong turn on what I thought was Taxiway Foxtrot I did see a sign with an F on it with a black background on my right which is why I thought I was on Taxiway F. As I proceeded towards Runway 7. I commented to my passenger that there were several dips in the pavement which was unusual. As I approached F2, I saw a red sign past F2 indicating no entry. That's what was literally the red flag. Fortunately, I was in a high wing aircraft which cleared all lights and signs. This may not have been the case in a low wing aircraft. This second road was not shown on my airport taxi diagram which might have helped. I don't know if anyone else had ever made this same mistake, but I think better signage would have helped. Perhaps a sign coming out of the ramp on F1 indicating 2nd left to Foxtrot or a red no enter sign like the one at F2 might have might have also helped. I had not flown into this airport in over 15 years. I did not request progressive taxi instructions because the route appeared to be very simple. I will be more vigilant during night operations at unfamiliar airports.
ASRS:1776759.s: A pilot taxiing a high-wing aircraft at night at an unfamiliar airport mistakenly entered a parallel vehicle road instead of Taxiway Foxtrot due to misleading signage and an outdated diagram. The pilot stopped, received approval from Airport Operations to correct the path, and proceeded to Runway 7 without incident.

ASRS:1776761.n: Flying the published missed with autopilot in NAV and VS ALT to capture 4,000 [feet] as assigned by ATC. I was instructed to fly heading 070. After setting the heading bug to 070 I forgot to switch AP from NAV to HDG mode. The autopilot then started into the hold turning right to 161. [ATC] asked where I was going and at that point lost control trying to turn too steeply back to 070. In an unusual attitude I was trying to recover. Eventually, [I] hit the straight and level button on the autopilot and climbed above the cloud deck, got reoriented and rejoined the approach and landed without further problems.
ASRS:1776761.s: During a missed approach, the pilot forgot to switch the autopilot from NAV to HDG mode after receiving a heading 070 clearance, causing an unintended turn into a hold. The pilot lost control while attempting a steep recovery but stabilized the aircraft above the clouds and landed safely.

ASRS:1776772.n: When I arrived at DUY there was another aircraft parked in the ramp area and it began to taxi out before I vacated the runway. The previous aircraft had offloaded cargo in the center of the ramp but I failed to see it due to the ramp being unlighted and the difficulty of seeing over the engine cowling. The aircraft's taxi light is also located in one wing and doesn't illuminate objects on the other side of the aircraft very well.While taxiing onto the ramp, the propeller contacted a cardboard box from the previous aircraft's cargo. There was no damage to anything outside of the cardboard box and there were no injuries involved.The ramp area at Kongiganak is very constricted and requires a lot of effort to operate safely in the best of circumstances. I feel that this episode might not have happened had the previous aircraft unloaded its cargo in a less hazardous location. At DUY the runway is lighted but the ramp is unlighted. If the ramp area had better lighting, then this unfortunate episode might have been avoided.
ASRS:1776772.s: A pilot taxiing at DUY struck a cargo box left on the unlighted ramp by a previous aircraft due to poor visibility and limited taxi light coverage. The propeller contacted the box, causing no damage or injuries, though the pilot attributed the incident to the constricted, unlighted ramp and hazardous cargo placement.

ASRS:1776784.n: My Recommendation: Because there is what I believe to be a low but uncertain chance that the primary pressure vessel of the Aircraft X has a current active failure, the aircraft should be immediately grounded, and an investigation be initiated into whether this issue is just a classification and engineering oversight, or indeed a failure to the aircraft's primary structure. Aircraft X (Boeing-767-300) is potentially operating on an inapplicable airworthiness sign off and may fly (already has flown) with a possible serious defect to the aircraft's primary structure (pressure vessel). Aircraft X arrived at ZZZ station December 2020. Upon arrival the following defect was found and recorded into the maintenance log book:Discrepancy: Undocumented Speed tape found concealing stripped & unsecured mounting screw to extruded Main Cargo Door (MCD) Manual Vent Door Drive (Pressure Vessel) cover panel.I notified Maintenance Control of the defect and submitted via email a proposal for a temp repair utilizing non-standard substitution parts available on-hand at our station that I hoped would allow for a timely repair keeping the aircraft on scheduled revenue flights despite the need for an Engineering Order (EO) and additional authorizations. After an appropriate time, an outline of maintenance action to be completed was submitted to our station for a yet unapproved EO numbered: XXXXXXXX, that was a substantial deviation from my own earlier proposed temp repair. This EO after performing a Detailed Visual Inspection (DVI) merely called for reattaching the panel in place with RTV-106 sealant, no hardware, and a covering of multiple layers of aluminum speed tape. Knowing that an external application of tape over a hole in the primary pressure vessel of an aircraft did not meet the basic criteria for acceptable maintenance standards, I contacted maintenance Control to inform them that we (aircraft technicians under my purview) at ZZZ would not be able to comply with the EO maintenance instructions as they were currently written because of the safety implications.After expressing my unwillingness to press forward with the draft EO I began receiving pressuring communications from various maintenance controllers, maintenance duty managers, and Company management, saying everything from 'just do it;' to 'it'll be fine.' Additionally, it was overheard in background talk on more than one phone call with maintenance controllers that they did not believe the panel in question was actually a primary pressure vessel fitting as I had asserted in multiple emails and phone conversations, and was merely a weather seal. Worried that I had somehow made an egregious mistake about the panel in-fact being a pressure hull seal, I enlisted both additional night shift mechanics to assist with a cabin pressurization leak check (referencing AMM 05-51-24-782-001) with the damaged MCD Manual Drive cover panel removed. As I operated the cabin pressure manually, utilizing APU bleed source, the two assisting technicians reported a strong, unrestricted flow of air emanating from the uncovered hole, while I was observing only 1 PSI indicated differential cabin pressure. Believing that this observation adequately supported my previous assertation, I terminated the test, returned the aircraft to its previous configuration, and felt confident that my continued refusal to repair the aircraft as outlined in the draft EO to be a safe and correct judgment call.The scheduled departure of the aircraft was altered from XA:15z to XE:00z. At XB:16z I received an email asking me to 'please call In to Maintenance Control to advise on current status of approved EO compliance;' (no approved EO had been received or transmitted to anyone at ZZZ station). Given the ongoing pressure from phone calls and condescending emails to comply with an EO I had yet to see, I advised [the] maintenance controllers that I would not be complying with the EO and to direct all future communications to be in writing. I then suggested at that point that they 'just AOG (aircraft on ground) ship the required parts necessary to return this defect to its original condition;' with the observation 'that the original undocumented speed tape repair has already been proven to fail;' as my own justification for non-compliance with an EO that called for doing the same thing, only with more tape.At XD:50z we received the first approved copy of the EO XXXXXXXX via email from the Maintenance Manager, which upon review was consistent with the advised sealant and tape repair already rejected. The scheduled aircraft departure was once again pushed back to XG:00z, well after the scheduled arrival of the oncoming maintenance day shift. At XE:15z I received a phone call from my Company Regional Manager asking me why I was not complying with the EO and then, regarding taping over a hole in the pressure vessel, to 'explain how this is a safety concern?' After briefly elaborating to him about how the loss of cabin pressure makes flight crews go to sleep and planes to become lawn-darts, he said that I would 'have coverage in terms of liability because the engineer signed off on three layers of speed tape.' After mutually disagreeing, he proceeded to switch the subject to asking me which maintenance technicians were coming in on day shift, then, seeming unsatisfied, continued to ask me about the status of other technicians not scheduled for shift. Several minutes after hanging up, another call was received from a subordinate technician, not scheduled to come in, inquiring as to what was going on and why the Regional Manager was asking him to come into work on his weekend and 'override' us. At the advice of another technician overhearing the conversations, I took a written note of the above quotes from the calls.With continued inquiries for resolution on the aircraft, the oncoming day shift Lead informed Maintenance Control that the EO was still unworkable as it was and reiterated that the original temp repair proposal forwarded to Maintenance Control that included substituted hardware installation would be a fix deemed acceptable and believed conforming with standard practices that we would still be willing to sign off on. Giving in, the Maintenance Controller agreed to get the hardware installation added to a revised version of the EO along with an additional step for a cabin pressurization check that the day shift Lead smartly felt necessary for repairs performed on the pressurized structure of an aircraft. With assurances that the revised EO would include the agreed upon amendments, the day shift Lead and myself expedited the repair to the aircraft in an effort to make the scheduled departure pending timely receipt of the revised EO. The cabin pressure leak check of the repair was then successfully accomplished with only a small movement observed in the repair at a peak indicated differential pressure of 4.5 PSI, and no leaks or excessive loss rates noted. Upon departing the aircraft to accomplish paperwork closeout we were greeted by the oncoming flight crew, who had apparently been kept apprised of the ongoing situation and wanted to personally thank us for looking out for their safety.At XF:18z we received the approved EO XXXXXXXX Revision 1. Required paperwork was completed, signed log pages were sent, flight crew was briefed, and the aircraft was returned to green status at XG:10z. The aircraft subsequently blocked out of the gate at XG:39z for a delay from scheduled departure of 39 minutes. Why is this a safety concern? Upon later realization and review, I have found several possible deviations to Federal Aviation Regulations (FARs), the airline General Maintenance Manual, and uncertainty to the validity of the accomplished repair that should be investigated immediately as it may represent a serious safety issue to the aircraft. Having been so narrowly focused on getting the point across to the necessary parties involved in the tribulations of Dec Xth that the damaged part was indeed part of the pressure vessel of the aircraft and that a workable repair would have to be tailored to the additional physics involved with that part of the structure, I failed to realize the broader implications of what a repair to the pressurized structure of an aircraft entailed in terms of adherence to regulations, maintenance policy, and accepted practices. The FARs define 'Primary Structure: is that structure which carries flight, ground, or pressurization loads, and whose failure would reduce the structural integrity of the airplane.' Even though steps were added to Revision 1 of the EO to conform the repair to acceptable practices 'equal to its original or properly altered condition;' because the installation hardware was a reasonably close approximation of the original parts, the additional step of adding three layers of overlapping speed tape is in direct contradiction to the airline General Maintenance Manual policy for its use: -HIGH SPEED ALUMINUM TAPE- High speed tape is a convenient material for use as an interim repair for non-structural materials. Under no circumstances will it be used on primary aircraft structure. A Log Book entry is required when high speed tape is applied unless instructed to do so by an EO with DER approval.Under this policy, the use of speed tape in this manner is strictly forbidden and forgiveness when it comes to doing the maintenance under the provision of an EO only absolves the requirement of a log book entry for its use. However, even though agreement was made in Revision 1 of the EO for addition of attachment hardware and an added cabin pressurization leak check, the EO creator did not alter the original classification of the repair to acknowledge that the repair was in-fact being accomplished on an aircraft primary structure: 'The Main Deck Cargo Door Manual Vent Door Drive Cover is considered secondary structure. The time limited repair per this EO is minor, and the temporary repair per Part 1 does not affect the fit, form or function of the skin.'I would imagine this to be an oversight, and if it is, then an additional revision needs to be made which would at a minimum alter the category of the defect deferral and its associated time-limited re-inspections and permanent repair due date/cycles. If this is not an oversight, however, as this EO has been twice over reviewed and approved, and the MCD Manual Vent Door Drive Cover is indeed a secondary structure, then the original investigative cabin pressure leak test failed for a reason other than indicated (i.e. there is an existing failure of the primary pressure vessel somewhere internal to the Main Cargo Door). Which would in turn mean that a damaged secondary structure is now fulfilling the function of a primary structure pressure seal. I do not believe this to be the case, but, as the MCD is a modification from the original aircraft structure, the existing reference material available for my use to confirm the hypothesis that the cover plate is indeed a primary structure component is vague and uncertain. Tech Engineering likely has additional references not available at a line station that could perhaps shed light on the issue.Since issuing equivalent versions of the above safety report to both Airline and Company on [the next day], Aircraft X has remained on a regular flight schedule with recurrent re-inspects per Part 2 of EO XXXXXXXX Rev 1, until receiving Part 3 Permanent Repair [4 days later]. I can currently find no record that any further investigation has been conducted.
ASRS:1776784.s: A maintenance technician at ZZZ station refused an initial Engineering Order to tape over a stripped screw on a Boeing 767-300's primary pressure vessel, citing safety risks. After management pressure and a successful cabin leak test, a revised repair using hardware and tape was approved, returning the aircraft to service with a 39-minute delay.

ASRS:1776806.n: During a Flight Attendant crew change and passenger boarding, our Flight Attendant B advised Flight Attendant A and myself, Captain, that she received a call from her personal Physician that she had a positive result for COVID-19 test resulting from a pre-surgery screening. A Flight Attendant immediately advised B Flight Attendant to contact Crew Scheduling and request to be removed and replaced for the flight. The Captain immediately advised Operations Agent to discontinue boarding and have passengers in jet-bridge return to boarding area in terminal building, while B Flight Attendant gathered her belongings and removed herself from the aircraft.I then requested the Operations Agent to call Flight Attendant crew lounge to see if a Reserve Flight Attendant was available to assume vacant position. The Flight was originally advised of a 30 minute delay for inbound Flight Attendant from another flight. After approximately 10 minutes, we were advised that a Reserve Flight Attendant was enroute from the crew lounge to cover flight. The Flight took a 17 minute delay due to the Flight Attendant exchange.
ASRS:1776806.s: During passenger boarding, a Flight Attendant tested positive for COVID-19 and was removed from the aircraft. The Captain halted boarding to secure a Reserve Flight Attendant, resulting in a 17-minute delay before the flight could depart.

ASRS:1776812.n: We were at FL410 in continuous light chop. The seat belt sign was on before we entered the known area of turbulence and remained on till we passed the turbulence. ATC [was] reporting light chop for the next 150 miles. I had the speed intervene window open. The N1 was set for turbulence penetration. The speed was Mach .76. Within a matter of seconds we were in severe mountain wave. The speed increased to Mach .80 and we were in the over speed band. The over speed clacker went off right away. We began losing altitude. I immediately reduced thrust which was ineffective so pulled the speed brake. The speed slowed to Mach .76. We lost 300 ft. quickly. Then the second wave hit and we climbed rapidly back to altitude then 200 ft. above the assigned altitude. The aircraft returned to FL410. The event was probably 30 to 45 seconds. During the event I had the FO (First Officer) seat the flight attendants immediately. I had the FO ask for a descent to FL390. We were given the descent. The FO reported the mountain wave and the trends to ATC. There was no traffic in the area on TCAS and none was reported by ATC. We reached FL390 with no further wave but the light turbulence continued. I checked the flight attendants in and they reported no one was up during the event. I reported the event to Maintenance as severe mountain wave and over speed. I reported the event to Dispatch as well. In my 25 years of flying I have never seen mountain wave this bad.
ASRS:1776812.s: The flight crew encountered severe mountain wave turbulence at FL410, causing an overspeed to Mach .80 and a 300-foot altitude loss. The pilot reduced thrust and deployed speed brakes to recover, then descended to FL390 where turbulence lightened but continued.

ASRS:1776830.n: After getting clearance to push from both Towers to the 'Y' I initiated the pushback. As soon as I started my turn into the taxiway the pilot notified me of a jet speeding in our direction. I immediately braked and pulled back toward the gate. The pilot stated again that we had the clearance and the jet should have stopped. It did not stop and sped right by.
ASRS:1776830.s: The ground handler initiated pushback after receiving clearance from both Towers, but a jet sped toward the aircraft on the taxiway. The handler braked and returned to the gate while the pilot insisted the jet should have stopped, yet it passed without stopping.

ASRS:1776833.n: While driving the bridge to the aircraft the 737-900 door was opened prior to the bridge docking or the required two knocks by myself. While driving I don't expect to see the door get popped which is extremely distracting while I am moving heavy equipment towards an aircraft. If the slide had been deployed it could have caused me serious harm or even death. I file an average of 3 or 4 [safety reports] on this exact issue every single week. This has got to stop.
ASRS:1776833.s: A ramp driver reported that a 737-900 door was opened before the jet bridge docked or the required two knocks were given while the driver was moving heavy equipment. The driver stated this unexpected action was extremely distracting and could have caused serious harm or death if the slide had deployed.

ASRS:1776835.n: Aircraft X was showing out of the gate when the ramp tried to final. Once I finished working another flight I saw I had 5 Weight and Balance Check messages showing Hazmat not secure w/15 bags for flight Aircraft X. I called ZZZ Operations at first the zone controller did not want to be bothered said ramp will call me. After the ramp tried to final another 5 times the Lead [Ramp Supervisor] then decided to call the Load Planner. When he called he at first stated the Hazmat was below the line, which I corrected him and said nothing was ever below the line because the flight was not weight restricted. That line isn't what got my blood boiling, the lead then stated on a recorded called all of the Hazmat was no show and wanted me to hold it off. I refused because I couldn't understand why if it were a no show he would attempt to finalize the Manifest 10 times before calling me. When I asked him that question he hung up the phone. The lead then attempted another 6 time to finalize the Manifest with no bags in the pit, afterwards he called back to say the plane is going to have to come back because the Hazmat is onboard. If I would have been one of those push over load planners I would have simply held off the Hazmat taking the lead at his word and we would have had a plane takeoff with Hazmat onboard, not secured, and no pilot paperwork. That really irks me the fact that he lied on a recorded line to have me hold off Hazmat that he knew he loaded on the aircraft.
ASRS:1776835.s: A Load Planner reported that a Ramp Supervisor attempted to finalize the manifest for Aircraft X ten times despite unsecured Hazmat and missing bags. The Supervisor allegedly lied on a recorded call to claim the Hazmat was a no-show, forcing the aircraft to return to the gate with the cargo onboard.

ASRS:1776836.n: No COVID policies being enforced. More than 5 people in new small breakroom. No mask.
ASRS:1776836.s: Cabin crew reported that no COVID policies were enforced, resulting in more than five people gathering without masks in a new small breakroom.

ASRS:1776838.n: There was no disinfectant or sanitation spray in the lobby today. This is not what has been promised to us to protect us from COVID.
ASRS:1776838.s: Cabin crew reported that no disinfectant or sanitation spray was available in the lobby, contrary to promises made to protect staff from COVID. The narrative cites this lack of equipment as a failure to provide the agreed-upon safety measures.

ASRS:1776841.n: ATIS was advising ILS approaches in use. We requested the RNAV Y for pilot proficiency reasons. The request was approved by the final approach controller. At the end of the RNAV arrival, we were put on the published heading and told to expect vectors onto final for the RNAV Y approach by the final approach controller. We requested but were denied direct both initial approach fixes to start the approach. We were given 2 vectors, the last being [Heading] 290 and the clearance to fly heading 290 maintain 4,300 ft. until established on the final approach course cleared for the RNAV Y approach as we were vectored toward the course between the initial approach fixes. The approach became challenging at that point because the final approach course and glidepath anticipation cues were not visible and therefore we were unable to arm the approach. Additionally, the 4,300 ft. restriction left us high rather than leave us in a position to descend to 2,900 ft. in the space between the initial approach fixes because the width of the lateral course at that point is much narrower than a localizer signal. The IMC and terrain rich environment added to the concerns at this point. I feel that part of this challenge was created by the technique US air traffic controllers are using to get aircraft onto RNAV approaches. Rather that clear an aircraft to a fix on the approach, they are trying to vector them onto final as they would for an aircraft flying an ILS approach. My first safety concern is that there is not final approach course to intercept when flying an RNAV approach such as the localizer transmitting out bound from the runway for many miles. Rather there seems to be courses from one fix to the next all the way down the published approach. When ATC says 'fly heading xxx until established on the final approach' there isn't a final approach to intercept. I question whether a clearance of that wording is procedurally correct on RNAV approach. There are no examples I can find in company manuals or the Airman Information Manual the depicts starting an RNAV approach at anywhere other than a fix on the approach. I have had this type of vector onto final clearance for an RNAV approach for RNAV approaches in other U.S. destinations also so I feel the safety threat posed by this type of RNAV clearance is widespread in the USA. I have never received a clearance like that outside of the USA. Outside the USA, I have always been cleared to fix to start the RNAV approach. My second safety concern is that if that type of RNAV approach clearance is correct, we do not train that at any point during initial or recurrent training. All of our simulator training clears the aircraft to a fix on the approach when cleared for an RNAV approach. If the type of ATC clearance we got is procedurally correct we never see it in training.
ASRS:1776841.s: Pilots flying an RNAV Y approach reported that ATC vectors to intercept the final course, rather than clearing to a fix, left the aircraft high and prevented arming the approach due to missing glidepath cues. The crew attributed this safety concern to a mismatch between US ATC vectoring techniques for RNAV approaches and standard training procedures.

ASRS:1776843.n: We had to bring back [taxing] flight because of [load configuration error] requirement of the15 bags [missing] around the Dangerous Good cargo.
ASRS:1776843.s: The crew returned the taxiing flight due to a load configuration error involving 15 missing bags required around the Dangerous Goods cargo.

ASRS:1776872.n: During passenger boarding I started the APU to cool the aircraft. I selected the APU bleed on and immediately began to smell a foul pungent odor. I turned the bleed off and waited a couple minutes. I tried the APU bleed again and encountered the same pungent odor. I waited a minute to see if it was a temporary smell but it persisted. I turned the bleed off and wrote up the airplane in the maintenance logbook. The smell was predominantly in the flight deck and forward galley however passengers deplaning from the rear of the aircraft were inquiring about the odor. Maintenance checked to see if the APU was possibly over serviced. The APU checked out normal. Maintenance continued their work and eventually cleared the write up. When we returned to the aircraft to get ready to board all crew members again smelled the same smell. Although it was not as strong as before it was still there and seemed to get slightly worse if we turned the Number 1 Pack off. I again wrote the aircraft up in the maintenance logbook. No medical attention was requested or required for crew or passengers.As for the probable cause, no causal factors that I can think of. Maintenance said it could have been the fumes from an aircraft starting upwind of us however that wouldn't explain why we smelled it the second time hours later. APU was started in preparation for departure, upon turning on the APU bleed to begin cooling the aircraft there immediately was a strong fume that made my nose and eyes begin to burn. I told the CA (Captain) that was the bad fume smell we need to be careful about and said I was leaving the flight deck to stand on the jet bridge. The bleed was turned off and I left for fresh air. After multiple retries by MX (Maintenance) who agreed the smell was there the passengers and remaining crew were deplaned. Later the MX personnel had done nothing other than run the packs using the external air cart and were ready to sign the plane back into service, but simply walking into the galley every single crew member could still smell the fumes. We tried to isolate the problem pack by switching packs and the fumes became worse again. We then left the aircraft again. This is an ongoing problem worldwide in the industry. The potentially disastrous health consequences of this type of pyrolization should be addressed before more crew members and passengers are impacted.
ASRS:1776872.s: Crew members detected a pungent, burning odor during APU bleed activation for cooling while boarding and again before departure. Maintenance cleared the aircraft after finding no faults, but the smell persisted, causing crew to deplane and raising concerns about potential pyrolysis fumes.

ASRS:1776883.n: On climb out to ZZZ both airspeed disagreement cautions came on with +/- 10 knot difference between the Captain and FO (First Officer) airspeed [indicators]. Once at cruise all cautions went away and we continued. Upon descent and on the arrival we again got the 'airspeed disagreement' caution for about 5 minutes then it again disappeared. Continuing on the descent at around 16,000 ft. and in icing conditions the Captain's airspeed went to +/- 50 knots causing the throttles to chase the airspeed. I turned off the autopilot, autothrottles and both flight directors as per the QRH and quickly realized the FO side was working fine. The FO continued the descent. Climbing out, passing approximately FL280 in IMC conditions, with the CA (Captain) flying, we received an 'IAS DISAGREE' indication. There was a split of approximately 10 KIAS between the CA and FO (First Officer) instruments with a corresponding split in Mach. I, the FO, got out the unreliable airspeed checklist in the QRH to look up the possible indications. After a few moments the indication disappeared and the IAS returned to normal. After beginning a descent the same indications returned and then disappeared as they had before. Passing approximately 16,000 ft. there was a large fluctuation in the CA's airspeed causing a large fluctuation in the autothrottles. The CA disengaged the autopilot and autothrottles. We transferred aircraft control since my indications seemed normal. The CA ran the QRH for unreliable airspeed [and] I flew the approach using the autopilot with the autothrottles disengaged to an uneventful landing.
ASRS:1776883.s: The crew experienced intermittent airspeed disagreement cautions during climb, cruise, and descent in icing conditions, causing autothrottle fluctuations. The Captain disengaged automation and transferred control to the First Officer, who flew the approach using reliable instruments for an uneventful landing.

ASRS:1776899.n: As we taxied out to our assigned runway of XXL in ZZZ, we received several EFIS COMP MON [airspeed disagree] caution messages. They would only stay on for a few seconds, then disappear as I would reset the master caution that would accompany the ding. Once we were cleared to 'line up and wait' on our assigned runway of XXL I taxied on the runway, and handed the controls to the First Officer (FO) and we waited for our takeoff clearance. A few moments later, we were cleared to takeoff with clearance of 'RNAV to ZZZZZ Runway XXL, cleared for takeoff.' The First Officer then initiated the take off sequence. As she pushed the thrust levers forward and we started to move down the runway, yet another EFIS [Electronic Flight instrument System] COMP MON caution came on with an associated ding and master caution warning. I looked to ED1 (primary EICAS) to find the caution and said aloud 'continue.' and the The First Officer continued with the takeoff roll. As soon as I looked back at the airspeed indicator tape, I saw we already were at V1 speed, and Vr speed. So I said aloud 'V1, rotate' as soon as we rotated the STALL FAIL caution illuminated on ED1. The stick shaker activated shortly thereafter, followed by a warbling tone to indicated a stall had happened. I look at my airspeed indication 'tape' and now saw both red 'barber pole' indicators starting to come together. As I saw this, I quickly looked at the FO airspeed indication and back at the backup airspeed indication. I noticed they both were reading the same thing and said aloud, 'looks like we have a stall fail caution, and my airspeed is showing incorrect indications.' I then began to run the QRC and QRH for the stall fail and loss of reliable airspeed indications. After running the QRH, we promptly returned to ZZZ without incident and taxied to a gate. According to Maintenance, water entered into the left-side pitot tube and caused an erroneous airspeed error, and potential STALL FAIL caution.
