ASRS:1776899.s: The crew experienced intermittent EFIS COMP MON and STALL FAIL cautions during takeoff from Runway XXL due to water in the left pitot tube causing erroneous airspeed indications. After executing the QRH for loss of reliable airspeed, they returned to ZZZ without incident.

ASRS:1776907.n: The Captain and I met at the airplane in the morning and the first topic of discussion was the automated parking guidance procedure as neither of us had used the system yet and they appeared to be operating. We referenced the flight manual as well as the local notes concerning the system and still felt that we were not sure exactly what we were supposed to do approaching the gate. We asked rampers prior to departing and their explanation, which did not help much. We departed and further discussed our plan for approaching the gate in our briefing for the return leg. As we approached the gate 3 rampers were present and the guidance panel worked well and was intuitive. We found a Ramp Supervisor and he discussed the details with us and answered questions we had. The guidance in the flight manual is inadequate as it does not address definitively whether or not marshallers are required to be at the spot. It does not specify the procedure for requesting assistance from ramp personnel if required It does not address what to do in the event that equipment is in the safety zone. Finally, the guidance as to when the screen symbology is required references 'the nose of the aircraft passing the jet bridge' which does not apply to the Aircraft X in where the system is active. My interpretation and common sense answers to these questions are likely to create a safe operation but safe and compliant are not always the same thing. We entered the gate area in compliance with the flight manual to the best of my knowledge and interpretation, however I feel that the guidance in the manual was inadequate. Part of the information we used to determine a plan for parking came from talking with rampers. They obviously have good insight but their word does not meet acceptable standards for determining compliance with a procedure. I would recommend a simple update to the manual that goes beyond description of the guidance panel and sets definitive procedures for entering the gate.
ASRS:1776907.s: The flight crew encountered inadequate automated parking guidance procedures in the Flight Manual while approaching the gate. They relied on ramp personnel for clarification, concluding that the manual lacks definitive instructions on marshaller requirements, safety zones, and system activation triggers.

ASRS:1776920.n: There was a break before the next flight to ZZZ. Flight attendants left the aircraft. First Officer (FO) left the aircraft. Captain left the aircraft as one of the FAs came back to the aircraft. Captain came back to the aircraft. Both FAs and FO were on board. Also a Ramp Agent (RA) was on board sitting in the back of the plane resting. One of the flight Attendants told the Captain she was concerned that the RA did not complete the security search. From her perspective it seemed as if the security check was not complete. Captain went back and asked the RA if he had completed the security search. He said yes. Captain asked what was involved with the search and he described that it was a visual search and where he looked. Captain told the Flight Attendant that the Ramp Agent said he did it. Flight Attendant was not sure because the RA hadn't lifted up the seat cushions and looked behind them or put the tray tables down as the FA had seen done in previous security searches. Captain asked the RA if he could do the security check again and that there was a concern that it was not complete. The RA started doing another security check lifting up the seat cushions in the first couple rows. Captain went to the flight deck to prepare for the flight. Captain assumed that the security check got completed the second round and all was good to go. Flight departs for ZZZ, Captain and FO review the security section of Flight Ops Manual (FOM). After arrival in ZZZ, the Captain goes to review the security section with FAs. It is then that he hears that the Ramp Agent did not go completely through the cabin on the second time and check seat cushions and tray tables at ZZZ1. The RA talked with another RA and then told the Flight Attendants that the search had happened and it was complete. The Captain called the Duty Officer and had a discussion about the situation and the wording in the FOM. Duty Officer told the Captain that he would call back after a few minutes while he made a call to find out what the Ramp manual says to do. After the Duty officer called back to the Captain he referenced the Services Manual about aircraft search to and from ZZZZ, wording was not the same as what is in the FOM. The Duty officer agreed that there is room for some confusion between the wording in the two manuals. Captain decided to stop the operation and have ZZZ ramp agents do a Full Search before continuing on to ZZZ2. A Big thank you to ZZZ RAs in knocking out a Full Search. My thoughts (Captain) there is some confusion in how the FOM describes a cabin search and what a visual inspection actually is on the security form.Pay closer attention to details. Don't assume anything, make sure everyone is on the same page in understanding of what's happening. Ask questions, try and understand the full picture. It's been awhile since our airplanes have made ZZZZ trips and it was the first time for our crew the other day since prior to COVID-19. We need to show each other respect, and give grace in this super stressful time. After talking with the Duty Officer, I more fully aware of the staffing issues with ramp, COVID-19 cases and just under staffing in different areas which has been extremely difficult. I also see a value in debriefing the crew at the end of the trip or after abnormal situations as a learning time for all as we grow as professionals.
ASRS:1776920.s: During a break before departure to ZZZ, a Flight Attendant questioned a Ramp Agent's incomplete cabin security search, prompting a second attempt that was also not fully executed. The Captain halted operations to order a full search by ZZZ ramp agents after discovering conflicting instructions between the Flight Ops Manual and Services Manual.

ASRS:1776929.n: We were fully boarded, with checklist Before Start To The Line complete. Flight Attendant B reported passenger submitted, when Flight Attendant A reported the ramp agents requested we contact Station Ops. Operations informed us Flight Attendant B was being replaced on the trip by a reserve. I assisted Flight Attendant B off loading bags, and advised them to catch a breath and gather all effects. The pressure of the last minute situation and the ramp, and the timeline, needed to be ignored at that moment. The replacement flight attendant arrived, I assisted loading bags, verified ID and returned to the flight deck. Weight and performance numbers came up and the Captain stated ready for door closure. The main cabin door and cockpit door secured, weights entered and verified on FMS. Without communication from ramp agents, they re-opened the main cabin door. Flight Attendant A knocked on the cockpit door, which we opened. Flight Attendant A stated the First Officer was now also being replaced on the trip. I queried Crew Scheduling and was told name ordered me off the trip with no further information given. The replacement First Officer arrived and I offloaded the bags. The Captain was astonished that such an action would take place without communication, consult, or apparent consideration for safety of flight.Passengers expressed surprise, and some measure of concern and alarm. The main cabin door being opened without the crew's awareness is not a procedure I have seen before. Replacing crew members who are not ill at the last minute affects our morale and pocketbook, and creates unnecessary concern for the revenue passengers. Safety of flight is inevitably affected by this kind of turmoil, and it falls on the Company to alleviate stress and safety rather than contribute to it. The Company exercised authority in contradiction to common sense and safety of flight. The timeline, already compressed, became distressingly so given the apparent chaos this action caused in view of passengers. Ordering the ramp to open the main cabin door without communicating first to the crew is an extraordinary act of harassment and intimidation. If a pilot needs to be replaced on a trip for administrative reasons, surely that can wait until after a short turn is completed. This action requires the crew, the new crew, to re-brief and reinitialize a flight under stress, delays our passengers, compromises our timeline, and potentially costs us our bonuses. It should be taken only under extraordinary circumstances, which apparently do not exist. The Company should be an asset to safety of flight rather than a liability.
ASRS:1776929.s: During pre-departure, Station Ops replaced the First Officer and a flight attendant without notifying the crew, causing ramp agents to reopen the secured main cabin door. The Captain reported this uncoordinated action created passenger alarm, compromised safety of flight, and constituted harassment by forcing a re-brief under stress.

ASRS:1776958.n: During boarding Family A was sent down to aircraft not wearing face covering. Passengers were asked the age of the child at the entry door and stated 3 years old. Passenger stated at the doorway she had the child's mask in her purse and would put it on at their seat location, I apologized and stated the mask would need to be on the child before boarding the aircraft. Family A then stepped out on the Jetway, pulled the mask out and said it would be difficult getting the child to wear and keep the mask on. I wanted to have the passengers go back up and speak with customer service, but thought they would comply. As other passengers were boarding, Family A followed behind, I did not notice they had not put the mask on the child.After we completed the safety briefing and doing the walk through, Family A were sitting with the child, had not placed the mask on the child, mother had placed the mask back in her purse. I apologized again and stated she would need to put the mask on child. Captain had signaled for takeoff. I also mentioned to the parents the Captain wanted to go back to the gate and I told them I did not want to go back to the gate. The mother tried to put the mask on the child, the father tried, then stated he wanted to give her some medicine that would make her go to sleep. I informed the Captain what was going on and of our progress, Captain made the call to go back to the gate. Several managers met the aircraft. Family A was asked to deplane.
ASRS:1776958.s: A cabin crew member reported that Family A boarded with an unmasked three-year-old child despite warnings. The Captain ordered a return to the gate after the parents refused to mask the child, resulting in the family being asked to deplane by managers.

ASRS:1776961.n: I came to my gate early to work my next flight. A flight was still there and boarding. I watched as passenger after passenger scanned their boarding pass or mobile device across the gate reader. I even watched as one gentleman sneezed with his boarding pass in hand. The reader was never wiped down with sanitizer between scans. I believe we should be wiping down gate readers before and after each flight.
ASRS:1776961.s: A pilot observed passengers scanning boarding passes on a gate reader without the device being sanitized between uses, noting one passenger sneezed while holding their pass. The reporter recommends wiping down gate readers before and after each flight to improve hygiene.

ASRS:1776974.n: Due to COVID-19 the following statements need to be remove or change for the Technician performing the task.task# XX(A) put the mask-regulator unit on your head and your face.task# XX1Breathe through the mask-regulator unit with dilution control lever set to N (normal) and when it is at the 100% position.Remove or make an amendment to skip the step, it's also on the Y type aircraft manual.
ASRS:1776974.s: A technician reported that COVID-19 protocols require removing or amending oxygen mask regulator steps in the Y type aircraft manual. The specific tasks involving donning the mask and setting the dilution control lever need to be skipped or revised.

ASRS:1776980.n: On [Date 1], I was reviewing paperwork on the current Aircraft X in the [Maintenance Visit] in ZZZ and noticed that a robbed transponder on Aircraft X was installed the previous night and did not get a signoff in the logbook releasing the aircraft for RVSM (Reduced Vertical Separation Minimum) operation. This aircraft was still scheduled to be in the [Maintenance Visit] for another 5 days so I just had the nightshift avionics tech complete the entry the next day. But I knew that the avionics tech that forgot the RVSM signoff on the [Maintenance Visit] also replaced a transponder on Aircraft Y during the overnight on [Date 2]. I pulled the paperwork from the night of [Date 2] and found that the #2 Transponder was changed to clear a MEL (Minimum Equipment List), but a RVSM release was not done in the logbook. I called Maintenance Control and told them what happened and Aircraft Y was inbound to ZZZ1 at the time so when it landed in ZZZ1, Maintenance went out and deferred the RVSM. The ZZZ Avionics tech that replaced the transponder is [Name].Found during paperwork reviewShould of, but did not realize the transponder is RVSMCalled Maintenance Control and had the system deferred (RVSM)[Parts Document] lists the PN (Part Number) of the transponders that go on our aircraft that are post ADS-B (Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast) mod. This PN [XXX] is not listed in the aircraft IPC (Illustrated Parts Catalog), so there is no statement (RVSM Critical Item) like all the other transponder PN's listed in the IPC. This statement (RVSM Critical Item) should be added to the [Parts Document], to bring attention to it like the PN's listed in the aircraft IPC. On [Date 2] I was assigned to clear a Transponder #2 MEL (Minimum Equipment List) on Aircraft Y. I determined it needed a new transponder, however, we did not have the proper transponder in stock required for ADS-B (Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast) mod aircraft. I was directed to rob the transponder from Aircraft X which was the [Maintenance Visit], after robbing (from Aircraft X) and installing (on Aircraft Y) the transponder, I went through the operation checks and everything was good. I went to sign off the paperwork and seen, from the beginning of Chapter 34 in the AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual), that it was not CAT II (Category 2). I forgot that RVSM (Reduced Vertical Separation Minimum) isn't included in the beginning of ATA (Air Transport Association) chapters and since I picked the part number based on [Number] I didn't see the RVSM reminder note seen in the AIPC (Aircraft Illustrated Parts Catalog). I went to open the GMM (General Maintenance Manual) on the tech computer I was using and it wouldn't open. It was known within the base that PDF's can act up on the 2 provided tech computers. My ignorance of not remembering that RVSM wasn't included in the beginnings of ATA chapters, and not going into AIPC, and assuming that since RVSM wasn't downgraded it wasn't an RVSM component, along with my laziness of not confirming with a lead or Supervisor on their computers contributed to missing the RVSM release sign off. The plane made at least one flight with out having the RVSM release. The next night I installed new transponder in Aircraft X and Operations checked everything and since I assumed it wasn't RVSM the day before I repeated my mistake for the [Maintenance Visit on Aircraft X], and didn't write up a RVSM release sign off. It was caught before the aircraft left and the other avionics technician went through the operation checks again and provided the RVSM release sign off.The day shift Supervisor caught the [Maintenance Visit] not having the release and knew that I did the aircraft the night before and seen that I didn't release that one either and took corrective action.I didn't put max effort into looking into seeing if the component was RVSM critical. I went off of a handful of assumptions and didn't double check with my leads or Supervisor. The [Number] didn't reiterate it was an RVSM critical item, the GMM PDF didn't want to load on the tech computers, RVSM isn't located at the beginning of ATA chapters like CAT II and RII (Required Inspection Item) are.Put RVSM in beginning ATA chapters like CAT II and RII. Add a reminder in [Number] that the transponder is RVSM critical component. Remove old transponders from stock that can't be used with ADS-B aircraft seeing that our whole fleet has ADS-B mod. Leadership verified wrong part number in stock the night before contributing to this issue being on 2 aircraft due to robbery. Update/upgrade/fix tech computers so we can open the files we need.
ASRS:1776980.s: An avionics technician failed to sign off RVSM releases after installing robbed transponders on Aircraft X and Y due to incorrect part documentation, computer failures, and procedural assumptions. Maintenance Control deferred RVSM on Aircraft Y upon landing, while the error on Aircraft X was caught by a supervisor before departure.

ASRS:1776990.n: On a training flight with a student, we had alternator failure an hour into our lesson. I did not notice the ammeter reading negative until the transponder began to flicker on and off. When I was troubleshooting, I asked the student to look at the ammeter, since it was on his side, and he told me that it was showing a negative reading, and that there was a red light. I immediately turned towards ZZZ1 and began to reduce the electrical load, hoping to lengthen the amount of time that we would have a working radio. At this point I checked into our traffic avoidance system, and noticed that there was heavy traffic at my airport of intended landing. I queued up Approach and told them the nature of my situation. I told them I wasn't sure if I would have enough battery to safely make calls to get into the traffic pattern, considering my transponder was dying. A few minutes later, right after they transferred us to Tower, who quickly cleared us to land, we lost all ability to communicate. We were unable to use our electric flaps on the landing. I taxied back to the ramp and gave Tower a call to see if I needed to fill out any paperwork, and they told me that they had taken care of it. In retrospect, I should have caught the failed alternator sooner. My student had noticed the light, but did not know what it meant, and his yoke was in the way for me to notice it. During our cruise checklist, that is one of the items that we check, and I did not notice anything wrong when we did the checklist 20 minutes prior. Additionally, after noticing the issue I could have just completely turned off the master switch and used pilotage to get us close to [the airport], after which I could have turned the master back on and then used my radio. I had never had this happen before, so I was trying to make quick, confident decisions.
ASRS:1776990.s: During a training flight, the pilot and student experienced an alternator failure that caused electrical load issues, transponder flickering, and eventual radio and electric flap loss. The pilot landed safely after receiving a clearance from Tower, noting the failure was missed during the cruise checklist due to the student's yoke obstructing the warning light.

ASRS:1776992.n: After doing 5 touch and goes on runway 28R, I received clearance to land. I did a wheel landing, let the tail come down, and when the aircraft was traveling slowly at about 15 kts or less, I started turning left to aim for the taxiway exit, and the aircraft kept turning to the left and did a complete 360 ground loop on the runway. The aircraft did not suffer any damage or touch any part of the aircraft to the runway, except the wheels of course, and I did not leave the runway. Due to this unexpected delay the aircraft landing behind me had to go around. I attribute this ground loop to unexpected strong crosswind, and the fact that we just put air in the tires and the aircraft was a lot more responsive to rudder control inputs that on my previous flight. She just got away from me for a moment.
ASRS:1776992.s: The pilot ground looped the aircraft 360 degrees on runway 28R during the landing roll after a wheel landing. The pilot attributed the incident to strong crosswinds and increased rudder responsiveness from newly inflated tires, causing a following aircraft to go around.

ASRS:1777003.n: This was my first flight at the controls of a tail wheel aircraft. I was in the left seat receiving flight instruction from the CFI in the right seat. A thorough pre-takeoff briefing including experience levels and positive transfer of controls was accomplished before departure.As we approached ZZZ, we briefed the fact there was a right crosswind with gusts and the appropriate actions to take regarding this. The approach was stabilized. A normal wheel landing was accomplished and the tail was successfully lowered to the ground. The left main tire failed, at which point the instructor stated 'my airplane' and I released the controls. The resulting swerve was not controllable and the airplane ground looped approximately 150 degrees, coming to rest on the runway. We immediately shut down the aircraft and exited. No propeller or wingtip contact with the runway occurred. The aircraft remained on the runway. No injuries occurred. The mission was to fly with 2 friends and give them tail wheel instruction. There was a crosswind from the right and we discussed crosswind correction and the plan. [The pilot flying] conducted the wheel landing and shortly after putting the tail down, the airplane started shaking violently. I thought this may have initially been a tail wheel shimmy, which was odd since it didn't shimmy since the tail wheel springs were replaced in month, but the airplane started veering to the left so I announced 'my controls' and corrected it with right rudder. The shaking got worse and the plane then swung around to the right and ground looped. The wings did not contact the surface and there was no prop strike. The airplane was then towed to the hangar where I worked with a mechanic to change the wheel and tire so that the plane could be moved while inside the hangar. I did identify some contributing factors. There was a strong right crosswind, it was my student's first landing, and I had previous issues with my tires slipping on grooved runways. They are 8.50 oversize tires. I do believe the left main tire went flat on landing, and with the strong crosswind and delay of taking the controls from my student, it was unrecoverable. I'm filling out this report to detail human factors issues that contributed to damage to my precious airplane, and as the investigation unfolds it will determine if there is need for additional caution when using larger tires.
ASRS:1777003.s: A student pilot and CFI ground looped a tailwheel aircraft during a crosswind landing after the left main tire failed. The instructor attributed the unrecoverable swerve to the tire failure, strong crosswind, and a delay in transferring controls from the student.

ASRS:1777006.n: After takeoff Runway X on the ZZZZZ3 departure ZZZZZ transition, the Pilot Flying called for clean wing configuration, Climb Power and VNAV. Pilot Monitoring failed to properly select and verify the selected vertical command. PF flying did not receive the correct level off climb guidance. Human error focused on initially to cross ZZZZZ1 above 7,000 feet NOT at or below 7,000 feet. ATC immediately instructed aircraft to 'STOP CLIMB' and level off in which we complied with.Contributing factors:Pandemic and lack of flying time in last 6 months.Unfamiliar airport operations. At departure called for clean wing, CLB, VNAV. PM cleaned wing and selected VNAV;CLB. I as PF failed to verify new VCLB mode on PFD. Contributing factor: - on initial brief i misread SID as cross ZZZZZ above 7,000 feet. The SID requires a cross ZZZZZ below 7,000 feet. - last flight was July 2020.
ASRS:1777006.s: The Pilot Flying and Pilot Monitoring on a departure flight misread the SID, causing an incorrect climb above 7,000 feet instead of below. ATC issued a 'STOP CLIMB' instruction after the PF failed to verify the VNAV mode, attributed to pandemic-related lack of recent flying time.

ASRS:1777007.n: Took off from ZZZ in VFR and picked up IFR plan and was given clearance to 190. After passing through a thin layer I encountered a very large build up and the base was lower than the MEA. I was concerned for the safety of flight and descended below the MEA in order to clear the buildup. I did this without calling center. Center was very upset and canceled my flight plan. After clearing the buildup I began my climb again and was reissued my clearance.
ASRS:1777007.s: The pilot departed ZZZ in VFR, switched to IFR, and descended below the MEA without notifying Center to avoid a large cloud buildup with a base lower than the MEA. Center canceled the flight plan due to the unauthorized descent but reissued the clearance after the pilot cleared the weather.

ASRS:1777008.n: I was on an IFR flight plan to ZZZ descending out of 7000 to 4000 while talking to approach control. It was solid IMC. Tops were 7200, bases were 3800. While descending through 5500 I noted another aircraft on TCAS about 5 miles same altitude traveling toward me also descending. I queried ATC and they said he was a VFR aircraft not talking to ATC. I told ATC it appeared we were closing rapidly, I was given a 30 degree left turn which I immediately performed. The other aircraft at the same time seemed to turn toward me and kept descending. We were within a few miles, I then got a TCAS traffic alert. I started another left turn but the aircraft continued its track toward me. My TCAS showed our aircraft at same altitude and on top of each other on the screen. I then started a climb. I estimate the aircraft passed behind me and we missed by less than 50 feet. I then landed without any other issue. I told ATC that I feel that was real close and I was going to file a NASA report. When I cancelled my IFR on the ground control asked me to call them. I did and spoke to the controller. He verified that there was a loss of separation and that the aircraft was VFR and not talking to ATC. He was able to give me the aircraft type and tail number. I was able to find out who the pilot flying was and I called him to discuss. He said he was VFR, saw a mile wide hole in the clouds and wanted to descend which is when he turned toward me and descended. He said at one point he had me in sight but it was solid IMC. He does not have an instrument rating..
ASRS:1777008.s: An IFR pilot descending in IMC experienced a near-miss with a non-instrument rated VFR pilot who entered a cloud hole and descended toward them. Despite ATC issuing a left turn, the VFR aircraft continued its track, resulting in a loss of separation of less than 50 feet before the IFR pilot climbed to avoid collision.

ASRS:1777015.n: I was working two radar sectors combined with a trainee and trainer as my coordinator. The traffic volume was high with the normal arrivals, departures, overflights, and practice instrument approaches. The complexity was high due to a 10 minute notice of a flight check aircraft that needed to check an opposite direction approach. Once the flight check aircraft started his opposite direction approach I started briefing the relieving controller in training for a sector split. As the flight check aircraft had just finished with the opposite direction approach and continuing to brief the relieving controller for the split, I radar identified the flight check aircraft and turned him on course for the next approach. As all that was happening, I was descending and vectoring Aircraft X for the ILS approach to a different airport. Aircraft X was the second aircraft in the sequence of three for the ILS approach. As Aircraft X crossed 2 miles north of a satellite airport, Aircraft Y was departing VFR north bound climbing to 3,000 ft. without any communication with me. I called the traffic as soon as I saw the issue and Aircraft Y reported that he was maneuvering to avoid collision. A few seconds later Aircraft Y called VFR looking to pick up his IFR flight plan. Also the weather at each facility within the airspace was overcast or broken around 2,200 ft.
ASRS:1777015.s: An air traffic controller managing high traffic and a flight check aircraft lost radar contact with a VFR departing Aircraft Y while vectoring Aircraft X for an ILS approach. The controller issued a traffic alert after Aircraft Y climbed to 3,000 ft without communication, prompting the pilot to maneuver to avoid a collision in overcast weather.

ASRS:1777027.n: I signed Dangerous Goods Form for wet battery HAZMAT, only later did I realize that there needed to be a HAZMAT on board notation from Dispatch on the Dispatch Release notes section. This notation was missing. This notation is a recent change to the Dangerous Goods Form procedure.
ASRS:1777027.s: The pilot signed a Dangerous Goods Form for a wet battery but later discovered the required HAZMAT on board notation was missing from the Dispatch Release. This error occurred because the notation is a recent procedural change that was overlooked.

ASRS:1777033.n: During pushback a Flight Attendant called and informed me that a passenger was refusing to wear their face mask. I asked if she wished to have the passenger removed for non-compliance to which she responded in the affirmative. I had the push crew pull us backed to the gate and requested a Supervisor from operations. Arriving at the gate, the Flight Attendant informed me that she made four attempts to have the customer replace his mask over his nose to which he refused or was otherwise non-compliant. The Gate Agent boarded the plane and was unable to get the customer to wear the mask appropriately so he was removed.
ASRS:1777033.s: During pushback, the Captain and Flight Attendant reported a passenger refusing to wear a face mask. The aircraft was returned to the gate, and after failed attempts by crew and a Gate Agent to secure compliance, the passenger was removed.

ASRS:1777039.n: Departing ZZZ cleared to 6,000 ft. right turn [Heading] 240 off Runway XX after takeoff cleared direct to ZZZ1 [VOR] executed that on CDU (Control Display Unit), but it did not show on NAV (navigation) display on either Copilot or Captain side. Then issued direct to ZZZ2 [VOR] executed that in CDU still no magenta line for course guidance on either NAV display. CDU was working properly with course and distance. We then noticed we could not select STA WPT ARPT DATA POS from the NAV display selector panel. So we hard tuned the VOR in the CDU and asked for radar vectors to ZZZ2 [VOR] because it was 300 plus miles away. We noticed the lack of GPS on NAV display so I checked GPS in the CDU, it seemed to be working correctly. We informed ATC we were no longer slant Lima equipped. I called Dispatch for help and to get approval from ATC to operate that way. We received a reroute from ATC and Maintenance Control did not see any malfunctions with NAV system. Also our TCAS had malfunctioned during climbout, so we were no longer RVSM capable. We advised ATC of this also and descended. I went through the NAV unreliable checklist that was no help. After about 60 minutes of flight GPS and NAV display control panel started working normally TCAS was still inoperative.
ASRS:1777039.s: The crew experienced NAV display and TCAS failures during climbout from ZZZ, causing a loss of RVSM capability and requiring a reroute. Although CDU data remained valid, the displays failed to show guidance until GPS and NAV controls recovered after 60 minutes, while TCAS remained inoperative.

ASRS:1777055.n: Aircraft being pushed back from gate XX in ZZZ. Just prior to our pushback, another company had started to tow a type X aircraft from gate XX1 to XX2 (I didn't see which gate specifically as I was the wing-walker). The crew towing the type X aircraft cut across the ramp when they had plenty of room to maneuver around our flight and in the process give us plenty of room. The other company tow team's action forced me to motion to our pushback driver to stop the push ASAP. We stopped our push and the other company continued to their gate. Our crew then continued our push back and dispatched the flight normally. The X gates are being used for RON aircraft due to ongoing COVID-19 flight reductions.
ASRS:1777055.s: A wing-walker stopped a pushback at gate XX after another company's tow team cut across the ramp with a Type X aircraft, creating a conflict. The push resumed safely, and the flight dispatched normally despite the congestion caused by RON aircraft usage.

ASRS:1777113.n: Encountered severe ice and could not exit the conditions before losing ability to maintain altitude. Continued on with the approach to landing starting the approach 400 feet low.
ASRS:1777113.s: The pilot encountered severe ice, lost the ability to maintain altitude, and continued the approach starting 400 feet low. The report attributes the low approach to the inability to exit the icing conditions before altitude was lost.

ASRS:1777115.n: While in cruise flight Flight Attendant (FA) A called the flight deck. The First Officer answered the call. He told me the FA had a non-compliant passenger with the mask. He reported that she was tapping him trying to waken the passenger and he pushed her arm away. We transferred control and I called her back and asked it everything was OK and to repeat what happened. We ACARS Dispatch to have a Supervisor at gate. We were in range when we received the call and elected to continue to ZZZ. The passenger was mask non-compliant. He was told to cover his nose with the mask. He was sleeping when mask slid down. FA woke passenger with a tap, it may have startled him, but he pushed her hand away and swore.I believe the company has to make sure the passengers are aware of the seriousness of non-compliance.
ASRS:1777115.s: During cruise, a Flight Attendant tapped a sleeping passenger to correct mask non-compliance, causing him to push her hand away and swear. The crew contacted Dispatch for a supervisor at the gate but elected to continue to ZZZ.

ASRS:1777141.n: We noticed when we were doing the in-flight service that passing out the bottle of water/snack bag first, meant that all the passengers had their masks off as we were serving them from the bar cart. It would be safer for passengers and crew to serve the beverages first, then the snack bags as the amount of time the masks were off would be shorter. This would also limit our exposure time while passengers have their face masks off.
ASRS:1777141.s: Cabin crew reported that serving water and snacks simultaneously during in-flight service caused passengers to remove masks for extended periods. They recommend serving beverages first to shorten mask-off time and reduce exposure for both passengers and crew.

ASRS:1777142.n: Passengers were sitting in seats across from the jump-seat. There was not 6 feet between us. We were face-to-face! Our knees were touching. I'm concerned about the safety of not socially distancing between Crew jump-seats and passenger seating.
ASRS:1777142.s: Cabin crew reported that passengers seated opposite jump-seats were less than six feet away, resulting in face-to-face contact and touching knees. The crew expressed safety concerns regarding the lack of social distancing between crew jump-seats and passenger seating.

ASRS:1777151.n: Upon boarding [Passenger X] was noted to have a valve connected to his mask board. As Flight Attendant A was able to ask the valve be covered with one of the on board masks or swapped at his discretion due to the company not permitting direct exhaust valves. He indicated his mask had filters on the interior and was disappointed he could not use his preferred mask. After discussing with crew we agreed the valve at least needed to be covered or swapped out. Mask was swapped prior to departure. Advised I had asked for a Supervisor to ensure we were on the same page regarding masks and valves noting it was not my intent to single him out or pick on him, but wanted to ensure we were on the same page for policy. The passenger thanked me and we departed for ZZZ1.Enforce policy at gate.
ASRS:1777151.s: A flight attendant and a passenger disagreed over a prohibited exhaust valve on the passenger's mask during boarding. The passenger swapped the mask to comply with company policy before the flight departed for ZZZ1.

ASRS:1777153.n: During accomplishment of portable water system disinfect done by using ozone cart, as instructed by fellow mechanic assigned as support, (name unknown). I might have improperly connected the water supply line. This happened at ZZZ [Gate] around XA:00 [Date]. As soon as I noticed water coming out of the aft fuselage drain holes, I immediately stopped the re circulation process, notified crew chef, dumped over serviced wasted and requested for assistance form tech crew personnel.Lack of work experience with this specific task on my part, lack of assigned training, inability to complete work interdependently due to not having D1 endorsement and being able to drive on airport premises and move around with equipment and tools. Hostile work environment.Assigned training required to completed before being assigned to perform ozone cards, different diameter or tread pattern on water fill line attainment port preventing from improper installation, picture diagrams included in revised work card, hands on ozone unit classroom training, ZZZ ramp driving credentials, hangar access in below freezing conditions, better gate illumination, larger port markings allowing to differentiate between both ports housed only 3 ft. apart. I was assigned to drive new transfer AMT's around since none of them had their DR1/3. One group required the 'blue cart' for water servicing, and the tech responsible for the job asked me questions about it. I gave him a basic description of the job, helped hooked the FILL line to the FILL nipple, and showed him the correct adapter for the job and threaded it in to show it was the right fit. After which I left to move other techs around. When I came back to the gate, that's when the results of the improper servicing occurred. The event occurred at [Gate] at roughly XA:00 on [Date] during the cycling phase of the disinfect.
ASRS:1777153.s: A mechanic improperly connected a water supply line during an ozone disinfection cycle at a gate, causing water to leak from aft fuselage drains. The reporter attributed the error to lack of specific training, inability to drive equipment due to missing endorsements, and a hostile work environment.

ASRS:1777166.n: This submission is not to report and accident, rather a serious incident under FAA and NTSB definitions. The day before the flight, my wife and I planned to attend a meeting in ZZZ1. I moved the helicopter out of the hangar and had it fueled to the 1/2 full point. We contacted the church where we were going and obtained permission and authorization to land on the property. Early the morning of the flight, I opened ForeFlight and briefed weather, winds, and the anticipated location, and sent a screenshot of the map and location to my rotorcraft instructor. He and I then had a conversation about the steps and procedures to assess the location once I arrived, and we discussed how to set up for the landing. At XA:00 my wife and I met our friends at the ZZZ airport, performed the preflight, calculated a weight and balance, loaded up in the helicopter and headed for ZZZ1. The weather was excellent with good visibility and cool temperatures in the 50's to 60's. After the 20 min flight, upon arriving at our landing zone, I circled twice as a part of our reconnaissance and did our steps of the 600 ft. recon: size, surrounding, surface, slope, safety and then the 300 ft. recon: wind, wires, way in, way out, where to auto. The landing was normal and I secured the helicopter and we attended the meeting and luncheon. After the luncheon, I went out to the helicopter and started my preflight. During my walk around, I walked out to the road next to the church and looked in all directions. I observed wires to the north across the highway, to the east I observed wires, the church building was to our south, and I cleared the area to the west visually, and saw it was open and unobstructed, the wind was from the west. Once the preflight was complete, I recalculated the weight and balance, all was good, we were more than 200 lbs. under the gross weight limit, and with the temperature in the mid 60s, performance showed to be real good, so we loaded back in the helicopter. After going over the passenger briefing and seeing that all passengers were buckled up and ready I started the helicopter. After all checklist items were completed, and the warmup was accomplished, I lifted into a stable hover, maneuvered up and out toward the highway. Once again I looked for any traffic, and noted that the intended flight path was into the wind, and to the west, was clear and unobstructed. As we were in the hover, I pushed forward cyclic and just as we started a normal takeoff, my front seat passenger said 'WIRE' and I suddenly saw a wire just ahead of us! I immediately applied aft cyclic and pulled up collective. I felt the impact with the wire, and I identified that the center of the highway was clear with zero traffic. I initiated an immediate landing. Approximately 2-3 seconds after not clearing the wire, we were on the ground, and I recall the landing as straight and level, firm and smooth. I shutdown the helicopter, made sure all passengers were out safely and well clear of the helicopter and off the highway. I then secured the helicopter. Next I installed the ground handling wheels on the helicopter and with the help of my passenger, we pushed the helicopter off the highway to the north, then 200 ft. up a side road and into my friend's side yard. At that point I was able to take a moment, thankful for all the help and assistance received, and beyond thankful for no injuries. To prevent a recurrence and to avoid this situation in the future: I contacted my flight instructor and walked through the incident scenario, and I have discussed how to avoid this situation in the future. This incident could have been avoided or prevented by driving by vehicle instead of flying. Also, this incident could have been prevented by performing and executing a confined area takeoff, thus avoiding areas that might have lines and wires. I did walk the area to be used for my takeoff path during my preflight, and I had already performed my 600 ft. and 300 ft. recon prior to landing, so by asking a larger area, and looking closer and further down the takeoff are, might have been of value.
ASRS:1777166.s: A pilot and passengers in a helicopter struck a wire during takeoff from a church landing zone despite prior visual reconnaissance. The pilot executed an immediate emergency landing on the highway, resulting in no injuries, and attributed the incident to failing to identify the wire during the preflight walk-around.

ASRS:1777169.n: I am reporting my misinterpretation of the COVID relief provided by SFAR 118-1, which resulted in my acting as PIC beyond by required flight review date.My last flight review was in Month X 2018, so normally I would need another one by Month X 2020. But I saw a headline online (maybe from [organization] or another similar site) that the end dates had been extended due to COVID relief, so I didn't worry about the expiration too much - many official agencies have been extending deadlines for things like driver's license renewals etc., and I assumed FAA had done the same. So I flew once in Month Y and once in Month Z, the last flight being to take my plane to a maintenance shop for its annual.I then started thinking about getting a flight review, so I decided to read SFAR 118-1 to determine exactly what relief the FAA had provided and whether it would last until my plane was ready. To my surprise, there were requirements about recent experience, type of operation, the need to take Wings courses, etc. - it was much more complicated than just an extension of time.But I determined that I did meet the requirements, provided I took the required Wings courses, I decided that both getting my plane back from an annual when it was finished, and traveling to a flight review were operations required by the FAR's and were thus permitted. The annual took longer than expected, but I saw headlines that the relief had been extended with SFAR 118-2. When the plane was ready to be picked up on Month C day 2, I took the required Wings courses and flew my aircraft back from the maintenance base, thinking that I had until Month C day 31 to complete a BFR.Then on Month C day 14 while preparing for my flight review later that day, I carefully read SFAR 118-2 so I could explain to the CFI how I had adhered to it. At that point I realized that while its relief should have applied to the end of my plane's annual, the delay in the annual's completion plus the fact that the FAA's further extensions did not apply to me meant that I had exceeded the relief allowed by SFAR 118.To summarize, the SFAR is new and complicated and I mis-interpreted it despite a good-faith effort to comply.I think the substance of the SFAR is reasonable now that I understand it, and although it's vague in places, I understand that it's an emergency regulation, so it doesn't seem too bad. I think what would have helped me is a requirement that, in order to use the relief offered by SFAR 118, one of the required Wings courses should have been a tutorial on SFAR 118 itself.My flights past the Flight Review deadline were uneventful and I am of course no longer flying until my next Flight Review is complete (I started it on Month C day 14 as stated but the flight portion was delayed due to weather). I doubt that SFAR 118 will be relevant much longer, but I think adding a Wings course the next time some complicated new SFAR comes out would go a long way towards increasing compliance and understanding.
ASRS:1777169.s: The pilot acted as PIC beyond their flight review date while operating a personal aircraft due to misinterpreting COVID relief provisions in SFAR 118-1 and 118-2. Although the flights were uneventful, the pilot ceased operations upon realizing the relief did not cover their specific situation and began a new flight review.

ASRS:1777170.n: Following issuance of a first class medical under special issuance for sleep apnea, conducted a flight for a flight review with a qualified flight instructor. This flight was conducted a few weeks after the first possible dose of an investigational vaccine for COVID-19. The vaccine was unapproved for general use, and the trial the pilot is participating in phase 3 at the time of the flight and currently. The pilot has subsequently taken a second possible dose, but was unaware of any potential FAA interpretation that participation in a vaccine trial was potentially medically disqualifying, he treated the situation as with any vaccination and self certified himself as fit to fly having no adverse symptoms. This may have been incorrect for the moment, but was done in good faith at the time.
ASRS:1777170.s: A pilot with a special issuance medical certificate conducted a flight review shortly after receiving an investigational COVID-19 vaccine. The pilot self-certified as fit to fly in good faith, unaware that participation in the vaccine trial was potentially medically disqualifying under FAA regulations.

ASRS:1777174.n: Upon landing on the centerline of runway at ZZZ the airplane made an uncommanded turn to the left. Even with rudder input and braking I could not keep the airplane on the runway. The left wing clipped the 3,000 ft. remaining sign. Winds were 340 (degrees) at 12 (knots) gusting to 19, (pretty much straight down the runway). Inspection of the airplane showed that during the excursion the nose gear was completely sideways such that the 'Goodyear' was worn off of the sidewall.I do not have 'lazy feet.' I believe that my quick response to the airplanes movements prevented more damage as I was able to stop the airplane just off the runway. I have been flying PA46 airplanes for eleven years including 300+ hours in the Matrix and 1000+ hours in the Meridian/M600.There is no good explanation for the airplane's diversion. Subsequently I found out that there have been 5 other M600s that have experienced no less than 7 similar excursions. I and others believe there is a material problem with the PA46 M600.
ASRS:1777174.s: The pilot reported an uncommanded left turn during landing on a PA46 M600, causing a runway excursion where the left wing clipped a sign and the nose gear was damaged. The pilot attributed the incident to a suspected material problem with the aircraft, noting similar excursions in other M600s.

ASRS:1777190.n: My wife and I planned a round trip to visit some friends at a church in ZZZ and have lunch after the meeting. Our granddaughter stayed the night with us prior to our flight the next morning. She travels with us often and enjoys the trips, and has flown with us since she was born. The next morning, we arrived at the airport and boarded the aircraft along with our friend and his wife. I did a weight and balance, and it came out more than 200 lbs under the gross weight limit. I verified and center of gravity and weight were well within limits. My wife had our granddaughter sit next to her in the seat, and I made sure they were buckled. Together they weighed less than 170 lbs and seemed to fit comfortably in the one seat. We departed mid morning. We had a good meeting and lunch in ZZZ, and after lunch we all got back in the aircraft and buckled up ready to go back. It occurred to me that our granddaughter is now 6 years old, and even though she is approximately the same height and weight as when she was 4 and 5, she should have her own seat and seat belt. In the future I will make sure each occupant of age has his or her own seat and seat belt, so they can be properly buckled and restrained.
ASRS:1777190.s: The pilot reported that a 6-year-old granddaughter shared a seat with her grandmother during a round trip, weighing under 170 lbs combined. The pilot concluded the child required her own seat and seat belt for proper restraint in future flights.

ASRS:1777195.n: Please consider changing/eliminating the Deer Valley One procedure!The Deer Valley One obstacle departure is improbable if not impossible in a high-performance airplane.1. Chart does not tell you how close the turn is.2. Turn needs to be completed by 1.6 nm from end of runway! This alone should never never be permitted.3. Turn radius at 200 kts. is likely about 1.3 nm.4. 400 ft. V2 +10 flaps up igniters off Venr takes about 2nm min. And way longer in this scenario.5. And wait until you add what happened to me, a traffic call for departing traffic on parallel runway in the direction of my needed turn.6. That took time to find and alter course to avoid the traffic that was about 500 ft. away at the same altitude!6b. That traffic prohibited a turn to [Heading] 336 as required to occur at about 100 ft. if I was to make the turn in time.7. Then the TCAS resolution screen took time to resolve that first conflict.8. Then the instant that screen was resolved, a second additional 'traffic traffic' call occurred for another item of traffic that I could never visually acquire. Box said above and slightly ahead as I recall. Right near my course, so it was a serious safety concern.9. Then the second TCAS screen took time to resolve that second traffic call.10. Now it's finally time for 400 ft. V2 + 10, flaps up igniters off, recall Venr.11. By this time I'm coming upon 5,000 ft. considering engaging the autopilot, but the Flight Director is not aligned because so close and capturing.12. Stuff it down to capture, but overshot 5,000 ft. slightly.13. And now it's finally time to do the turn, but ATC asked what's up.Well ...How can you design a turn that needs to be completed in 1.6nm which would mean it must be started at about 100 ft. AGL = unsafe & no jet should turn before 400 ft. as trained.And look at the chart, no indication how close that is.And compounding my situation is that the PXR VOR was out of service.I submit it's impossible in a high performance airplane. Do it in the sim without telling the pilot in advance and with and without being a regular at the field, and I estimate you'll get max 10% compliance. Who would design for a 90% potential of non-compliance?Please have them redesign/eliminate this departure!
ASRS:1777195.s: A pilot reported that the Deer Valley One departure is unsafe for high-performance aircraft due to a required turn within 1.6 nm and conflicting traffic calls that delayed the maneuver. The pilot attributed the difficulty to the tight turn radius, multiple TCAS resolutions, and an out-of-service PXR VOR, resulting in an overshoot of 5,000 ft.

ASRS:1777197.n: Just a little confusion on my part. I was cleared direct to the FAF for the approach. The crossing altitude was high. I was cleared for the approach, being cleared direct to the fix, I was a little confused as to whether I should execute the procedure turn, because of the direction I was coming from. When I went to query the controller to confirm this, he became saturated with radio calls from other aircraft. I began the turn to intercept, got established on the inbound course, began descending to intercept, but was far too high on the glide slope, to safely get stabilized while inside the FAF. The controller gave me the hand off to tower. Knowing I was going to have to execute a steep descent to intercept the glide slope, I made the decision to level off and begin the missed approach. When I contacted tower, I notified them I was going missed, they instructed me to fly the published missed and contact Center. I reestablished contact with center, flew the published missed, and got the plane set-up for my next approach. What I could have done different. Exercised my PIC (Pilot in Command) authority and executed the procedure turn based off the angle I was approaching the final approach course from, and my high crossing altitude and communicate with ATC earlier and more assertively about my concerns. How the system can be improved. Provide clear guidance in the AIM, Instrument Flying Handbook, and Instrument Procedures Hand book, about when to execute a procedure turn when cleared direct a fix. Depending on the angle you are going to intercept the course and where the fix is located on the approach one may or may not necessitate a procedure turn to get established. When cleared to a fix are you technically on a vector because you are going from a point in space direct to a fix? Are you essentially flying a self-assigned heading via GPS to that point? This is a bit of a gray area that could use some clarification. On GPS approaches this is fairly clear, especially on approaches that are constructed within a Terminal Arrival Area (TAA). On GPS approaches without a TAA and non GPS approaches, this can be a little confusing.
ASRS:1777197.s: The pilot, cleared direct to the FAF with a high crossing altitude, became confused about executing a procedure turn and was too high to stabilize on the glide slope. Consequently, the pilot executed a missed approach, attributing the event to unclear guidance on procedure turn requirements when cleared direct to a fix.

ASRS:1777205.n: [Aircraft X] was on an IFR flight to ZZZ1 on [Airway1] at 9,000 ft. There was another aircraft on [Airway2] also landing ZZZ1 just handed off to me also at 9,000 ft. The adjacent sector asked me if I would like [Aircraft X] at a different altitude and I gave them 8,000 ft., which they complied with. Upon further review that was below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude of 8,600 ft. and [Airway2]'s Minimum IFR Altitude of 8,400 ft. I should have been more aware of the Minimum IFR Altitudes along [Airway2].
ASRS:1777205.s: An air traffic controller cleared Aircraft X to 8,000 ft while it was on Airway1, but this altitude was below the 8,600 ft Minimum Vectoring Altitude and the 8,400 ft Minimum IFR Altitude for the adjacent Airway2. The controller attributed the error to a lack of awareness regarding the Minimum IFR Altitudes along Airway2.

ASRS:1777222.n: Family of four delayed flight due to their 2 year and two month old and 5 year old not wearing masks. Mother told Agent, Supervisor and flight attendants [the] children would be fed for entire flight to avoid wearing masks. After I was briefed on the situation we had the Supervisor repeat the mask requirements which they agreed to follow. During the flight the father was asked to put on his mask and he pointed at his cup of soda and cookie, but would not speak. By pointing at the soda/cookie he was indicating he did not have to wear his mask. This went on for a long period of time during our 3 plus hour flight. Our flight was close to capacity. I also informed Dispatch and asked for a Supervisor to meet the flight as the family was supposed to connect on another flight.
ASRS:1777222.s: Flight attendants reported a family of four on a near-capacity, three-hour flight who refused to wear masks, claiming children would eat continuously. The father repeatedly gestured at food to avoid compliance, prompting the crew to notify Dispatch and request a supervisor for the family's connection.

ASRS:1777230.n: Aircraft X, ZZZZ-ZZZ1 was the continuation of a planned [refueling stop] for ZZZ-ZZZ1. Thus the passengers remained on the plane while there was a crew change and fueling. The crew inbound from ZZZ reported that the APU failed multiple start attempts after landing. ZZZZ Maintenance was working to fix the APU and was in and out of the cockpit and the lower E&E bay.Upon boarding the aircraft my FO requested that external air be connected to the aircraft. After some time we were told that air conditioned air was not available, as the airport had 'switched' over to heat. Wanting to get some (any) airflow on the aircraft we requested that it be connected. Again after some time we were informed that no external air was available at the particular gate. At that point we requested a start-cart unit be connected so that we could use it to run the packs. Eventually this was accomplished, but only after the passengers had been onboard without any cabin airflow for an extended time, perhaps 90 minutes.Early upon arriving in the cockpit, I called dispatch to inform her of the problem and to let her know that we'd keep her in the loop as maintenance worked the problem. During our initial time in the cockpit the two mechanics were coming and going and I multiple times, offered to get out of the cockpit to allow them access to the displays as they worked the problem. Eventually, I left as they were paying no attention to social distancing, often reaching over us to access the FMC keypad. Though they were wearing masks, they were often pulling them down to talk on the radio or the phone. Multiple times I had to ask them to replace their masks over their mouth and nose. I felt they were too focused on their work and forgetting the COVID precautions.After some time, my concern changed from maintenance getting the APU fixed, to them not being able to get it fixed. Normally, I'd have little to no issue operating a flight without an APU, however with the on-going pandemic there are additional considerations. I thus called the dispatcher and let her know of my concerns and asked if she would reach out to the Operations Center OM for what airline plans are for an inop APU in today's environment and to get more information / guidance to aide in our decision making. Eventually, I was informed that the Operations Center OM had simply said that 'We had to get the passengers to ZZZZ1.' This was not information, guidance nor helpful. My responsibilities are to do that safely and given the pandemic we needed more information to help us assess and understand the passenger safety implications. I was VERY disappointed with the lack of understanding, information and support from the Operations Center. Our dispatcher, and her relief, did a FANTASTIC job!I also attempted to find the information related to running the APU during the pandemic. Unfortunately, given the format, there is no way to read the titles without opening each one. It was too time consuming at that time, thus I was unable to access the needed information. The display really needs to be made user-friendly.The Dispatcher was able to coordinate with ZZZZ1 and we were told from the dispatcher that ZZZZ1 had external air and a start cart and could support a no APU operation. I asked that they be informed that we would plan on keeping an engine running until both external electric AND air were connected so as to maintain cabin airflow.We eventually agreed to accept the flight with the APU deferred believing that we had a viable operational plan, no thanks to the Operations Center. Upon arrival in ZZZZ1 there was much confusion, likely due to language barriers. It took some time to understand that there were local rules that prohibited them from connecting external air or a start-cart while an engine was running. Once we shut down the left engine it was +10 minutes before external air was connected to the aircraft.Given the on-going pandemic the key is airflow. Yet it appears there has been no planning or consideration of what to do in the event of an inop APU. I feel that on this flight we completely blew our promise to passengers and employees with regards to airflow and air filtration. I've continued to assess how I could have made better decisions, but can find no guidance or related plans. I'm not sure but perhaps refusing the aircraft and deplaning the passengers would have been safer from a COVID standpoint than leaving them on an aircraft without any airflow for such an extended period. I believe that we need to come up with some clear plans, guidance and actions to support a flight if we are going to operate with an inop APU. Perhaps we need to even ask if given the pandemic and Airline's associated messaging if we should even operate with an inop APU.I'm not sure why ZZZZ was unable to fix the APU, as the ZZZZ1 mechanics were able to identify and fix the problem in less than 30 minutes from block-in!
ASRS:1777230.s: The flight crew and maintenance personnel faced an APU failure during a refueling stop at ZZZZ, leaving passengers without cabin airflow for 90 minutes due to unavailable ground equipment. The crew deferred the APU to continue to ZZZZ1, where local rules delayed external air connection, highlighting a lack of pandemic-specific guidance for operating with an inoperative APU.

ASRS:1777238.n: After takeoff at approximately 1600 ft. there was a loud rumbling and shudder from the right engine with a loss of power from around 98 N1 to 27 N1. No vibrations or exceedances and engine remained running at idle with no response. After the thrust loss in the right engine we treated it as an engine failure and proceeded to clean up the airplane. I declared a Pan Pan Pan and notified ATC of the engine failure. After the airplane was stabilized we leveled at 3000 ft. and started the turn to downwind for the return to the runway. We initially started with the Engine Fire Severe Damage Checklist but switched to the Engine Stall Surge after we realized the engine was running fine at idle. Engine did not respond to throttle movements. I elected to keep it running since there were no vibrations or exceedances. Since the First Officer (FO) had the airplane well in hand I continued planning for the return and Flaps 20 landing. The approach and landing were uneventful and the Fire Brigade was standing by. We shut down the right engine clearing the runway. The Fire Brigade verified the engine and airplane were okay so we taxied to the ramp. Lessons learned: During the cleanup, I missed turning off the auto throttle arm switch hitting my flight director switch instead. Error was caught as FLCH and MCT (Flight Level Change and Maximum Continuous Thrust) was selected after flaps up as the auto throttles started to advance. I originally started in one checklist then switched due to the engine was still providing electrical, pneumatic and hydraulics at idle. Not sure I totally voiced that change to the FO but we did discuss leaving the engine running and agreed it was the best course of action. I used the Performance page in the ACARS to get landing data...it was cumbersome and could lead to errors. I changed the airport to pull up the runways but the fuel was as if we had flown to destination. I was able to change it but prefer the simple charts in the QRH when time is short. All in all, great CRM between us caught errors and made for a good outcome. After takeoff at approximately 1800 ft. there was a loud bang and the airplane shook as if we hit something. I asked the Captain, 'what was that?' The Captain responded, 'Right engine failure / No N1' with a loss of power. No vibrations or exceedances and engine remained running with no EICAS messages. I felt very comfortable with flying the airplane to let the Captain handle most of the managerial issues. We continued planning for the return and Flaps 20 landing. SOP saves the day. The scenario [was] very similar to annual training. We felt very comfortable with the handling the situation.
ASRS:1777238.s: The Captain and First Officer experienced a right engine power loss at 1600–1800 ft after takeoff, with the engine remaining at idle without vibrations. They declared a Pan Pan, returned for an uneventful Flaps 20 landing, and attributed the successful outcome to effective CRM and adherence to SOPs.

ASRS:1777281.n: After an auto brakes 3 landing, we taxied to the gate. Upon arrival to the gate, we accepted ground power and shut down the number one engine. I went to the back to crack the door. Returning to the flight deck, the external power was flickering and kicking on and off. The Captain started the APU as we noticed a smell. Thinking it was associated with the electrical fluctuations we looked around the flight deck for evidence of a tripped circuit breaker. After a few moments, a mechanic came up to the aircraft to inform us the aircraft is on fire. We expeditiously exited the aircraft. Maintenance explained it was a main landing gear fire due to a hydraulic leak.Hydraulic leak in the left main landing gear well and associated fire. 'Fire' was left out of the maintenance write-up. The fire department was called and responded. The mechanic that came on board to inform us after the fire had been fought described the aircraft as 'on fire;' but 'fire' was not communicated in the write-up. During shutdown after block in, I noticed an acrid smell in the cockpit. My First Officer (FO) smelled the same thing, we had no cockpit indications that indicated any problems. I asked the FO to leave the jet via the stairs as I shut the aircraft down. Shortly after maintenance came into the cockpit and told me to evacuate the jet because there was a fire. Maintenance notified the ARFF (Aircraft Rescue and Fire Fighting) service and they were on the scene as I got to the foot of the steps.Per maintenance, a hydraulic leak associated with malfunctioning electrical hydraulic pump.
ASRS:1777281.s: The flight crew detected an acrid smell and electrical fluctuations during post-landing shutdown, prompting an evacuation after maintenance reported a fire. The incident was caused by a hydraulic leak in the left main landing gear well from a malfunctioning pump, which ignited and required ARFF response.

ASRS:1777306.n: On arrival into ZZZ from the south, we were vectored off of the ZZZZZ procedure and held high due to traffic. We had been previously queried as to our RVR requirements for [Runway] XXR. We were set up and briefed for CATIII approach to XXR. Just prior to ZZZZZ waypoint, we heard traffic ahead cleared to descend via ZZZZZ arrival landing north. We were then given clearance to descend via the arrival landing north and were unable to meet the new crossing restrictions. Due to 71 knot crosswinds our heading was 320. The vector we were given for descent was 340. This was assumed to be a 360 for descent. As we turned through a heading of 260 ish we were told to make an immediate right turn for restricted airspace. We complied. We continued on the arrival and had an uneventful hand off to approach.I believe that the ATC is currently overworked due to COVID cutbacks. Many communications are being missed in the last months because ATC are covering too many sectors. Our lack of fore warnings regarding the changes to airport configuration left us with inadequate situational awareness. We followed the vectors given to us with incorrect assumptions. I'm grateful that this situation was resolved without incident. My recommendation is that we begin to re-staff ATC to normal pre-COVID operation. Flight was left high on the ZZZZZ Arrival. ATIS had us landing on [Runway] XXR. We were cleared for the ZZZZZX but never informed by ATC that ATIS X special was issued at XA22z we only learned that there was a runway change due from listing to arrival aircraft in front of us. We were now high for landing [Runway] YYL by 6,000 feet at the same time we were instructed to slow to 190 kts. We can slow down but not go down at the same time. We were instructed to fly heading 340 as we descended the controller once again said turn left 340 which we were on and we assumed he wanted us to do a 360 which is common to loose altitude and rejoin the arrival. He was busy with several other aircraft left high the weather was poor in mild turbulence. The next call was for us to turn I believe 040 because he said we are going to hit a restricted area.I was heads down retrieving the new ATIS as well and programming the FMS for a different runway. This was a combination of change of runways, poor weather, and aircraft being left high by two controllers and high winds with an approach to mins. This was a series of events that lead to an aircraft being out of position.When the weather is poor we cannot skimp on air traffic controllers they need to be tentative to aircraft and where they are going. If the aircraft is out of position. It should be quickly realize especially when a runway change has been posted and an aircraft may not have received the special ATIS.
ASRS:1777306.s: Pilots reported being left 6,000 feet high on the ZZZZZ arrival due to ATC staffing shortages, missed runway change notifications, and conflicting descent vectors in poor weather. The crew made incorrect assumptions about a 340-degree heading instruction, leading to a restricted airspace violation before an immediate corrective turn was issued.

ASRS:1777348.n: Pilot left ZZZ with 2.5 hrs. fuel and .5 hr. reserve. Navigated to ZZZ1 and completed 3 TO/LD (Takeoffs/Landings). Navigated to practice area and did turns across road. Navigated to square field to practice square turns around a field. Ground reference maneuvers conducted at 800 ft. AGL. Leveling off out of second turn engine died. Pilot glanced at fuel gauges and noted left tank over half full and right tank empty. Applied full power, mixture rich, carburetor heat on. Engine revived a few times while approaching suitable landing field. Landed in soft mud. Momentum carried tail over. Aircraft came to rest inverted. Pilot sustained no injuries.
ASRS:1777348.s: A pilot practicing ground reference maneuvers at 800 ft AGL experienced an engine failure due to fuel exhaustion in the right tank. The aircraft landed in soft mud, flipped inverted, and came to rest with the pilot sustaining no injuries.

ASRS:1777357.n: On take off from PLU, an unsafe condition took place that could have resulted in an aircraft collision.PLU's runway mid-point is higher than both thresholds. There's a taxiway that crosses over the southern threshold of the runway. I was departing from the north to the south. I made routine radio calls. Just prior to the midway point, I was off the runway and climbing, but I was not yet high enough to see the other end of the runway. At that point, another aircraft made a radio call that it was crossing the runway. No more than about a second later, I was high enough to see the end of the runway, and I saw the aircraft. It was passing left-to-right from my point of view. I veered left slightly and continued my climb.I don't know if the operator of that aircraft heard my radio call. The operator did not respond to my follow-up call that I was in the air departing and veering to the left. The operator could not have made the crossing threshold call more than a second or two before actually crossing the runway. I suspect the operator did not make a full stop prior to encountering the threshold.Had I experienced any sort of engine problem on my take-off roll or during the very early portion of the climb, the safest action would have been to land straight ahead on the remaining runway. However, in that case, I consider it likely I would have collided with the crossing aircraft.Threshold-crossing aircraft should listen to the radio before approaching the runway, and then should come to a complete stop before crossing the runway, should then only proceed with crossing after hearing no conflicting aircraft.
ASRS:1777357.s: A pilot departing PLU north to south encountered a runway incursion when another aircraft crossed the southern threshold while the pilot was climbing. The reporter suspects the crossing aircraft failed to stop or listen for conflicting traffic, creating a collision risk that was avoided by veering left.

ASRS:1777376.n: While working Radar West a C-130 came off of LRF requesting direct to HERCK intersection to hold. I misread the approach plate with the holding procedures and issued an altitude of 2000'. The hold at HERCK is depicted at 3000'. The aircraft entered a 2200' MVA while holding at 2000'. I noticed the MVA as they entered it and immediately climbed them to 2200'.
ASRS:1777376.s: An air traffic controller issued a C-130 an incorrect holding altitude of 2000' at HERCK due to misreading the approach plate, while the procedure required 3000'. The aircraft entered a 2200' MVA, prompting the controller to immediately climb it to 2200'.

ASRS:1777379.n: I was working the R1 position. Aircraft X was inbound from the south requested RNAV [Runway] XX approach to get below the deck and requested to proceed via own navigation to ZZZZZ. I cleared Aircraft X to maintain and cross ZZZZZ at or above 5,700 ft., RNAV [Runway] XX ZZZ Approach. Aircraft Y was inbound from the east, and instructed to hold east of ZZZ at 6,000 ft. for sequence behind Aircraft X. Aircraft X was radar service terminated and switched to ZZZ Tower. ZZZ Tower had not been advised of Aircraft Y in holding. At approximately 5.5 mile, ZZZ Tower called and advised Aircraft X was requesting a 360. I approved Aircraft X request. When I observed Aircraft X continuing to travel eastbound, I called ZZZ Tower to verify Aircraft X had canceled IFR. ZZZ Tower advised they had not canceled IFR. When I observed Aircraft X began to climb higher than 4,600 ft. eventually up to 5,200 ft., I issued Aircraft Y to continue in holding except to climb to 7,000 ft. CA went into alarm, I issued a traffic alert to Aircraft Y and advised a right turn heading 360 and to climb and maintain 7,000 ft. I called ZZZ Tower and asked them to switch Aircraft X back to me. Aircraft X was still on Tower's frequency and they rejoined the RNAV [Runway] XX at 10.5 miles and continued inbound.On initial call from ZZZ Tower, I should have verified that Aircraft X had canceled IFR with Tower. I could have instructed Aircraft Y to hold at 7,000 ft. from the initial call.
ASRS:1777379.s: An air traffic controller managing Aircraft X and Y experienced a conflict when X climbed above 4,600 ft while Y held at 6,000 ft, triggering a CA alarm. The controller attributed the incident to failing to verify X's IFR cancellation with Tower and delayed instructing Y to climb to 7,000 ft.

ASRS:1777385.n: Training on North radar, Aircraft X a VFR CN35 at 065 just maneuvering about 15miles south of the CRP airport. Aircraft Y, IFR at 060 flying southbound underneath the CN35. No traffic restriction was given to the CN35 nor was traffic issued to either aircraft. About 7 minutes later the Aircraft X wants to report a near midair and says he had to respond to a TCAS hit for traffic. There was no other traffic close to the Aircraft X so it had to be the Aircraft Y at 060 who he was referencing. Too much confidence in the trainee led me to not ensure the traffic was issued. Take action and instruct trainee to issue traffic or restriction when you see the situation.
ASRS:1777385.s: An ATC trainee failed to issue traffic advisories to a VFR CN35 and an IFR aircraft flying 1,000 feet below, resulting in a TCAS alert and near midair collision. The controller attributed the incident to overconfidence in the trainee's ability to manage the situation without supervision.

ASRS:1777396.n: Flight Attendant was preparing for door closure checking bins and seat belts. Upon reaching Passenger X in XX2 noticed young man mid twenties wearing mask below his nose. She asked him to pull his mask up and got no response. She motioned to him to get his attention and repeated herself, but he just stared straight ahead in defiance. She had to repeat herself and asked if he understood English. He made an eye roll and told her, 'You can leave now;' dismissing her instructions.The Flight Attendant approached the cockpit and told me the situation. We were now past departure time and I stepped back to reiterate the mask policy verbally. When I approached his seat, he was staring straight ahead with the mask just barely over his nose. I explained Airline has a mask policy for everyone on the airplane except when actively eating or drinking, and that he was not being singled out and needed to follow the instructions of the flight attendants. His response in a raised voice was, 'I'm wearing the [expletive] mask!' and 'You're making me angry.'I asked him why he was angry and then what he thought he would do when he got angry. He just tried to stare me down and I decided there was no point in continuing this conversation with him. I made the decision to have Customer Service remove him from the full flight to prevent anymore altercations once airborne.
ASRS:1777396.s: A pilot and flight attendant encountered a defiant passenger on the ground who refused to wear his mask properly. The pilot decided to have Customer Service remove the passenger from the full flight to prevent potential altercations once airborne.

ASRS:1777423.n: While boarding for our ZZZ-ZZZ1 flight, the Fwd FA came into the flight deck to tell us about a rude passenger. Passenger boarded the plane without wearing a mask and took a seat in X1. The Fwd FA approached and reminded passenger about the required mask policy. Passenger reluctantly complied and as the FA turned to walk away, the passenger called her an '[expletive]'.
