After the FA informed us about this, I first asked the FA if passenger is being disruptive. The FA stated that passenger was not. I then asked if she would like me to go speak to the passenger. The FA stated that was not necessary. Finally, I asked if she would like me to request a customer service representative. The FA again said no, the situation is under control and she would let us know if the problem continues. I messaged my Dispatcher to keep them in the loop of what was said. We pushed, de-iced, and while taxing to our assigned runway, I asked the FO to call and make sure there were no further issues in the back. The FA stated that the passenger had fallen asleep, so we elected to continue. About mid-way through the flight, the Fwd FA called up and stated that the passenger had woken up and was starting to cause some disturbances. The FO was already the PF and I asked him to take radios as well. The passenger asked for a cup of water so passenger didn't have to wear the mask because she was 'drinking'. The FAs let this go on for about '30 minutes' (quoting them) and the passenger had not drank any of the water. Passenger again was non-compliant with the mask and both FAs asked passenger three times to wear the mask. At this point, I sent another message asking for a customer service representative to meet us at the gate in ZZZ1 and explained to the Dispatcher everything the FAs had told me. About 5 minutes after that, the Fwd FA called up again. Again, I told the FO his controls, his radios. The FA then explained that the passenger was now starting to 'scream' on the plane and yelled very loudly, '#@%^! I'm not from [foreign country]!' While doing this, proceeded to flip off both FAs. I again messaged our Dispatcher with this information and now requested Security along with the customer service representative. The FAs and I talked back forth regarding passenger danger level. The passenger was remaining in the seat and making no other threatening gestures, so we did not see the need to declare an Emergency. We continued the flight to ZZZ1 with no further incidences. After landing, I had the FO call Ops just to make sure a customer service representative and security were waiting for us at the gate. Upon arrival into the gate, a customer service representative and security officer where indeed right there. The customer service representative immediately came onto the plane and removed the passenger.The FAs did not make any indication and no one told me they suspected the passenger was drunk. Seems as if passenger was just a genuinely disturbed person.We probably should have gotten security or customer service involved at ZZZ because of the name calling. Because the passenger had put on the mask and was making no further threatening behavior, we decided to make a note of it and continue. We all agreed though, that if passenger made one more derogatory comment, we would most likely be removing passenger from the flight. We had no further problems until mid-flight.
ASRS:1777423.s: The flight crew and cabin crew encountered a non-compliant passenger on a ZZZ-ZZZ1 flight who refused to wear a mask, used expletives, and screamed during boarding and cruise. The crew contacted dispatch to request security and customer service at the destination, where the passenger was removed after landing without an emergency declaration.

ASRS:1777425.n: On subsequent flights I experienced the same issue with my EFB. Once airborne both pilots became aware that the 'Content' App was inaccessible thus making all company manuals also inaccessible. On both occasions we were forced to use SATCOM (satellite communication) to reach the Chief Pilot (on the first incident) and the Dispatcher (on the second incident) to retrieve the necessary information. Under normal circumstances this application is not referenced unless there is a need for the company manuals, however on the first occasion the Captain was attempting to study prior to upcoming training and the issue was discovered. On the second occasion, there was necessity to reference the manuals and we became aware that neither of us had access. I am not confident in the cause of the problem, but it appears once the tablet goes offline (no internet connection) the manuals become inaccessible. I raise this issue to the safety department because I feel that likely there are many flights departing with these issues, but normal operations don't necessarily involve accessing this application on our EFBs. However when the necessity does arise it is important that we have immediate access and not reliant on relay of information via SATCOM. Not having computer/tablet expertise, I hesitate to make any suggestions, but I do feel it's important to investigate the cause of this issue and hopefully we can find a work around, in the short term, and a solution going forward.
ASRS:1777425.s: Pilots reported that the EFB 'Content' App became inaccessible after takeoff on two flights, preventing access to company manuals. The reporter suspects the issue occurs when the tablet goes offline, forcing reliance on SATCOM to retrieve necessary information from the Chief Pilot and Dispatcher.

ASRS:1777450.n: I was Check Airman conducting Captain IOE on flight DCA-ZZZ1 . Light Snow Pellets falling at the time with small accumulations observed on aircraft surfaces. Decision made to de-ice type 1 only since we were number one for takeoff and de-ice pad is near departure end of runway 1 at DCA. We received our type 1 application, the Post de-icing report was received, and we taxied out and departed within specified holdover time. Takeoff was uneventful with no abnormalities noted.After landing in ZZZ1 a deadheading [DCA Pilot] based Captain came into the cockpit and presented to me a picture of our left wing immediately following de-icing. This picture showed significant accumulations of ice on the rear of the wing. The discussion we had was that the de-ice crew in DCA did a very cursory job of de-icing the aircraft and merely pushed the sum total of accumulation that was on the wing to the rear of the wing without melting it or pushing it off the wing. This calls into question a number of issues to include the competence and training of the de-ice personnel as well as whether the fluid used was at the correct ratio and temperature. Unfortunately, I do not have a picture of the right wing for comparison purposes.Immediately following this flight and within minutes of being made aware of what occurred, the new Captain and I went to the ZZZ1 Chief Pilots office and met with Chief Pilots [names] so they could communicate to the DCA station to make certain no additional airplanes left that day without being properly de-iced and that I would follow up with a report. [Reporter stated the cause of the incident was] DCA de-ice personnel not properly trained and supervised.More training and oversight of station de-ice personnel.
ASRS:1777450.s: During a DCA departure in light snow, a Check Airman observed significant ice accumulation on the left wing rear after de-icing, alleging ground personnel merely pushed ice back without melting it. The reporter attributed this to inadequate training and supervision of DCA de-ice crews, prompting immediate notification to station management to halt further departures.

ASRS:1777460.n: Just clearing the bridge prior to Taxiway 1 we were cleared for takeoff Runway ZZR at approximately XA00z for an on-time departure. After brake release and prior to 80 knots our takeoff clearance was canceled. We aborted departed [Taxiway] 1X and were instructed to hold short of [Taxiway] 1Y for 45 minutes both engines running (vaccine on board) and wait for departure control to resume duty (allegedly COVID cleaning).Tower and ATC need to coordinate their operations. We shouldn't be getting a takeoff clearance cancellation after brake release. Over 80 knots we may have had to press anyway as opposed to a high-speed abort putting everyone in a precarious position. Since company is the only significant operation during the AM push in ZZZ there isn't any legitimate reason ATC isn't aware and able to accommodate our operations.
ASRS:1777460.s: The crew received a takeoff clearance for Runway ZZR but had it canceled after brake release and before 80 knots, forcing an abort. They held for 45 minutes with engines running due to alleged ATC coordination issues regarding a COVID cleaning delay.

ASRS:1777467.n: I took over this flight from another shift. Normally this flight is scheduled to operate ZZZZ-ZZZ, but due to ZZZ weather it was rescheduled to arrive ZZZ1. Flight was sent with a redispatch and ETOPS alternates of BIKF/CYYT and no destination alternate for ZZZ1. While enroute and well past the EEP (ETOPS Entry Point), the crew sent an ACARS:What airport is defining ETOPS exit"I checked the flight plan and noticed the EXP1 (ETOPS Exit Point) was showing ZZZ1. The EEP airport was correctly identified as EINN and the ETP (Equal Time Point) location seemed accurate when looking at the route. I tried to figure out the reason for this, including creating dummy flight plans (non-redispatch, etc) and was unable to get a proper EXP. I advised the crew the correct EXP defining airport was CYYR (using range rings to define) and that while the ETOPS Exit Point on the release was not correct, the critical fuel scenario based on the ETP between BIKF/CYYT seemed accurate. I asked a few peers to review this to make sure I wasn't missing something and they all agreed. Another dispatcher found a similar issue on a similar routing of (Aircraft X ZZZZ-ZZZ1 on date). I advised the Dispatcher on Duty and he contacted Name1 immediately. Unfortunately, capturing line mode is not working for any flight right now."
ASRS:1777467.s: A dispatcher identified an incorrect ETOPS Exit Point airport on a redispatched flight en route to ZZZ1, determining the correct defining airport was CYYR. Although the critical fuel scenario remained accurate, the dispatcher reported the error to management, noting that capturing line mode data was currently unavailable.

ASRS:1777468.n: During this flight, we encountered wake turbulence near the flare portion of landing twice. The first resulted in a uncommanded right roll of approximately 30 degrees followed by a left roll of 15 degrees. A go around was executed. The second was a uncommanded 20 degree left roll, with a prompt recovery and landing. No further wake was encountered. A go-around could also have been executed here, I planned to if the turbulence did not subside after the first correction. Fuel remaining was a factor in this decision, as it would put us below minimum (but above emergency) fuel for return. In both cases, a momentary (1 sec) stick shaker occurred as a result of being at Ref in a high bank angle.
ASRS:1777468.s: The flight crew encountered wake turbulence twice during the flare, causing uncommanded rolls of 30 and 20 degrees. A go-around was executed for the first event due to fuel constraints, while the second was recovered for landing; both incidents triggered momentary stick shakers due to high bank angles at reference speed.

ASRS:1777479.n: Ice build up on all landing gear from inbound flight. Every work group I spoke to noted the lack of guidance on the issue. The initial reaction from the first rampers I spoke to was 'call Maintenance' but other people would have been fine with just using the PCA. On calling Maintenance control they noted how stations are very inconsistent on this issue. Dispatch noted the same. Since about half the ramps reaction was to have Maintenance handle it, we took that path to not have half the ramp uncomfortable with the action. Large delay to wait on Contract Maintenance. No further info.Provide consistent guidance and procedures for all work groups on deriving landing gear.
ASRS:1777479.s: Rampers and Maintenance encountered ice on landing gear after an inbound flight, causing a delay while waiting for Contract Maintenance. The reporter attributed the delay to inconsistent guidance across work groups regarding whether to use the PCA or call Maintenance for de-icing.

ASRS:1777484.n: Well, fatigue did play a role. It slowed us down. Earlier the hotel we were at started with construction outside at XA:00 am. This flight was already an hour late, and it was XO:30 pm at night before we could even taxi. I might also need to use the tools the Ipad has to draw a taxi route when I am not super familiar with the airport. Yes this is a hub for us, but the deice pad was in a place I [had] never been to.The First Officer was also overly concerned about cleaning the aircraft flight deck due to the COVID virus, as we changed planes from an earlier flight. I was having a slight reaction to the spray as I breathe it in, which gave me a allergy response. I had to step out of the flight deck for a few minutes. So my pre-flight taxi brief was lacking and I should of and will going forward instruct my future First Officer's that I need the extra set of eyes outside.On top of that, I will send an email of my concern for the proper use of this spray. We don't have much guidance on it.After being de-iced on the X taxi pad area, we were given taxi instructions to cross Runway XXR-XXL at Taxiway F, but the instruction to get there was a little vague because we started on Taxiway H. Because the ground being covered by snow, the taxi signs became the primary way to identify the taxiways, the painted tarmac signs were covered by snow. I believed I passed Taxiway F because the sign was further away and I was distracted because the First Officer was having difficulty with the de-ice checklist and holdover times. I then (most likely) made a left turn on Taxiway Bravo and right turn down Taxiway V. While on Taxiway V and approaching the intersection of Taxiway Y & V, I made an all stop as I was confused and approaching two runway intersections.I saw I went past Taxiway F and then had to get my bearings where I was. I declared to the First officer that I was lost and needed help. Once I figured out where I was, ground control gave me a new set of taxi instructions. The ground controller did not seem to be too concerned about the taxi deviation. However, at the time the confusion was real and I did not want to cross a runway without figuring out where I exactly was.After this I brought CRM back into the game and had a frank discussion with the First Officer. I told her that I can't taxi the plane and look up deice holdover data at the same time, and that the current issue is that we don't have much time to mess around with since we only used type 1 fluid (15 min). I then asked her that it looked like it stopped snowing anyways, so would she agree or disagree to that assessment? She did so we proceeded to taxi to takeoff.
ASRS:1777484.s: The Captain, fatigued and distracted by a First Officer's cleaning duties, became lost while taxiing a snow-covered aircraft due to obscured signs and vague ground instructions. After deviating from the assigned route and stopping near runway intersections, the crew reoriented, received new instructions, and proceeded to takeoff.

ASRS:1777489.n: After pushback from gate in BWI, the ground crew removed the steering bypass pin. They did not verify the bypass handle had returned to the normal steering position. Pushback was stopped early because tug began to slide on the ramp. We disconnected within 10 feet of the normal engine start position. After engine start as I attempted to taxi due to a very slippery ramp condition we immediately began to slide without nose wheel steering. I stopped the aircraft and reported poor to nil braking on the ramp thinking the slide was caused by outside conditions. We advised ATC we were holding our position. Maintenance came out to the aircraft and after plugging in reported that the bypass lever had inadvertently been stuck in the bypass position after the pin was removed. The aircraft had been on the ground for four to five hours in freezing precipitation. We had deiced at the gate but I am unsure if remaining frozen contamination caused the lever to not spring back to the normal position. We advised ATC that we had found a stuck bypass lever and were now ready to taxi. Ramps and taxiways were poor as [Air Carrier] had an Aircraft X slide off Taxiway F across from the Midfield Freight area.
ASRS:1777489.s: The flight crew and ground crew at BWI experienced a loss of nose wheel steering and braking during taxi after the steering bypass lever remained stuck in the bypass position. The crew suspects freezing precipitation prevented the lever from returning to normal after the pin was removed, causing the aircraft to slide on the slippery ramp.

ASRS:1777501.n: The mechanic who was assigned to work Aircraft X by chance found that the hydraulic reservoirs and accumulators for the green and yellow systems still had danger tags stating 'do not pressurize hydraulics' still hanging from them. These tags were dated XX/Sep/2020 and were from another company.
ASRS:1777501.s: A mechanic assigned to Aircraft X discovered danger tags on the green and yellow hydraulic reservoirs and accumulators. The tags, dated September 2020 from another company, warned not to pressurize the hydraulics.

ASRS:1777503.n: I am filing this for the technician that was tasked with this job. Aircraft X had a log to flush blue system hydraulics due to contaminated hydraulic fluid. The procedure in the AMM called out for a tool to purify the hydraulic fluid which [our] company didn't have. The mechanics were then told to follow the AMM until they came to a 'roadblock' and then figure it out from there. Eventually they used the Hydraulic Mule, which got contaminated, and figured out a way to flush it through the RAT (Ram Air Turbine) system. Capturing the contaminated fluid became another issue as no one could determine at what pressure this fluid would exit the line. Furthermore, because there was no procedure in place for this task no one could give guidance on what pressure to dial into the Mule in order to get the fluid pushed out (they eventually started at 50 psi and worked their way up to approx 2000 psi which was adequate to complete the task. Whoever wrote the task card should have ensured there was a viable AMM or procedure to accomplish this task and that the correct tooling was in place. We are now aware of several other Airbus aircraft around the system going through the exact same hydraulic contamination issue. In the case of [another] aircraft, it is the Green and Yellow systems that are affected which would necessitate a gear swing if i understand correctly. Could the ERC (event review committee) pleased use all resources to ensure proper procedures and tooling are in place prior to tasks like this one being assigned. Also, is it possible to find out the source of this hydraulic contamination?
ASRS:1777503.s: Technicians flushing contaminated blue hydraulic fluid on Aircraft X improvised using a Hydraulic Mule and RAT system due to missing tools and procedures. They increased pressure from 50 to 2000 psi to complete the task, highlighting a need for proper documentation and tooling before assigning such maintenance.

ASRS:1777548.n: Our facility has been back on a normal schedule for around 2 months now but we are operating extremely short staffed due to the amount of people out due to the pandemic. This is forcing those of us that still come to work to work harder. I was working GC and LC combined since this is now the 'new normal.' I commented to the CIC who was also working FD (pre-pandemic we would have had a Supervisor a GC, a FD, and a LC). 'Why did the TMC switch flows when we have a 7 knot tailwind?' He agreed that it was an early call but this happens a lot and I believe it happens because ZZZ TRACON is still on 5 days on and 5 days off and they don't have the staffing to open positions which is causing ZZZ to operate in a way that I believe introduces more risk.On the west side we normally have three runways but one is closed due to a construction project, and numerous taxiways are closed as well. In a north flow we are forced to land on Runway XXR when we would normally not do this and the East side keeps all the departures. This causes the situation that happened to me. Aircraft X goes around and I issue the standard 340 and climb to 3,000, he went around due to the tailwind. I then issue instructions on GC to alleviate a conflict there. I then notice a suppressed data tag of a west bound departure off of the west side (Aircraft Y), and issue Aircraft X a further turn to 270 and coordinated with the departure controller. The suppressed data tag was a huge factor in me not seeing the east side departure heading west, and the conflict on GC was another distraction.ZZZ TRACON needs to return to a normal schedule so they can staff their final monitor positions. ZZZ does not need to be departing west bound departures off of the east side when ZZZ1 TRACON is landing XXR, especially when the weather is marginal like it is today. Additionally, ZZZ TRACON does not need to be landing XXR at all, because that forces us to depart XYL which involves multiple crossing on Runway XXR (more risk). ZZZ TRACON needs to land the normal arrival runways and if they can't do this due to their staffing then they need to return to a regular schedule. Most of us here are fed up with what is being asked of us and the safety of the system is quickly eroding to appease the users demands and ZZZ's TRACON staffing.
ASRS:1777548.s: An air traffic controller working combined Ground and Local positions reported a near-miss caused by a suppressed data tag and staffing shortages at ZZZ TRACON. The controller missed a westbound departure while managing a go-around and conflict, attributing the risk to reduced staffing forcing abnormal runway flows and position combinations.

ASRS:1777558.n: The aircraft listed entered my airspace without coordination.I previously reported dozens of airspace violations directly to management. Management has recently changed its stance, and they now view a violation of my airspace as a performance issue on my part. It is their stance I am to watch all surrounding sectors and prevent other controllers from failing to do their job. I will now be reporting these airspace violations here instead to preserve my career.Also worth noting, the Controller that violated my airspace was working their first session after XX days off of COVID leave, and was working a higher volume of traffic than they could handle with the rust of being off so long. Controller did not have a D-side or any other support. The supervisor was apparently unaware of the traffic volume, and I walked over to ask him to monitor Controller.Bring back the safety and reporting culture. A controller should not have to choose between complying with a mandatory reporting requirement or losing their job, especially when it isn't that controller failed to comply with regulations.
ASRS:1777558.s: An aircraft entered the reporter's airspace without coordination due to a controller returning from COVID leave handling excessive traffic without support. Management now treats such violations as the reporter's performance failure, forcing the reporter to use this channel to preserve their career.

ASRS:1777561.n: I was the D-Side for approximately 1-1.5hrs when ZZZ Approach went ATC Limited with Tower only open from 1800-2000 local time for COVID cleaning. It was clear from before ZZZ went limited that the contingency plan was lacking, and controllers were brainstorming on the fly how we would handle the situation. In the period of 2 hours, I would estimate we had 15 arrivals into ZZZ1/ZZZ2/ZZZ3. It seemed like an abnormally busy time. I do not believe there were any losses, however there seemed to be a complete failure of planning/explanation/preparation provided to us controllers on how to best handle the situation and what we could expect. Many aircraft experience lengthy delays with several getting low on fuel. I would recommend for better contingency plans and better preparation for controllers when such an event is to occur.
ASRS:1777561.s: An air traffic controller reported that during a two-hour ATC limited period at ZZZ for cleaning, 15 arrivals faced lengthy delays and low fuel due to a lack of contingency planning. The controller attributed the operational difficulties to insufficient preparation and explanation provided to staff before the event.

ASRS:1777562.n: Aircraft X was vectored to their final approach course approximately 3 to 4 miles in trail of a preceding Aircraft Y. We were VFR conditions but had low ceilings hovering around 1,000 feet. Aircraft weren't coming out of the clouds until a 1 to 2 mile final. When Aircraft X joined the approach they has an absurdly high overtake speed with the Aircraft Y in front of them of 80 plus knots. There was no way separation was ever going to be maintained. When the realization set in of what was happening Local Control issued instructions to cancel the approach and to climb to 3000 feet and to turn 20 degrees to the left. I began coordination with Departure Control for a handoff with vectors to bring the aircraft back around for another approach. In the meantime Aircraft X advised Local Control that they were minimum fuel and were continuing the approach. Local Control advised me of this, so I canceled the coordination, and redirected my attention to an aircraft awaiting clearance. Then Local Control advised me that Aircraft X was indeed going around with the 20 degree left turn, and 3000 foot altitude assignment. Traffic was light, so I instructed Local Control to climb Aircraft X to 6000 feet and issue a turn to get them into the dispersal area as per our joint agreement. I again initiated coordination with Departure Control for the handoff, with Aircraft X climbing to 6000 feet and on a 100 or 105 heading.Then I came back to the aircraft on Clearance Delivery and had them read back their clearance. During the read back, Departure was trying to call me and say that Aircraft X needed to climb immediately for an aircraft that was departing southeast bound off a satellite airport. I responded that the altitude had been issued and would find out why Aircraft X stopped their climb at 3000 feet. I relayed the information to Local Control as I was receiving it. Local Control told me that Aircraft X would not accept the climb due to their minimum fuel situation, which I relayed back to Departure. Departure Control requested we ship Aircraft X to them, so that they could maintain separation with the traffic departing the satellite airport which I relayed to Local. Local was able to get Aircraft X to climb to 4,000 feet before shipping them. There was a loss of lateral separation on final approach, but there may have been altitude separation, although I am not sure about that. The problem is that we are struggling with spacing issues on final and even have a collaborative work group established with Approach to resolve these problems. Approach is continually handing Tower these overtakes, and less than coordinated arrival spacing for departure gaps, but Tower is always held accountable for the consequences of each event. This is the standard here at even though the separation problem originates with the Approach Controller. Even our local management tends to initially stand behind Approach and their actions while pointing their fingers at the Tower controllers trying to tell us that what we did was incorrect, even though we are only trying our best to prevent an separation error from occurring or getting worse. Standardize spacing requirements here at 3 miles or required and coordinated arrival spacing distances and never transfer communications of aircraft on final until there is less than a 30 knot overtake speed. In other words, follow the guidance in the 7110.65 and ensure separation before transferring communications to another controller. And on top of this, performance management to ensure controllers are being held accountable to the basic standards.
ASRS:1777562.s: An Air Traffic Controller reported that Aircraft X, on final approach behind Aircraft Y with an 80-knot overtake speed, lost lateral separation due to poor spacing from Approach Control. Although Local Control ordered a climb to 3,000 feet, Aircraft X initially refused due to minimum fuel before eventually climbing to 4,000 feet to avoid a departing aircraft.

ASRS:1777563.n: ZZZ TRACON planned to surrender their ZZZ1, ZZZ2, and ZZZ3 sectors to ZZZ ARTCC initially around XA:00 pm local due to facility cleaning of a COVID-19 positive. Area X (controllers and management) objected to the proposed time frame and was able to push the event back to around XD:00 pm local.Shortly before the XD:00 pm acquisition of airspace from ZZZ TRACON, we learned that there would be no radar service to any of the City satellite airports. We were given the following stipulations: No IFR service to ZZZ4, ZZZ5, ZZZ6, ZZZ7, etc. No VFR Flight Following will be provided in ZZZ TRACON's airspace. Any IFR aircraft not willing to cancel IFR and proceed to their satellite destination VFR without any radar service from ATC will be kept out of ZZZ TRACON's and offered an alternate airport for landing in ZZZ Centers airspace.At XI:04z, ZZZ2 ARTCC called ZZZ ARTCC Sector XY to coordinate a possible emergency situation with Aircraft X. The aircraft (a type) was originally off of ZZZ8 to, as ZZZ1 ARTCC stated, 'Somewhere in the midwest' but changed his destination to ZZZ4 because a service center was located there. The issue affecting the flight was with a fuel pump trying to incorrectly pump fuel to a wing (or tank) that it wasn't supposed to. This was not an emergency at the time but serious enough to change the destination and have the aircraft inspected by maintenance.At XI:07z, the aircraft checked on with ZZZ ARTCC sector XY. As the situation developed, it was discovered through management that if the pilot declared an emergency, it would have no impact on the reduced level of service he would receive from ZZZ TRACON enroute to ZZZ4.Shortly after this time, I relieved CPC [Name] at [Sector] XY and began working the sector. Upon realizing the possible developing situation and the corner that I was being put in, I declared to continue under Article 65 of the 2016 FAA/NATCA CBA. My experience painted a picture of a night time, single-engine and (possibly single pilot), IFR flight being operated in IMC, with a fuel pump issue that likely could become an emergency situation, wanting to land at an airport that would have no radar service for the last 45 miles of flight, IFR or VFR. At some point Management requested the pilot provide an alternate airport. In a brief discussion with the pilot on the frequency, I suggested ZZZ because in my mind, it's the only airport that would have any kind of radar service. As the pilot reluctantly continued on to ZZZ4, he was forced to descend to find VFR conditions. It wasn't until he broke out of the clouds below 4,000 feet that he announced he could continue VFR. This now meant that this aircraft had to fly the last 45 miles to ZZZ4 at 3,000 feet. Any level of safety that altitude provides to an aircraft (in distress or otherwise) was forcibly sacrificed. Additionally, to remain clear of the Class Bravo, the flight was vectored to the east of side of the city toward the ZZZZZ way point and then northbound. The pilot mentioned his plan was to fly north from there and then turn west toward ZZZ4 and call the tower when he got 10 miles out. This added additional miles and flight time to the situation. Again: Single-engine (possibly single-pilot), night, IMC, with a mechanical issue and no radar service.At XI:33z, the pilot informed me that he could proceed VFR to ZZZ4, and radar service was terminated by ZZZ ARTCC.Other factors during this ZZZ TRACON COVID cleaning period:VFR aircraft off of ZZZ4 enroute to ZZZ9 could not maintain VFR and needed a short range IFR clearance with an RNAV approach clearance.Volunteer (call sign unknown) aircraft inbound to ZZZ9 requested and received radar vectors to the ILS [runway] X approach.Finally, at the end of the cleaning period, ZZZ TRACON suggested that ZZZ ARTCC just keep the airspace for the rest of the night which was agreed to by ZZZ ARTCC.Consider the impacts of Covid-19 cleaning, not to just the affected facilities but also the flying community.
ASRS:1777563.s: A ZZZ ARTCC controller managed a single-engine aircraft with a fuel pump issue en route to ZZZ4 during a TRACON closure caused by COVID-19 cleaning. Due to the lack of radar service at the destination, the pilot was forced to descend below 4,000 feet to fly VFR, sacrificing safety altitude and adding flight time.

ASRS:1777570.n: We were at 4,000 feet on a vector to final about 15 southeast of ZZZ when a TA came up on TCAS on the nose co-altitude. Right after it came up we were given one more turn to join final for [Runway] XXL. In the turn the TA became a descending RA and we complied per the maneuver's section in the QRH. We descended about 800 feet and finished the turn at which time we were Clear of Conflict. As we leveled the wings we saw the traffic go by our right wing a little high as they were still at 4,000 feet, appearing to be no more than a half mile away. It appeared to be a smaller GA aircraft but went by quickly. We told ATC we descended for an RA, at which time he said to just maintain 3,000 feet. He seemed unconcerned and asked no questions nor gave us any information. We never received a Traffic Advisory call prior to the initial TA. The Controller was busy, but did not seem to be swamped. Maybe staffing as a result of COVID-19 is a factor.
ASRS:1777570.s: The crew received a TCAS Resolution Advisory while turning to final at 4,000 feet and descended 800 feet to avoid a nearby general aviation aircraft. The controller instructed them to maintain 3,000 feet without providing prior traffic advisories or further information.

ASRS:1777575.n: While enroute and at cruise altitude of 39,000 feet, with between 1:00-1:15 hrs of flight time remaining of a 3:40 hour flight: my stomach began to feel queasy, I started sweating, and in a short time felt the urgent need for a bowel movement. I advised the Captain of my need to use the lavatory and contacted the flight attendants. I quickly got out of my seat due to the urgency in my stomach and went to the door. When I stood up rapidly, I felt a rush of nausea as well as feeling light-headed. When the flight attendants knocked, I opened the door. The next thing I know I am sitting on the galley floor with a nurse sitting next taking care of me, with a doctor assisting. The doctor and nurse monitored my vital signs, which initially both blood pressure and oxygen levels were low. I began to feel normal shortly after they had me drink some water and ½ cup of orange juice, utilize the onboard oxygen and began to administer 2 bags of IV fluid. Blood pressure and oxygen levels returned to normal.I told them that I had been fasting and had not eaten for nearly 2 days. I also said I could tell I was dehydrated due to the limited amount of urine output on our first lavatory break 1-1/2 hours into the flight. Both agreed that this was probably a cause for what happened and called it a vagal response, which can cause a person to faint.Upon landing, we were met by paramedics at the gate. They took my vital signs to include a blood glucose test. After completing their assessment, they said I was fine and there was no need to take me to the hospital. After being released from the paramedics, the entire crew of went to the crew van and the overnight hotel.Medical Assistance provided a Hospital for me to be seen, to ensure I was medically able to fly (as a passenger) back to ZZZ. I went to the Hospital and received: initial screening, EKG, and blood tests to include Electrolytes, Hemoglobin, Triage Cardiac screen 'CUANTITATIVO, (INCLUYE TROPONINA I, BNP, MIOGLOBINA, CKMB Y DIMEROS D)'The doctor stated that I was in excellent shape and saw no problems or issues with any of my test results. I was released with no further action nor medications required. On Aircraft X ZZZ to ZZZ1 my FO (First Officer) said he needed a lav break, and I said go ahead, I have the aircraft. He got out of his seat and waited for the (FA) Flight Attendant to call so we could open the door. As the door opened and the FA came into the cockpit, he said boy your FO is very sweaty. Not more than 30 seconds later, the back end called and said the FO had passed out in the forward galley or first class. At that point, the FA stayed with me on the flight deck for the duration of the flight as he was talking on the phone and giving me vitals so I could send too Dispatch. We had an ER nurse taking care of FO and she set up an IV and he began to get better and told us he wants to continue to ZZZ1. FO was checked at the gate as well as going to ZZZ1 hospital and everything was good with no further action.
ASRS:1777575.s: Two First Officers on separate flights fainted in the galley at cruise altitude due to dehydration and fasting, causing a vagal response. Both were treated with fluids and oxygen onboard, recovered, and were medically cleared after hospital screenings with no further action required.

ASRS:1777589.n: On arrival into IAH we were assigned to descend via the LINKK1 RNAV arrival and subsequently cleared the ILS Runway 27 approach. We selected 1,500 ft. in the MCP to comply with the restriction at the FAF. Over GILLL intersection ATC asked me to maintain present speed of 240kts. I speed intervened to comply with the clearance as the aircraft would have started to slow to 210kts over RDFSH. The aircraft came out of VNAV Path into VNAV Speed and descended below the path. I went into vertical speed mode and selected a descent rate to approximate the path using the VDI (Vertical Descent Indicator) scale. My expectation was that I was going to be given a 'resume normal speed' clearance fairly quickly as there was not any traffic behind us as was apparent to me. Unfortunately, we were not given the clearance and I was slow to stop the descent using vertical speed mode over SYYKO intersection and elected to disengage the autopilot and hand flew the aircraft to stop the descent in a more expeditious manner. We climbed back to 3,000 ft. and resumed the profile uneventfully.
ASRS:1777589.s: The pilot descended below the ILS Runway 27 approach path at IAH after speed intervention for a 240-knot clearance caused VNAV Path disengagement. The pilot hand-flew the aircraft to stop the descent over SYYKO and climbed back to 3,000 feet to resume the profile.

ASRS:1777591.n: We went to Aircraft X to further review deferrals. We found 2 deferrals on the Mode Control Panel. The MELs described LNAV, VNAV, HDG HOLD, FLT CH, ALT HOLD, VS, all possibly affected by the MELs. I asked the mechanic to have someone come out and describe what we'll have available after departure. I called Flight Control and asked if we were RVSM legal. I was told we can't fly the SID, that we would have to get direct all the way to ZZZ. This very degraded state was concerning to the First Officer and me especially with the winter storm warnings at our destination. We were also told that the aircraft would not be legal to return to ZZZ1 with deferrals. We were also concerned about having an inflight emergency and diverting to an airport with only RNAV approaches available as we weren't capable of that approach. After discussions with Maintenance Supervisor, Flight Control and the Assistant Chief Pilot someone decided to tail swap the trip.
ASRS:1777591.s: The crew and maintenance personnel found Mode Control Panel deferrals on Aircraft X that degraded navigation capabilities and prevented RVSM compliance. Due to winter storm concerns and the inability to return or divert safely, operations decided to tail swap the trip.

ASRS:1777608.n: This event had to do with both Primary Flight Displays airspeed indications giving crew error readouts. The aircraft had been sitting outside during the snowstorm we had in the northeast. We followed deice and anti-ice procedures per Cold Weather Ops. Checklist. Passing through 210 kts (211) both IAS indications turned red indicating we were in a overspeed indication. Both landing gear and flaps/slat were verified up by checklist usage and visually from the cabin. With our resources we verified IAS were correct even though they were indicating in the Red. We ran appropriate checklist and verified aircraft performance charactertics utilizing all aircraft instrumentation. We advised the maintenance (coordinating with cessna) and agreed continuing on to destination would be the right decision with our situation. Both of us agreed with solution and agreed we we're safe to continue. Upon slowing in to ZZZ at 210 kts both Primary Flight Display IAS indications returned to Green Normal color. We landed with all normal indications. With my XX years of aviation commercial experience, I don't agree with the Cold Weather Checklist. It tells us to extend flaps to 35 for de-ice and 0 degrees for anti-ice. My experience has always kept Flaps up during both these procedures, so to prevent fluid getting on full flap area that sits under wing when retracted. Selecting Flaps once nearing runway so to prevent snow and slush from getting on Full Flap area would be a better practice, while protecting a major portion of flap area from icing conditions waiting to takeoff.Suggest looking at how we perform de/anti-icing procedures on the fleet.
ASRS:1777608.s: The flight crew experienced erroneous overspeed indications on both Primary Flight Displays at 210 kts after cold weather deicing, which resolved upon slowing. The pilot attributed the issue to the current checklist requiring flap extension during deicing and recommended modifying procedures to keep flaps up until near the runway.

ASRS:1777614.n: During the crew brief we discussed the departure procedure and I selected LNAV on and confirmed it was armed via the PFD. After a maintenance issue at the gate and a rushed before takeoff checklist during a short taxi we took off. Shortly after takeoff, ZZZ tower asked why we didn't turn. Confused I looked at the PFD and LNAV was not operating. I told the Captain to turn in the correct direction and moved the heading bug to the correct heading. We don't know how or why LNAV disengaged after we both confirmed it was armed in the brief.Rushing the before takeoff checklist caused us not to verify everything in the MCP/ND check so we don't know if LNAV was still armed at takeoff. Other than training in the aircraft type simulator, I have not flown since early November. The Captain only has X00 hours in the aircraft.Suggestion - Don't rush the before takeoff checklist.
ASRS:1777614.s: The crew rushed the before takeoff checklist after a maintenance delay, failing to verify that LNAV remained armed on the MCP. Consequently, LNAV disengaged shortly after takeoff, requiring manual heading selection when tower queried the missed turn.

ASRS:1777619.n: Normal (very early) departure. We taxied out, ran checklists, lined up for takeoff, when I added power, we got the takeoff configuration warning horn. We both saw immediately the flaps were not set. I notified tower we needed to exit the runway. Exited the runway at the first taxiway. I don't think our ground speed got above 25-40 (?) knots. Set the flaps, re-ran the before takeoff checklist, notified the Tower ready, and completed the flight normally.Haven't been flying as much as normal. First flight, very early morning. Possible distraction(s). This is a humbling event. I don't think I've done it in X0 years of flying. There was nothing specific that I remember, but something interfered with our regular routine or 'flow'. I did the 'after start' checklist and missed it, and we both did the 'before takeoff' checklist aloud and missed it. I thought I was checking the position and the indicators carefully, but obviously I need to be more stringent, and will be in the future. When cleared for takeoff, and starting to line up and advancing throttles, a configuration aural warning activated because the flaps were in the up position. Neither of us realized the flaps in the incorrect position before taking the runway and I immediately took control of the aircraft and returned the thrust levers to the idle position, disconnected the auto throttle and cleared the runway, never exceeding 10-12 knots (still at taxi speed). Once clear of the runway, I commanded the flap lever to 1 and first officer moved lever to 1 and we got the green light. Ran the entire before takeoff checklist again and was cleared back onto runway for an uneventful takeoff and climbout.I had completed a 3 day trip late the previous night and this was an early XA30 departure time with minimum required rest. I stayed at the hotel and was interrupted in my sleep routine at around midnight by a noisy neighbor conducting a phone call in the room next to mine. Maybe I wasn't fully rested and still a little groggy. My expectation was that the flap lever was placed to 1 after engine start and I was used to that routine so I didn't register that the flaps were not in the correct position. This was the first time this has occurred for me.Only suggestion is to double and triple check all items, especially configuration items, and to use the crew concept better.
ASRS:1777619.s: Pilots on an early morning departure failed to set flaps before takeoff due to fatigue and routine disruption, triggering a configuration warning horn. They aborted the takeoff at taxi speed, corrected the flap setting, and completed the flight normally after re-running checklists.

ASRS:1777622.n: Flight was uneventful until cleared the ILSZ RWY 36 via direct QIT VOR at 18,000 feet assigned. A large build up was directly situated over QIT therefore ATC was asked for a left deviation due to the buildup. During the decent briefing the approach and contingencies were briefed, however, a storm disrupting the approach was not anticipated. A left deviation was started and I decided to proceed direct to point D111G as the best course of action. The FO had his terrain display in terrain mode allowing me to see any conflicts ahead. The FO correctly pointed out that going direct point D254I would be a better course of action and allow more time for the approach. I agreed and we asked for and was given direct to that point by ATC. At this point the situation was less than ideal. The weather was mostly cloudy with only brief glimpses of the terrain. I had the altitude of 10,500 feet in my mind thinking I was heading for my original point (D111G) when in reality we were required to be at 14,200 feet point D254I. I had started the descent when the FO pointed out the error and I immediately started to climb. At this point we were still not on the approach due to the weather. We were still proceeding direct to D254I. I was also slowing and configuring for the landing. I ended up disconnecting the autopilot in order to reestablish myself on to a stable approach. The terrain display never showed any conflicts and no verbal warnings of the system was encountered. I knew approximately where the aircraft was at all times. My error was in the decent altitude while forced off of the approach due to weather. We eventually did get on the approach, were stable when we broke out of the weather and had an uneventful landing. The large cell situated over the UIO VOR forced an unprepared diversion around it resulting in an off route decent in order to land. This in turn resulted in attaining a lower than desired altitude in heavily mountainous terrain. This was my first time into UIO. Although I reviewed the required airport familiar special qualification briefing, in this situation it was not adequate. I consider myself very experienced in mountainous terrain and I believe this particular field should require a Check Airman checkout. 'Picking the brain for gotchas' would have been invaluable.
ASRS:1777622.s: The Captain and First Officer diverted around a storm over QIT VOR while approaching UIO, resulting in an off-route descent to 10,500 feet instead of the required 14,200 feet. The Captain corrected the altitude error after the First Officer's intervention, disconnected the autopilot to stabilize, and completed an uneventful landing.

ASRS:1777654.n: Everything during the preflight, engine start, and taxi out went normal. During the taxi out our clearance was picked up with a 5 minute void time. We had calm winds and [Runway] XX is the calm wind runway so we had briefed and planned for a [Runway] XX departure. There was work on the taxiway so it was going to require a back taxi to the end of [Runway] XX at an uncontrolled field. Coming out of the ramp we informed over the CTAF what our intentions were and taxied and held short of the runway. While holding short of the runway with some traffic in the pattern for [Runway] XX and a plane inbound on the GPS [Runway] XY doing a practice approach we realized we wouldn't get out in the 5 minutes. I put Center back in on Comm 1 and had my Captain on Comm 2 monitoring the CTAF. I asked Center for an extension explaining why we need it and they gave us another 10 minutes before the void time. I put the CTAF back on one and asked the Captain if I missed any important calls and he said no. We watched the plan in the pattern land [Runway] XX and I informed over the CTAF that we would hold short of the runway until the guy on GPS approach went missed and that we would then be back taxiing for full length takeoff on [Runway] XX. No one over the CTAF says anything else. We complete all checklists and are ready to go. After the GPS approach guy goes missed I inform over the CTAF that we are taking the runway and back taxiing on [Runway] XX. No one says anything. I looked right towards the [Runway] XX end and final and cleared that direction and the captain looked left towards the [Runway] XY end and final and cleared that direction. We then began our back taxi. During the back taxi I informed again over the CTAF that we were still back taxiing for a [Runway] XX departure. Nothing was said over the CTAF. We get to the end and line up for a full length departure. I inform over the CTAF that we are taking off [Runway] XX with a right turn out on the SID for a north departure. We wait a few seconds and nothing on the CTAF. We then began our takeoff roll with nothing out of the ordinary through 110ish kts. The runway was kinda of rounded and approaching V1 and cresting the rounded part of the runway I noticed something moving to the right of the runway. I said 'what's that?' Looked back down and it was V1 call out. At this time we realize it's an airplane that took off Runway XY and is making a left turn to our right. He was already a few hundred feet off the runway centerline and we were passed V1 so we continued with a normal departure sequence. During the departure we heard someone on the ground asking over the CTAF if the other plane had a radio. No response. It was asked a couple times with no response. We were asked by the person on the ground if we saw the plane. I was PM (Pilot Monitoring) so I responded with a yes and we asked for a radio check and were told that our radio was working. The other airplane finally responded saying he made at least 3 takeoff calls. The guys on the ground said that no calls were made from the other aircraft. He insisted again that he made the takeoff calls. Another plane flying just past the field who was on the CTAF also informed that he heard no takeoff calls from the other departing plane. We made a final call informing which direction our departure was and through what altitude we were climbing. Switched over to Center and had a standard flight the rest of the way. The cause was GA plane with a possible broken radio and or what seems to be more likely a wrong frequency tuned in was the biggest problem. If we had heard another plane wanting to takeoff in the opposite direction we would have never even started the back taxi let alone the takeoff. I'm not really sure what can be done about planes with no radios, broken radios, or wrong frequency's. We did everything to our power correctly and we were in no hurry with the extended void and were taking our time. Maybe operating even slower we could haveavoided being around the runway at the same time as this other plane. Hard to pin point something when everyone who was on frequency knew our intentions and what we were doing.
ASRS:1777654.s: The flight crew of a turbine aircraft at an uncontrolled field experienced a runway incursion during a back-taxi and takeoff on Runway XX. The incident occurred because a general aviation aircraft on Runway XY likely had a broken radio or wrong frequency, failing to announce its departure despite the crew's extensive CTAF communications.

ASRS:1777660.n: While operating the flight controls as PF (Pilot Flying), and beginning the takeoff roll, after brake release, as power was applied and throttles passed through approximately 10,000 ft-lb torque, the Captain/Pilot Monitoring and I simultaneously heard and felt a 'thud' which we immediately interpreted as a possible load shift. The Captain called for a rejected takeoff which we conducted in accordance with company procedures. We taxied back to the ramp, parked and shut down all engines. All hands conducted an inspection of the load. The skid load consisting of approximately eight long steel drill pipes, approx 15 feet long by 18 inches in diameter appeared to have shifted approximately two linear feet aft from the original loaded position. (Caused by) inadequate securing of cargo skid load, suspected due to improperly affixed and/or inadequate number of aft securing straps and/or chains. On takeoff roll a noise was heard and felt in the cockpit. The takeoff was rejected and the aircraft returned to the ramp for evaluation. Upon examination it was determined that a portion of the cargo had shifted aft. Insufficient aft restraint on the affected portion of the cargo.
ASRS:1777660.s: During takeoff roll, the crew rejected the flight after feeling a thud caused by a cargo skid of steel drill pipes shifting two feet aft. The incident resulted from inadequate securing straps and chains, leading to an inspection that confirmed insufficient aft restraint on the load.

ASRS:1777663.n: During boarding procedures a passenger was advised of the mask wearing requirements, nose/face. Flight Attendant (FA) advised passenger nose exposure to FA B who also had to re-advise passenger. Passenger appeared disgruntled about requiring nose coverage and Gate Agent advised she also had words with passenger with same response. FA B advised Captain of passenger's position against compliance. Prior to door closure the Gate Agent was present in case passenger removal was necessary.An announcement was then made saying 'non-compliance passengers were noticed and removal option would be used for non-compliance.' Passengers were advised they had an agreement at ticket purchase this had been clear this was not an optional requirement for flight.Using this method passenger realized this wasn't a joke and removal would occur. Captain advised FA B to do walk through for compliance and removal before door closer option. This passenger had been advised over 3 times by 3 different individuals with non-compliance results and now aware airlines was serious about compliance.Entire plane was compliant during walking through and continued flight. During entire flight passenger continued to pull mask off nose and appeared disgruntled. Passengers around passenger kept saying 'FA caught you again each time' so passenger then laughed like it was a game. We are to 'inform' at this point, which continued at every walk through, 'not enforce .' This was a constant occurrence during flight.After arriving and during departure this non-compliant passenger stopped and made rude remarks to FA A. FA B went to Gate Agent during cleaning to advice of this passenger's attitude and non-compliance so Gate Agent could make a note for future travel. This passenger felt he was not going to wear mask as required. FA B advised gate agent row and seat area and agent opened up the location and verified passenger's information. Due to constant resistance FA felt safer not to confront passenger directly. During 3 points this party was given clear instructions on mask covering requirements and possible travel denial. They continued during every stage with 4 different advisory points pre-board at gate, boarding (flight attendants), flight introduction (Captain's announcement) and inflight (flight attendants). With actions [during] deplaning this passenger let FA A know that they were above this rule.
ASRS:1777663.s: Flight attendants, a gate agent, and the captain repeatedly advised a passenger to cover their nose with a mask during boarding and flight, but the passenger remained non-compliant and made rude remarks. The crew documented the incident for future travel restrictions but did not remove the passenger, citing safety concerns regarding direct confrontation.

ASRS:1777667.n: On [a] flight to XNA we were cleared for the visual traffic pattern to land Runway 16. The Captain as the pilot flying had properly briefed the visual approach, to include the obstacles in the vicinity and highest obstacle on the approach plate. On right base, the Captain turned autopilot off with flaps 3 and gear down. I announced visual contact/no factor on the highest obstacles out the right window - a set of towers. We continued to slow and configure for landing and maintain an altitude of more than 1,000 ft. AGL. We received a caution from the GPWS, followed by a PULL UP verbal command. The Captain took the appropriate actions and immediately increased the airplane's altitude. We were in daytime visual conditions, and in accordance with company policy, determined we were still in a safe position to stabilize and conduct a safe landing after clearing the obstacle. We finished the turn to final, configured the aircraft for flaps 5 landing, completed the before landing checklist, were fully stable by 1,000 ft. and in a safe position to land the aircraft. Upon landing, we debriefed the situation, reviewing the approach plate for any obstacles. At more than 1,000 ft. AGL and no visual contact with an obstacle, we were unsure why the GPWS gave us the PULL UP command, but agreed that it was the most appropriate and safest action to respond to the command as we didGPWS PULL UP verbal command resulted in appropriate action of increasing aircraft altitude.A visual traffic pattern is one of the most difficult approaches we fly. I would suggest additional training during initial and recurrent training on distances and altitudes for different types of visual traffic patterns. I will personally work to improve my awareness as the pilot flying to ensure 1,500 ft. AGL on downwind and the 3:1 descent path ratio throughout the visual traffic pattern. I will review my flying skills to ensure I am flying this way as well. While I believe we took the appropriate action both during the event and after in the debrief, I will use this as a learning experience to ensure I am always a safe and skilled pilot.
ASRS:1777667.s: During a visual traffic pattern approach to Runway 16 at XNA, the crew received an unexpected GPWS PULL UP command above 1,000 ft. AGL despite visual contact with no obstacles. The Captain immediately increased altitude, and the crew subsequently stabilized and completed a safe landing.

ASRS:1777674.n: I departed ZZZ with the intent to ferry it to ZZZ1. At the time of departure, weather was reported as overcast at 1,800 feet, visibility 10SM. Field elevation is 2,500 feet. Highest obstacle of the enroute corridor was indicated as 3,325 feet, per ForeFlight profile. Reported weather allowed for a 1,000 foot clearance of the highest obstacle. Upon departing and climbing to 3,200 feet, I could clearly see over all the hill tops along my intended flight path. Approximately 10 minutes into the flight, clouds started to form and spill over from hill tops to the north and west into the adjoining valleys. I executed a turn to avoid the clouds. I decided I would return to ZZZ. Suddenly, clouds started to form all around me. The area around me was mountainous covered with thick forest. I felt that IMC was imminent so I initiated the IMC procedure. I leveled the aircraft and started a climb, after adjusted power & airspeed settings. I passed through the bottoms of 2 clouds as I started to set up the GPS for an instrument approach into ZZZ. A moment later I was in a pocket clear of clouds with a large field next to a residence below me. I decided it better to land VFR in the field than to continue IFR back to ZZZ. I performed a descending orbit towards the field to get a clear picture of any/all possible obstacles. A safe landing was performed without incident. Notifications were made to Center. After waiting approximately 2 hours, I was able to safely complete the ferry flight. Become IFR current within company.
ASRS:1777674.s: A pilot ferrying an aircraft from ZZZ to ZZZ1 encountered rapidly developing clouds in mountainous terrain and initiated IMC procedures. The pilot elected to perform a safe VFR landing in a nearby field rather than continue instrument flight, later completing the ferry after regaining IFR currency.

ASRS:1777681.n: Just after completing a climb to 12,000 ft in an attempt to get above an icing layer, the company issued iPad mount fell off the windscreen on to the floor. Initially, I reacted to this by reaching down to pick it up, but simultaneously noticed the G600 displayed a GPS failure indication on the moving map side of the screen. At the same time TAWS (terrain awareness and warning system) gave an aural alert 'TAWS NOT AVAILABLE'. There were no additional audible alerts or visual annunciations. I initially thought this was simply a GPS signal failure and was starting to react accordingly, I then observed that the aircraft had entered a descending turn and immediately reacted with an unusual attitude in IMC recovery procedure. Given that the aircraft was in continuous light turbulence, in the clouds, at night, I was momentarily completely focused on ensuring the aircraft remained in a controlled attitude. A few moments latter I began taking stock of what I did and did not have. I observed the GMX200 screen off, GNS530 screen off, the primary GTX330 was off, and the autopilot was off. The G600 was giving associated GPS/AHRS and GAD43 failures. There were no other annunciations on the primary panel, and no audible alerts. My next focus was to re-establish navigation to my next known waypoint, the ZZZ VOR. I had previously tuned the ZZZ VOR into the NAV1 and NAV2, so I had manual navigation and DME via NAV2. Since the GNS430 and secondary GTX330 appeared operable, I immediately squawked 7600 as I had been out of contact with ZZZ1 Center (which was on COM1) and had obviously deviated heading/altitude at the beginning of the incident a few moments earlier. Not knowing what was happening to cause these failures and what might be failing next, setting the squawk may at the very least alert Center that I am having a problem. I also needed a few moments to sort out which frequency I needed to be on, as at this point the stress level was high enough I could not remember the frequency. I had to retrieve the iPad which was still on the floor in order to look at the chart screen for the frequency. Once back in contact with ZZZ1 Center I described the situation as best I could: some kind of electrical and/or communication failure as most of my avionics were now off. I elected for a diversion to ZZZ, now about 17nm away, and worry about troubleshooting the problem on the ground rather in the air in IMC at night. I was given vectors for a visual approach and landed without further incident.Having time to analyze the situation, and noting after landing/parking that the Avionics 1 & 2 were able to be switch back on, I conclude that the root cause of the systems associated with Avionics Bus 1 failing was from the iPad mount falling off the windscreen and hitting the switch on the way down. In personal reflection, I can recognize the irony that simply reaching over to check the avionics switches would have likely resolved the issue. But, the totality of the circumstances I had been suddenly faced with: 'an unexpected flight attitude deviation following an otherwise innocuous distraction, an initial observation of having a GPS signal failure'. Normally a failure of the GNS530/430, even if the failure was a complete loss of the entire unit, would not have resulted in the loss of the autopilot modes. Typically any normal failure of the autopilot is also accompanied by an audible alert. I had no immediate indication that the autopilot was off until observing the aircraft starting a descending turn. This precipitated the human factor contribution to the scenario of dealing with an otherwise unexplainable loss of avionics and uncommanded attitude deviation and no indication to which trained emergency checklist actions would be a prudent course of action. Overall troubleshooting based on system knowledge is a higher level brain function and at the time I did not have the luxury of 'stepping back' to think what might be going wrong. All that to say, there are no checklists specifically for an avionics failure (such as the switch some how getting turned off) or even what to do if the GPS fails. The assumed reactions remain in the realm of pilot knowledge and ability to troubleshoot the problem in lieu of following a checklist... in all likelihood with the assumption that the autopilot is still functional. This isn't a suggestion that we make a new checklist item, but rather the addition of random failure modes such as this during training to either establish situational memory or reinforce what to do if you don't know what to do. Finally, the root culprit of the situation... the iPad mount. This has been an ongoing 'issue' that has been simply tolerated by Company pilots. It hasn't been reported likely because we didn't think it was a big problem, would have never imagined it would lead to any problem, or have not been explicitly told that it is a problem if it occurs. There is also the ongoing back and forth with pilots who do not like having the mount and will remove it from the windscreen. The result is the mount ends up on the floor, getting dirty and damaged to the point that many of the suction cups do not effectively stay on the windscreen. In fact, in talking with another co-worker I discovered that this exact scenario happened to him during an AM departure a few weeks earlier and had hit both Avionics 1 & 2 switches. Since he saw it (and had the benefit of being VFR during the day) he just turned the switches back on and remounted the iPad. It has been my observation the suction cups seem to most frequently fail when climbing into colder temperatures, but this is not always the case. At this point, I believe it is safe to say that the current mounting system does not work... either by nature of system or as a result of the poor care and handling it as received over the past year or so. I will have to admit, the iPad mount coming off is something that I have observed and didn't report... and frankly should have reported and made a big stink over sooner. But I am now: at this point I do not believe the current iPad mounting system to be either effective nor safe.
ASRS:1777681.s: A pilot reported that an iPad mount fell from the windscreen at 12,000 ft, striking the Avionics Bus 1 switch and causing multiple avionics failures and an uncommanded descending turn in IMC. The pilot recovered the aircraft, squawked 7600, and diverted to land safely, concluding the root cause was the unsafe mounting system.

ASRS:1777704.n: Aircraft ahead failed to exit landing runway in timely fashion. ATC instructed us to execute a go-around, Runway 34 right. Simultaneous departing traffic on 35 left was offset and behind. We were than instructed to turn right heading of 105. Almost immediately we got a proximity warning. We were then instructed shortly after to fly runway heading and climb maintain 9,000 ft. ATC came back after giving us vectors for Runway 35R, informing us they had a mix up in call signs. Their intent was to turn the aircraft heading 105 departing off of Runway 35L. It seemed that air traffic control had a high workload at the time of our go around and I assume the controller was fatigued. Suggest continued use of good situational awareness about surrounding air traffic environment during high workload for air traffic control.
ASRS:1777704.s: During a go-around on Runway 34R due to a runway incursion, ATC issued a conflicting heading of 105 intended for departing traffic on Runway 35L, causing a proximity warning. The controller attributed the error to a call sign mix-up during high workload and assumed fatigue.

ASRS:1777706.n: While I did perform a visual inspection of the flight deck in accordance with FOM requirements on all flights departing the US to Country X, I never received or completed a search form. I realized this about halfway to our destination. I called the flight attendants and asked them if they'd performed a visual inspection during their pre-flight, to which they responded in the affirmative. I also called ground handlers in ZZZ when I got to ZZZZ. The gentleman confirmed with me something along the lines of, 'the cleaners perform the search of the cabin while they're cleaning and disinfecting the aircraft.'This was a 'turn around' with maintenance items that needed addressing and [aircraft] disinfection that needed accomplishing, so some task saturation. Furthermore, my normal routine is typically to trade the Gate Agent's paperwork with my completed security sheet. With the auto passenger count closeout, that moment is no longer consistently there. I think we could benefit a lot from some more standardization (pilots, flight attendants, and Customer Service) regarding the completion of the security sheet. With the new below wing ground handling and the new procedures in ZZZ, there are changes in the way aircraft are turned and the people I interact with. I will most likely remind myself and my crew about the security sheet during my Pre-flight Briefing when I mention passports. This way, verifying the paperwork is received and goes out the door can be a collaborative effort. When airborne on our flight to ZZZZ the Captain realized that he didn't receive, fill out, and return the paperwork saying that he did the security sweep of the aircraft. He did perform the sweep when we first arrived at the aircraft and asked the Flight Attendants to see if they did their sweep as well. They also performed the sweep. When we landed in ZZZZ my Captain called the ground handlers and explained the situation and confirmed that he did the sweep.Our plane arrived late into ZZZ. We had to do a quick turn and wait for cleaning to [sanitize] the aircraft before our crew and passengers could get on the plane. Maintenance had to be performed on the aircraft. A lot had to be done in a short time.On the quick turns everyone needs to slow down and make sure they are doing things correctly even if it means we won't get out on time. If the Gate Agent, Flight Attendants or Pilots took time to remember the security sheet then it would have been filled out and given back to be filed.
ASRS:1777706.s: The Captain failed to complete the security sweep form during a quick turnaround at ZZZ involving maintenance and disinfection, despite performing the visual inspection. He later confirmed with flight attendants and ground handlers that the cabin search was conducted, attributing the paperwork omission to task saturation and procedural changes.

ASRS:1777754.n: The aircraft had been sitting for a great length of time so it was decided the aircraft should be test flown prior to its first revenue flight. During the initial checks, the radar system failed the test cycles, so the discrepancy was noted in the logbook and maintenance was performed (approximately one hour). All other checks were satisfactory. Taxi normal. Initial takeoff normal 80-kt call normal. At approximately 110 kts I noticed my airspeed indication had blanked. Taxi was indicated in the window. I glanced to the right the FO (First Officer) indications appeared to be normal. We were rapidly approaching V1/Vr 135 kts so I elected to continue. V1/Vr was called and I rotated at a normal rate after the nose wheel left the ground my airspeed tape reappeared, however, the indication was approximately 90-100 kts with visual stall indications. No shaker. Positive rate was called and the gear was raised. At about 100 feet. I transferred control to the pilot monitoring. I had IAS comparator in the PFD and multiple levels one and two alerts. SEL Manual Feel Sel Fadec ALTN (3). A combination of those alerts drives the user to 'Refer to Emergency Non-Alert procedure- AIRSPEED UNRELIABLE.' I called to the pilot in the OBS seat to get the QRH out. I was also handling multiple radio calls. Notified ATC that we had issues with airspeed indications and erratic altimetry issues and to keep us within 20 NM of ZZZ and that we would be returning to ZZZ. The FCP was blanking on numerous occasions we were cleared to 10,000 ft however the altitude window would blank on occasion. Between 6,000-7,000 feet we were trying to ascertain what readouts were accurate as the right-side airspeed was giving erroneous indications altitude readouts seemed erroneous as well. Captain side was reading 90 kts FO side 270 knots standby 230 kts. I asked for a ground speed readout from ATC 380 kts was the response. Then as we leveled at 10,000 feet my airspeed and altitude indications returned to normal as did the FOs. We returned to ZZZ with no other issues. Blocking in Maintenance noted two ADC failures generated by the CFDS below 300 feet.
ASRS:1777754.s: The Captain experienced unreliable airspeed and altitude indications shortly after takeoff due to dual Air Data Computer failures. The crew continued the flight, consulted the QRH, and returned safely to ZZZ after indications normalized at 10,000 feet.

ASRS:1777757.n: Upon arriving at the parking spot X the mechanic noticed engine two tail was missing parts and the metal skin looked burned. The aircraft was AOG [Aircraft On Ground]. When we parked at the parking spot the mechanic came upstairs to the cabin and notified us off the incident. [The failure may have occurred] when we took off on a Typhoon out off ZZZ.[Suggest to] delay the flight a few hours so we won't have to fly in Hurricane and Typhoons.
ASRS:1777757.s: A mechanic discovered missing parts and burned skin on engine two of an aircraft parked at spot X, grounding the flight. The reporter suspects the failure occurred during takeoff in a typhoon near ZZZ and suggests delaying the flight to avoid severe weather.

ASRS:1777759.n: Taxiing out to gate Captain had issues with his FD (Flight Director). Captain placed his FD source to #2. All appeared well. Normal takeoff until 400 ft. At 400 ft. the Captain commanded NAV proformance. I selected NAV and PROF from the GCP. Shortly afterwards the Captain asked for Autoflight. When pressing Autoflight the AP2 annuncated in the FMA. I pressed Autoflight again but AP2 remained enunciated. I mentioned this to the Captain. ATC then cleared us to fix ZZZZZ and I announced NAV Available because we were still runway heading, then noticed that Nav Armed was anticipated, but hadn't captured. The Captain used the heading select function. To keep the aircraft on the correct path. At this point we also noticed that the engines were still in Takeoff Thrust Limit. We tried several times to see if NAV would react or anything, but any FMS derived values to the GCP or autopilot did not work. As we continued climb we began to evaluate if we should continue the flight. As a team of three we double-checked all such settings and possibilities. There was no obvious action and the buttons pushed on the FMS and GCP didn't have the desired results. When the PROF key was pressed to display the climb page all values were blank or boxes. At this time we also were not sure of the reliability of our NAV function. With the degradation in our autopilot for maintaining course assigned route as we only had HDG and insecurity to the accuracy of the FMS NAV data presented to us and our route the Captain made the decision to return to the departure airport and we all were in concurrence with his decision. We then went through WAADS verifying weather at ZZZ, starting APU and starting fuel dump. During dump an ACARS message was sent to company advising of turn back. As we were dumping, ZZZ control vectored us south of ZZZ for dumping and eventual vectors Runway XX. After dump auto stopped and we turned dump off from the fuel pump switch there was a LVL 2 Dump VLV 2 Disag. The checklist was completed for this with the system in auto, a note was do not pressurize then cross feed manifolds. However we had a LVL 2 LAT FUEL UNBAL but could not follow the procedure as it requires us to pressurize the crossfeed manifold and the previous checklist was to not pressurize the manifolds. The system in Auto wasn't opening the crossfeed manifold and we chose not to. The approach was setup and briefed for ILS Runway XX and as we advised of ready for approach. On descent we noticed there were no overspeed or low speed warning bars on the airspeed indicator. As we slowed around 200 kts. in descent clean config the stick shaker turned on, power was added and airspeed increased causing the stick shaker to turn off. We then extended slats and we're vigilant about our speed since we realized we didn't have normal cues. When vectoring form the ILS the FMS was still enunciating NAV Armed. The all/land button was not responsive so the decision was to fly the approach manual as we could not determine if the autopilot was going to go on to the appropriate mode. Upon intercept of the localizer, we were right to the glideslope as well and got above the glide path and the approach became unstabilized. We executed a missed approach and advised tower. Tower asked if we were requesting priority handling, we responded negative but asked for a longer vector and ATC advised we'd get a 16 mile final and gave us a downwind vector. As the FMS was setup for a second approach the NAV Armed annunciation went blank. As we were vectored to the final, the APPR/Land enunciated normally. On localizer indication becoming active, the autopilot captured the localizer and a normal approach to landing was made. As our normal policy when a fuel dump is made emergency equipment followed us along the runway and taxiways to parking to insure that there was no hazmat leaks or FOD from the aircraft.
ASRS:1777759.s: The flight crew experienced multiple avionics failures, including flight director, autopilot, and FMS malfunctions, shortly after takeoff, prompting a fuel dump and return to the departure airport. After an initial unstabilized ILS approach due to degraded automation, the crew successfully executed a manual landing following a second approach where systems functioned normally.

ASRS:1777761.n: In ZZZZ loading was taking too long so I stopped our duty day because at our arrival point we would be over our legal XX hours. I asked the company for hotel rooms for the crew.
