The Handler informed us we would need to stay in a government designated hotel and undergo COVID-19 testing or stay on the airplane. We chose the hotel. The handler and a [company representative] informed us the immigration service of foreign country denied our crew entry into the country and we were not permitted to leave the airplane. I asked the Directors of Operations, Safety, and Standards, and the Chief Pilots if this would be legal Rest for our upcoming Part 121 assignment and got no response from any of them prior to our new (after minimum rest time) departure time, so I asked my crew if they felt safe to fly and they all said yes, we departed. We were in a foreign country subject to our Handler's communication with local immigration officials and them informing us what we could or could not do. We were even warned not to leave the aircraft by the handler to walk over to our other company airplane on the ramp as it could subject us to serious consequences if we were detected by Immigration. When we realized we had no alternate other than to obtain our Rest on board the aircraftA lack of planning on company Operations part in terms of how the Crew would be provided with normal hotel rest facilities should they get stuck in this location as we did. Even if you book a hotel if Immigration won't let you leave to go to it it is of no use.I kept my crew 100 percent in the loop as to all communications and any of them were free to decline the 121 assignment after we obtained Rest on the airplane. All of them told me they felt safe and were ready to fly.Plan for more than adequate time to load an airplane at this location. X.X hours were allocated obviously that was not nearly enough. Though we were as a flight crew rested, alert and fully capable of conducting the flight safely, local authorities had denied our entry into the country. We were forced to obtain rest prior this leg in the aircraft. Again, to restate, we had no choice other than to stay in the aircraft during our rest period. Our choice was originally to be tested for COVID-19 and risk quarantine to obtain adequate rest in the hotel. I personally witnessed company's efforts to get us into a suitable hotel. Those efforts were denied by local officials as relayed through emails from our handler.We were aware prior to the flight that it would be necessary to depart after resting in the aircraft.1) Mechanical delay departing ZZZZ on previous leg. 2) Failure of our handler to obtain rights to enter the country to ensure proper rest facility.All attempts were made to complete the flight within the originally scheduled duty day. We even suggested a shorter flight time to a different destination for a crew change. All efforts made by the crew were denied by the handler.Explain to the customer / handler that it will be necessary to obtain permission for the crew to stop enroute for a crew change if the loading is delayed. Please note here that the load being stopped and the crew departing within the appropriate duty day was an option given to the handler. The choice was made to continue with the full loading of the aircraft.
ASRS:1777761.s: The flight crew at ZZZZ was forced to rest on the aircraft after local immigration denied entry to a hotel due to loading delays and handler failures. The crew departed for their Part 121 assignment after confirming they felt safe, citing inadequate company planning for rest facilities in this location.

ASRS:1777765.n: Prior to entering the ZZZ Center airspace, during cruise at FL330, I had just returned back to my seat as 'as pilot monitoring' after using the rest room. As a matter of practice, I read aloud the FMA parameters (which all appeared normal), upon taking my seat and assuming the role as 'pilot monitoring.' Immediately after that, the Captain had also returned back to his seat as 'pilot flying' from his rest break, and exchanged his position with the IRO who had been occupying the captain's seat as the 'pilot flying' during the captain's break. At that time the Captain noticed that the aircraft had momentarily climbed to and leveled off at an indicated altitude of 33,500. The Captain immediately commenced a descent and returned the aircraft back to its original altitude of FL330, without any further consequence.We had become aware of the altitude when the Captain brought it to our attention In the cockpit. However, it was on the following day in ZZZ1 during my deadhead trip, that the captain recollected the event details and informed me that we had a deviation that may warrant the filing of a report. I believe that the aircraft may have climbed 500 feet and leveled off by the inadvertent touching of the altitude selector knob, either by the handling of the clipboard or by using disinfectant wipes in close proximity to the FCP, by one of the crew members, while getting in and out of the seats. None of the crew members is sure of what caused the movement of the altitude selector knob and the gain in altitude. The Captain immediately commenced a descent and returned the aircraft back to its original altitude of FL330, without any further consequence. As crew members, we were all equally surprised by the inadvertent deviation in altitude. Exercising greater level of situational awareness by all crew members, increased monitoring of the FMA, especially during the exchange of pilot seats and exchange of pilot roles while commencing and ending of crew rest periods. Exercising extreme care during handling of clipboard and using disinfectant wipes in vicinity of FCP during flight. Aircraft wandered off of assigned altitude in excess of 300 feet in cruise flight. [It was identified] when the Captain pointed it out. Mountain waves and or FO accidentally bumping the VSI or altitude pre-select while cleaning/sanitizing the FCP [may have caused it].I confirmed that the altitude was off the assigned, and needed to be corrected immediately. Advise all flight crews to use extreme caution when moving things around or cleaning the FCP inflight.
ASRS:1777765.s: During cruise at FL330, the crew experienced an inadvertent climb to 33,500 feet likely caused by accidental contact with the altitude selector knob while cleaning or moving near the FCP. The Captain immediately descended back to FL330 with no further consequences.

ASRS:1777766.n: We began our duty day at XA30 Z on date in ZZZZ, for a flight to ZZZZ1, continuing to ZZZ. Upon arriving in ZZZZ1 the ground handlers removed existing pallets and started loading the outbound cargo, before fueling started. Approximately 30 - 45 minutes later we had about a 16 ton imbalance with all of the fuel in the left wing tanks and center tank, and fuel was venting overboard, after the fuel spill clean up the fueling process resumed and again stopped due to the mechanic onboard the flight was not experienced on the aircraft type, and could not figure out how to operate the valves and transfer fuel to the right wing tanks. With us as the flight crew not allowed to exit the aircraft in foreign country, had no other option but calling [company], and keep them in the loop. At this time we are approaching our duty limit for the day in order to reach ZZZ, and we all agree to extend our day by X hours to get the job done, as described in the FARs. Numerous calls are being made to Dispatch, Maintenance Control in order to find help for the Mechanic who is outside supervising the fueling. Again we are approaching our duty limit, and calls are being made to Director of Operations Control, who hung up the phone on the Captain and to the Duty Officer who hung up the phone twice. What we were trying to accomplish was if the company had a contingency plan, or a plan B for us. As we had discussed this earlier, and rather sleeping on the aircraft, we were thinking more like proceeding to either ZZZZ2 or fly back to ZZZZ to rest, which was denied by the Duty Officer. We ended up spending the night on the aircraft, and after the curfew was lifted in ZZZZ1 we were able to get the required paperwork and fuel for departure. Finally arrived in ZZZ with no issues almost XX hours after the duty day had originally started. Would like to add that ALL phone conversations to operations control, maintenance control, Director of operations control and Duty Officer were made using speaker phone and was heard by the entire crew on the aircraft.[Caused by] inexperienced Mechanic operating and supervising the fueling process. The company needs to have a contingency plan, and plan B.By changing the scheduling procedures, have a dedicated crew fly between ZZZZ - ZZZZ, and use heavy crews for the rest, and provide better training for maintenance personnel in order to understand the aircraft type refueling process.
ASRS:1777766.s: Flight crew and an inexperienced mechanic encountered a 16-ton fuel imbalance and venting during refueling at ZZZZ1 because the mechanic could not operate transfer valves. The crew spent the night on the aircraft after company management denied requests to divert for rest, eventually departing after curfew and arriving at ZZZ.

ASRS:1777767.n: My duty day started in ZZZZ. I was part of a 2-man crew, scheduled to operate ZZZZ-ZZZZ1-ZZZZ. At the time I left ZZZZ, the TAF for ZZZZ had a small period of low visibility in the forecast, which was to occur while I was on the ground in ZZZZ1, and the weather was forecasted to improve to be above CAT I minimums prior to my arrival back into ZZZZ. While on the ground in ZZZZ1, I was checking the ZZZZ weather and found out that the ceilings were WELL below CAT I minimums. I called Flight Operations for a briefing and was told the same thing. I decided to delay the flight for an hour to watch the ZZZZ weather and to 'time' my arrival into ZZZZ to coincide with the forecasted lifting of the weather. Flight Operations then called me back and asked for me to delay another 30 minutes so we would arrive 30 minutes after the period of low weather in ZZZZ - I agreed, as it was a good idea. I also knew that I was currently at an outstation where I really have zero options for adequate rest if we got stuck there since we can't deplane the aircraft without mandatory COVID tests and quarantine until test results come back negative. So, in reality, flying to ZZZZ1 is really a gamble in the first place but, for sure, I knew that staying there wasn't even an option. I eventually departed ZZZZ1 at the newly determined departure time and flew towards ZZZZ.Through the use of ACARS ATIS updates as well as messages to/from the company - it was determined that the weather in ZZZZ had not cooperated with the forecast. Visibility was 125 meters to 225 meters - well below CAT I minimums. I talked with my First Officer and we decided to enter high altitude holding and set a 'bingo' fuel number for us to know when it was time to have to go to the alternate airport, ZZZZ2. We burned through our holding fuel and were forced to divert to our published alternate airport. That's where the real fun began. This is the point where we found out that an alternate that looks good on paper doesn't always work in actual practice. We landed, parked in spot XX, and sat, and waited, and sat, and waited some more. It took almost an hour just to get a set of stairs brought to the aircraft - and took an equally long amount of time to get a GPU and wheel choked so I could release the parking brake. At this point, I became doubtful that we would have the duty time to allow us to continue to ZZZZ1 - and that feeling was mirrored back to me by Flight Operations on my first phone call to them. A plan for crew hotels was then started, as well as the continued effort to contact our 'handler' there in ZZZZ2. Next came the biggest issue...Customs. The handler first started telling me that we can't stay there because we can't clear customs 'in their country'. I reminded him that we were scheduled to land in ZZZZ, which is the same country - but he didn't care. Clearly, the thought of a crew having to get rest at this published alternate airport hasn't been approached before? Finally, after 4 hours on the ground, the handler comes to the aircraft, asks me to shut it down so he can take us to a hotel close to the airport. I complied, and as soon as I carried my personal items downstairs, I was told by that same handler that it would be another hour before customs can clear us and to please wait on the aircraft - which was now shut down. I opened the aircraft again and that's where we waited for almost 2 more hours before the handler came back to tell us that there is 100% no way we were gonna clear customs there at that airport. At this point, we had absolutely no choice but to stay on the aircraft. After talking it over with my crew, we decided that the only option would be to depart ZZZZ2 as soon as we were legally able to do so - even though sitting on the aircraft isn't actually 'rest' - we had no other options. I talked with Flight Operations and they told me that we could depart at XA:00Z, which was another 3 hours from then. Out of lack of betterideas, we agreed, got the plane ready, and blocked out at XA:01Z for ZZZZ. The real point in this report is to illustrate that so many of our flight plans might look OK on paper, but when it comes time to actually put contingencies into practice, the plan immediately dissolves - leaving crews stranded without the ability to legally continue operating, and without the ability to obtain legal rest. Vetting of our 'approved alternates' certainly needs to take place.Not properly vetting filed, 'approved;' alternate airports to facilitate crew egress between aircraft and legal rest facilities.Worked tirelessly with the ZZZZ2 handler to try to secure rest facilities for my crew. When that failed, I worked with my crew and with Flight Operations to determine when we could 'legally' leave.Time and manpower needs to be put forth in this company to actually find out what processes would need to take place at alternate airports or at intermediate stops to allow crew members a place to get safe, legal rest when needed.
ASRS:1777767.s: A two-crew flight diverted to alternate ZZZZ2 due to low visibility at destination ZZZZ. The crew was stranded on the aircraft for hours because the handler could not clear customs or provide legal rest facilities, highlighting a failure to vet approved alternates for crew egress.

ASRS:1777794.n: Climbing out of ZZZZ to ZZZZ1 we were clear to unrestricted FL340. Empty of cargo we got to cruise level quick. We observed a pressure differential message and a rise 8.5 to 9.2 and up, as well as the cabin altitude rapidly climbing above schedule 7,000 ft quick, 8,000 ft and 9,000 ft at that point I told everybody, ' put the oxygen mask on' and verify the outflow valve. Quickly after that we got the level 3 ' cabin altitude' warning. I pulled the QRH and read to comply with the rest of the procedure for level 3 cabin altitude while the Captain was at the controls and the radios. I selected the cabin pressure on manual and turn the knob slowly and fast and there was no response. Since we had no control of the cabin altitude that kept on climbing, the Captain on the radio requested a descend to 10,000 feet follow by the wads and requested land back in ZZZZ with runway in use and weather. We recycle the air system controller and try the cabin pressure controller knob again no response. Then set on auto for the landing in ZZZZ Runway XXR + 3,000 meters visibility night conditions. After landing I verified the outflow open and pressure differential. We parked on apron. During the flight we were asked by the controller if we where having an emergency, The Captain answered: 'no, but we were experiencing a pressurization problem and we needed to descend'. On the ground the mechanic showed us the lower pressure relief valve stuck clogged with insulation. I am not sure how to prevent this event from occurring again, but next time I get a clearance to climb unrestricted and I am close to another heavy aircraft, climbing on the departure maybe request a vector. But that was the furthest on my mind, because of night flying and terrain the only thing I could think about at that moment was climbing at a good rate.
ASRS:1777794.s: The crew experienced a rapid cabin altitude rise and loss of pressure control during climb due to a stuck, clogged lower pressure relief valve. They descended to 10,000 feet and returned to ZZZZ for a safe landing after manual and automatic pressure controls failed.

ASRS:1777803.n: As the flying pilot during Initial climb we were told by ATC to climb unrestricted to FL 26,000 ft. After passing 9,000 ft. we had an alert Engine Fire on the #2 engine. Performed the memory procedure and continued flying the Aircraft while the Captain was going through the Quick Reference Handbook and after take off checklist. Dumped fuel for 5 minutes, approximately 10,000 kg, finished with dump checklist and proceeded with vectors to runway with no further problem.During SID approximately 9,000 ft. and climbing.An overheat or fire, we as crew responded to an Engine Fire Master Warning, aural alert and indication.Calm and responded as trained. We as crew responded to the emergency as we have been trained per SOP.Conduct a functional check per Maintenance Facility flight operation determination and detailed inspection of engine #2 and fire protection system to ensure the safety of the crew is at 100%.
ASRS:1777803.s: During initial climb at 9,000 ft, the crew received an Engine Fire warning on engine #2 after ATC cleared an unrestricted climb to FL260. The pilots executed memory procedures, dumped 10,000 kg of fuel, and returned to the runway for a detailed inspection of the engine and fire protection system.

ASRS:1777828.n: It was the middle of a very heavy snow [storm] and strong winds. We made it to the de-icing pad and were de-iced and had anti-icing applied (100% Type IV). I noticed on the way to the runway that the side cockpit windows were still snow covered. In fact, they did not do any sort of de/anti-icing of the front of the aircraft. I told the Captain I wanted to call back to the de-icing crew and ask them about it, but the Captain said it didn't matter. So we took off after I did the wing inspection. As we accelerated in the climbout, we hear numerous large chunks of ice fly off the airplane, loud enough that I wrote the airplane up and told maintenance they needed to do an aircraft inspection after landing. Upon further reflection, I am sure they did not de-ice the fuselage. With heavy, wet snow falling, they should have.
ASRS:1777828.s: The crew reported that during a heavy snowstorm, the de-icing crew failed to treat the fuselage and cockpit windows, despite the Captain dismissing concerns. Large ice chunks fell off during climbout, prompting the pilot to file a maintenance report for a post-flight inspection.

ASRS:1777832.n: This incident that occurred on our ZZZ-ZZZ1. As we approached Kabul airspace, our filed routing was from PINAX waypoint V848 to SURVI M881 to DI. Upon checking in with Kabul Control, we were rerouted PINAX P764 LAJAK then flight plan route. This routing was not in the our database and we informed ATC. They asked if we had NOTAM G2465/20. We asked them to standby while we checked. ATC then cleared us to waypoint GULNI then LAJAK. We informed ATC that GULNI was also not in our database. ATC then informed us that V848 airway was discontinued as of 03 Dec 20 per the Notam and replaced with airway P764 and read the NOTAM to us over the frequency. We were then cleared direct to LAJAK and requested to report abeam SURVI intersection. This new routing (and the new airway as well) takes us off of the preferred routing prescribed in the manual. A new route will need to be developed to comply with the new airway - P764. Additionally, this is certainly not an area where we need to be getting vectored off of an established airway because it is not in our database. We were caught completely off guard by this and in reporting it to our dispatcher, she was unaware of it as well. Along with the new airway, the new waypoint GULNI needs to be added as well.
ASRS:1777832.s: Pilots of ZZZ-ZZZ1 were rerouted by Kabul Control onto discontinued airway V848 and new waypoints not in their database due to a NOTAM. The crew was subsequently cleared direct to LAJAK, highlighting a need to update flight plans and databases for the new P764 airway.

ASRS:1777837.n: After being cleared for the visual approach and landing into ZZZ on Runway XX, we continued to configure the aircraft for landing. We proceeded to descend below 3,000 just inside the ZZZZZ fix. As we turned final around 2,600 feet MSL around 1,300 AGL we received a 'Obstacle' GWPS warning which we were given an RA to pull up. I immediately complied with the command until it confirmed and we visually confirmed that we were clear and continued the approach to land without incident. During the incident we did not observe nor did Tower observe any obstacles that we were in close proximity to. We maintained proper clearance of at least 1,000 feet AGL from all of the published towers that were on the approach plate.Cause - There were no noted obstacles that were within 1,000 feet AGL clearance and can only come to the conclusion that it was an anomaly with the GWPS system. At 2,800 feet we had turned inside the Tower that was 1,740 feet and turned well before the Tower at 1,809 maintain safe and legal separation from structures.Suggestions - Continue to follow protocol and respect a Resolution Advisory.
ASRS:1777837.s: The flight crew received a false GWPS obstacle warning and Resolution Advisory while on a visual approach to Runway XX below 3,000 feet. They executed the pull-up command, confirmed no obstacles were present, and concluded the event was a system anomaly before landing safely.

ASRS:1777840.n: At cruise the crew observed a projected -350 lb. fuel load at destination. This is unusually low for this phase of flight. The crew closely monitored the fuel situation and over the next 20 minutes and determined a worsening condition. The crew recalculated the flight plan, asked for direct to the airport to troubleshoot and identify the problem. All efforts did not resolve the issue. The crew [advised ATC] and diverted to ZZZ. On the way to ZZZ the fuel over destination worsened and the crew requested a closer alternate destination of ZZZ1.MFD indicating a negative fuel quantity upon or arrival.Reviewed flight plan, also requested direct routing to arrival fix for recalculation of fuel at FOD (Fuel Over Destination). Still showed a negative fuel balance and deteriorating. Aircraft fuel condition showed a predicted (landing) negative fuel amount upon level off and continued to worsen throughout cruise flight. Crew requested and received shortcuts with ATC to shorten total flight distance. As a precaution the crew opted to divert as the information being provided by the aircraft showed progressively worsening fuel status all the way to the touchdown at ZZZ1. Upon level off, noticed the fuel over destination (FOD) showed -300 lbs. of fuel. The condition worsened as the flight progressed. The total fuel on board was checked to see/compare against current duration of flight which showed we had used more than expected. The crew asked for a turn away from the current 100+ [kts.] headwind to see if the FOD would recalculate based on a tailwind. This made an insignificant difference and continued to worsen. We could have tried to further troubleshoot prior to diverting but with passengers onboard we opted to error on the side of caution and land sooner than later.
ASRS:1777840.s: The crew observed a worsening negative fuel prediction at destination during cruise, despite requesting direct routing and wind adjustments. Citing deteriorating fuel status and passenger safety, they diverted to an alternate airport, landing with a calculated fuel deficit.

ASRS:1777842.n: On approach to DAL at 3,000 ft. ATC called out traffic at about 5 miles, 500 ft. below that the TCAS showed climbing As he came closer ATC told us to do whatever to avoid. Simultaneously we received an RA to not descend and climb. Banked 30 degrees left and climbed 300 ft. Aircraft passed about 500 ft below us right to left. Per ATC returned to altitude and heading. Controller asked if we had an RA. Replied yes. We were notified of traffic by ATC and then by RA. Cause was VFR aircraft flying in approach control area.
ASRS:1777842.s: A pilot on approach to DAL at 3,000 ft received ATC traffic advisories and a TCAS RA to climb while avoiding a VFR aircraft. The crew banked left and climbed 300 ft, passing the intruder 500 ft below, before returning to their assigned altitude and heading.

ASRS:1777866.n: On pushback from gate, ground crew asked me to set brake because they had an issue with the tow bar. It was difficult to understand what they were saying outside of normal communication procedures because the tug operator spoke poor English. The ground crew was in the process of switching tow bars when I selected the external horn and informed the crew to remove all equipment and provide me a wing walker for the turnout as I had plenty of room to accomplish the taxi out. I watched the upper ECAM and waited for the 'NW STRG DISC' message to extinguish as confirmation of pin being removed. I also received a 'wand up with pin flag in hand' signal/salute. Taxi out was normal. On climbout, Center called and said the ground crew asked them to inform me that the nose wheel steering disconnect pin was still in the nose gear. I immediately knew this was false as I had confirmed before taxi out that it was removed and also the aircraft would not be able to be taxied with the pin installed. I contacted ops on company frequency and informed them that no pin was in the nose wheel. Again, I had a hard time understanding them as their English was poor. I then received a message from Dispatch and my understanding was they had lost the pin, assumed it was on the nose gear and then later found the pin. As a precaution, on arrival, I inspected the nose wheel and found no discrepancies. As a side note, it appeared that the tow bar being used was much smaller than normal. The tow bar they were going to swap it with was much larger.Cause - Poor English and communication.
ASRS:1777866.s: During pushback, the pilot and ground crew faced communication difficulties due to the tug operator's poor English while switching tow bars. Although the pilot confirmed the nose wheel steering pin was removed, ground crew later falsely reported it was still installed, causing confusion until the pin was found and the aircraft arrived safely.

ASRS:1777893.n: While operating Aircraft X, we experienced loss of thrust in the right engine while we were leveling off at 8,000 ft on the ZZZZZ 2 Arrival into ZZZ1. Earlier that morning, when we started the engines in ZZZ. We noticed that the right engine was approaching a hung start, however, it stabilized while it was still within the limitations. The Captain and I confirmed that the engine had stabilized and all engine indications appeared normal. Everything remained normal until our arrival into ZZZ1. The Captain was Pilot Flying, and when he increased thrust to arrest our descent and level off at 8,000 ft, we noticed that the right engine did not respond to the thrust lever. The thrust remained around 30% N1 regardless of the thrust lever position. We then notified ATC and requested radar vectors. Once we were on vectors, we ran the QRH for 'Thrust Lever Inoperative' 1-34. After discussing the situation, we determined that since the thrust was remaining at idle, it was in the interest of reducing complexity and increasing safety to keep the right engine operating at idle. We then ran the 'Single Engine Approach and Landing' QRH 1-27 and configured accordingly. We continued the approach and landed uneventfully. We advised ATC that we did not need assistance taxiing to the gate. Once we arrived at the gate, we performed the shutdown procedure. When we shut down the right engine, it took multiple attempts to get the thrust lever to shut the engine down. After completing the shutdown checklist, we advised Maintenance of the issue.
ASRS:1777893.s: The flight crew of Aircraft X experienced right engine thrust loss at 8,000 ft during the ZZZZZ 2 Arrival into ZZZ1, likely linked to an earlier hung start. They executed single-engine procedures, landed safely, and reported that the engine required multiple attempts to shut down at the gate.

ASRS:1777901.n: On departure climbing in icing conditions with engine and airfoil anti-ice on the Captain airspeed and altitude alerted to 40 feet [difference] from First Officer and airspeed 30 kts. [difference]. After a few minutes, alert cleared, and everything was normal up to cruise altitude. Flight continued normal until we descend into icing conditions. Radar showed scattered precipitation and ATC reported turbulence ahead. At 14,000 feet we got into heavy rime ice. Captain airspeed indicator went to zero, autopilot disconnected, FADEC went to alternate all 3 engines, LSAS (Longitudinal Stability Augmentation System) all failed. I started hand flying checking FO (First Officer) and standby instruments, First Officer notified ATC of the failure of our airspeed and altitude due to ice. The First Officer instructions looked to be reliable compared to the standby, so I transferred control of the aircraft to the First Officer and assumed Pilot Not Flying duties doing the checklist. After about 10 minutes Captain airspeed and altitude started working again. We were given a speed restriction of 260 kts. or less and to cross intersection ZZZZZ at 14,000 feet and then cross ZZZZZ1 at 12,000 feet. The incident happened just after ZZZZZ. We were not able to make the restriction at ZZZZZ2. I told the FO to stop descent until we were sure of the instrument readings while we were communicating with ATC telling them of our situation. We cross ZZZZZ2 at 13,800 feet about 280 kts. I took control of the aircraft back from the First Officer and continued the arrival and approach via ATC instructions.We were immediately aware of the malfunction. There were multiple alerts and warnings going off when it happened.After landing the mechanics did a CFDS (Centralized Fault Display System) check which showed a MSC (Miscellaneous Systems Controller) failure. Look like the Captain pitot tube was not being heated properly and descending into the icing conditions cause it to become blocked. Immediate corrective action was taken by both me and my First Officer to fly the airplane and contact ATC.
ASRS:1777901.s: During descent into heavy rime ice, the Captain's pitot tube blocked due to inadequate heating, causing airspeed and altitude failures, autopilot disconnect, and engine FADEC alternation. The crew hand-flew using standby instruments, missed ATC speed and altitude restrictions, and landed safely after mechanics identified a Miscellaneous Systems Controller failure.

ASRS:1777923.n: After being notified by Management & Safety about Aircraft X air return was due to a (new) nose gear down lock safety pin installed and 5 each (normal equipment) were found in E&E (electronics bay) equipment stowage. The ETOPS inspection was performed with no need for the use of 5 each landing gear down lock safety pins. At no time was red streamer visible during ETOPS inspection.
ASRS:1777923.s: Management and Safety reported that Aircraft X returned due to a nose gear down lock safety pin found in the electronics bay, though five normal pins were also present. The subsequent ETOPS inspection required no safety pins and revealed no red streamers.

ASRS:1777953.n: While executing the published missed approach for the Practice VOR approach at TUS Runway 11 left, Aircraft Y departed on Runway 11 flew under the Aircraft X and continued a climb to their departure altitude. The Aircraft X encountered wake turbulence from the departing Aircraft Y at approximately the VOR location, recovered, and continued with the missed approach procedure.Extenuating circumstances were that the Tower at TUS was closed due to staffing issues, and the TRACON was handling IFR and VFR traffic into and departing from TUS. We had no direct radio contact with the departing air carrier before, or after their departure. If the Tower had been open instructions to us or to the air carrier would have prevented this close encounter.
ASRS:1777953.s: Aircraft X encountered wake turbulence from departing Aircraft Y while executing a missed approach for the Practice VOR at TUS Runway 11. The reporter attributed the close encounter to the closed Tower and lack of direct radio contact with the departing carrier.

ASRS:1777963.n: I was cruising VFR at 7,500 ft., without flight following, but monitoring Center. My ADS-B (Automatic Dependent Surveillance - Broadcast) showed traffic 500 ft. below me, 12 miles out at my 1:30 position. This caught my attention because this condition indicates we will pass laterally very close. I heard Center alert the other aircraft about the traffic (my aircraft), but he was unable to get a visual. Center indicated my altitude was 7,200 ft. I turned on my taxi and landing lights to make my aircraft more visible to the other aircraft. We passed with 500 ft. vertical and about 150 ft. lateral separation. The other pilot called me on the phone later that day because he was concerned about a near miss (although he did get a visual on my aircraft just before we passed). His ADS-B indicated 150 ft. separation. My flights showed my ADS-B altitude 350 ft. lower than what it actually was, which was the cause for the other pilot's concern. I am reporting this to my avionics shop for repair, and in the future will pick up flight following earlier in the flight for better communication.
ASRS:1777963.s: A VFR pilot cruising at 7,500 ft. experienced a near miss with another aircraft due to an ADS-B altitude error showing 350 ft. lower than actual. The pilots passed with 500 ft. vertical and 150 ft. lateral separation, prompting the reporter to seek avionics repair and request flight following earlier in future flights.

ASRS:1777966.n: I landed on Runway XX and my airspeed was approximately 76 knots. As soon as I touched ground, I slowed down in order to follow Controller directions. The Controller asked if I could make Taxiway Alpha X. By that point, I had already passed the taxiway and responded to the Controller in which I stated negative. The Controller's commands were to make a left turn at Taxiway Golf. I then proceeded to slow down and pulled back on the yoke to the turn left onto Taxiway Golf. Before fully exiting the runway, the tires of the plane became stuck on the snow ground and I was not able to move forward. The Controller questioned me and asked if I was able to move forward. I replied that I was unable to and that I was stuck in the snow. The Controller responded back and said hold tight, ground operations was on their way. As ground operations came, I shut off the plane and aided the ground operations staff in pushing the plane backwards. We successfully pushed the plane out of the snow.I started the plane back up and I was then able to make a U-turn back onto the Runway XX and taxi onto Alpha Y. The sign for Bravo (B) was not visible and I exited off of Alpha Y, made the left turn for Alpha and then right turn for Bravo.This experience taught me to avoid any taxiways that appear to have ice or snow on them. I also learned that I must make the judgement as being the pilot in command. As the pilot in command, I have the ability to deny requests made by Air Traffic Controller if I cannot adhere to their request promptly. I must note that it is important that all parties involved must remain safe, since safety is a priority of mine.
ASRS:1777966.s: The pilot landed on Runway XX and became stuck in snow while turning left onto Taxiway Golf after passing Taxiway Alpha X. Ground operations pushed the aircraft free, allowing the pilot to taxi to Taxiway Bravo after noting that the Bravo sign was not visible.

ASRS:1777969.n: I intended to rent C172RG Aircraft X from a Company to practice landings today at ZZZ. The flight went according to plan until retracting the landing gear on climbout from RWY (Runway) XX. As the landing gear retracted, the aircraft's electrical system failed and I lost my radios and transponder. I flew the traffic pattern as I normally would until abeam the end of RWY XX, where I attempted to extend the aircraft's landing gear. The gear did not extend, so I departed the pattern straight out on a downwind to resolve the issue. After pumping my landing gear down by hand, I established communication with my cellphone with Maintenance on the ground at ZZZ, who made radio calls for me as I flew the aircraft in on final. I touched down and was able to terminate the flight without further incident. My main concern in filing this report is that after experiencing the electrical system failure, I did not have a functioning transponder. ZZZ is located within the Mode C Veil of ZZZ1, and a transponder is required while operating inside of the veil. Because of the electrical system failure, I was operating without a transponder. Based on the nature of this incident, the best course of corrective action that could be taken in order to prevent a recurring incident of a similar nature is for the electrical system to be examined and undergo whatever maintenance is necessary.
ASRS:1777969.s: The pilot of a C172RG experienced an electrical system failure during climbout from RWY XX, losing radios and transponder while inside the ZZZ1 Mode C Veil. After manually extending the landing gear and using a cellphone to coordinate with maintenance, the pilot landed safely and recommended electrical system maintenance.

ASRS:1777991.n: Prior to taking off I checked the UAS FM (facility maps) and observed that I could not exceed 50 feet AGL as I was in ZZZ Class B airspace. In an error, I did not file a flight plan and instead flew the drone, keeping it at an altitude of 50 feet AGL or below. After ending my flight I realized my error and immediately contacted my company UAS coordinator. In the future I shall always remember to file a flight plan and receive authorization before flying in controlled airspace.
ASRS:1777991.s: The pilot flew a drone in ZZZ Class B airspace at 50 feet AGL or below without filing a flight plan or obtaining authorization. Upon realizing the error post-flight, the pilot contacted the company UAS coordinator and committed to securing proper clearance in the future.

ASRS:1777994.n: I was flying right seat. After landing, Runway XX and exiting at [Taxiway] XX1, Tower radioed, 'taxi to ramp, this frequency.' PF (Pilot flying) proceeded to taxi south on Taxiway XX, and then turned right onto Taxiway XX4, into the FBO's ramp.I noticed Aircraft Y, parked close to our taxiway (on our right side), and asked PF to slow down, which he did. I then asked PF to come left (away from the aircraft) which he did. This put us left of the taxiway centerline (away from the aircraft). In the dim light, it looked as if we would clear the aircraft wingtip, particularly since we had come so far left. Unfortunately, the wingtips made contact.We then taxied to parking to deplane our passengers. After our passengers departed, I informed the FBO. PF walked to Taxiway XX4 and measured the distance from taxiway centerline to the wingtip of Aircraft Y. The distance measured 32 feet 8 inches. There was a cone under the wingtip. The wingtip did not have a static wick cover on it. Taxiing into ramp on center line we were turning into the FBO ramp and clipped the wingtip of Aircraft Y. The wingspan of our aircraft make/model is 69 feet 6 inches and from Center line to the edge of Aircraft Y was 32 feet. The PIC (Pilot in Command) who was in the right seat told me to adjust over some and I did. He then thought we were clear of Aircraft Y. While taxiing by the tips met by a few inches. It only scratched the winglet of [our aircraft], but bent the wingtip of Aircraft Y.
ASRS:1777994.s: The right-seat pilot and pilot flying taxied an aircraft with a 69-foot 6-inch wingspan into an FBO ramp in dim light. After the pilot flying moved left of the centerline to avoid a parked aircraft, the wingtips contacted, scratching the reporting aircraft's winglet and bending the parked aircraft's wingtip.
